The key is keeping your bait moving — these fish want to see some action.

Striped bass are around but scattered. I'm picking up schoolies in the 20 to 26-inch range working the inlet at first light, but the bigger fish seem to be holding deeper. A few boats have been connecting with keepers in 40 to 50 feet outside the inlet, but it's been a grind. Live bunker on fishfinder rigs is producing the best fish, but you need to get out there early before the boat traffic spooks them.

Looking ahead, we're building toward a full moon this weekend, which means big tides and serious current. That's when the inlet really comes alive. I'll be watching for the first real push of weakfish to move through on those strong ebb tides. The water temperature's been climbing steadily, and once we hit 70 degrees consistently, the summer pattern should lock in hard.

The canal's been running smooth, so access to the Peconic side is wide open. That's opened up some options for guys looking to escape the inlet crowds. Just remember — night fishing is when this place really shines. The daytime bite is decent, but when the sun goes down and the tide starts moving, that's when the magic happens.

reports.headline: Trophy bass blitz Moriches Inlet as night bite explodes on live spot
reports.subhead: Inlet's shifting bathymetry concentrates bait as summer patterns lock in across the system.
reports.body_markdown:
The inlet's running like a machine right now, and the bass know it. What started as scattered reports of decent fish two weeks back has turned into a full-blown trophy bite that's got every serious striper hunter making the drive out here after dark. I'm talking fish in the 35- to 45-inch class, with enough 20-pounders mixed in to keep your drag singing.

The pattern's textbook Moriches: live spot fished tight to the inlet's north jetty on the outgoing tide, right where the channel cuts deepest against the rocks. The key depth is that 18- to 22-foot zone where the current creates a natural feeding lane. Fish a Carolina rig with a 6/0 circle hook, 3-foot fluorocarbon leader, and keep that spot swimming just off bottom. The bass are staging in that deeper water during the day, then moving up to ambush bait as the tide pulls out.

What's driving this bite is the inlet's unique hydraulics right now. June's spring tides have been scouring the channel deeper on the north side while depositing sand on the south — classic Moriches behavior after we had those northeast storms in May. That deeper cut is acting like a conveyor belt, funneling spearing, rainfish, and juvenile bunker right into the bass's wheelhouse. Water temperature in the inlet's holding steady at 68 degrees, perfect for keeping both bait and bass active through the night hours.

The timing's critical. Best action starts about an hour after sunset and runs through the first two hours of the outgoing tide. Miss that window and you're looking at scattered fish instead of the steady pick that's been happening. I've been watching the inlet drain at 9 PM with the new moon cycle, and that's when the water really starts moving with purpose.

Cupsogue Beach has been producing during daylight hours for anglers working the surf. The sandbar structure about 150 yards off the beach is holding fluke in the 3- to 5-pound range, with enough keepers mixed in to make the walk worthwhile. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails are getting it done in that 12- to 15-foot trough behind the bar. The key is working the edges where the current creates that slight color change — that's where the fluke are positioned to intercept bait getting swept along.

Back in the bay proper, the shallow-water fluke bite has been surprisingly consistent for this time of year. The 6- to 8-foot flats between Tuthill Point and the marina are holding good numbers of fish, including some legitimate doormat candidates. I'm seeing reports of fish pushing 7 pounds coming from that skinny water, which tells me the bait concentration is exceptional right now. Tiny jigs — we're talking 1/4-ounce heads with 3-inch Gulp — worked slow on the drift are producing the quality fish.

Weakfish have started showing in the deeper holes around Smith Point, though it's still early in their summer pattern. The fish are small — mostly 14- to 16-inchers — but they're a good sign that the ecosystem's cycling properly. Look for this bite to improve as we move into July and the water temperature climbs another few degrees.

Looking ahead, this weekend's full moon is going to supercharge the tidal flow through the inlet. That means bigger volumes of water moving faster, which should concentrate even more bait in the feeding zones. I'm expecting the bass bite to peak Friday and Saturday nights, especially if we get those light southwest winds that have been setting up the perfect drift conditions. The inlet's primed for what could be the best week of striper fishing we've seen this season.

reports.headline: Moriches Inlet bass bite stays red-hot as live spot produces trophy fish at night
reports.subhead: Consistent striper action continues through mid-June with quality fish hitting after dark.
reports.body_markdown:
The inlet's been absolutely on fire for striped bass, and I'm talking consistent trophy-class fish coming over the rails after sunset. This isn't your typical summer doldrums fishing — we're seeing legitimate cows pushing 30-plus pounds hitting live spot presentations in the deeper cuts around the inlet mouth.

The pattern's been locked in for over a week now. Best action starts about an hour before sunset and runs through the first two hours of darkness. The key is positioning yourself in 15 to 25 feet of water along the eastern edge of the inlet channel, where the current sweeps bait out of the bay on the outgoing tide. I'm running live spot on fishfinder rigs — 6/0 circle hooks with just enough weight to hold bottom in the current. The bass are staging in that transition zone where bay water meets ocean water, and they're absolutely crushing anything that looks like it's getting swept out with the tide.

What's driving this bite is the thermal gradient setting up at the inlet. Bay water's running a solid 4 to 5 degrees warmer than the ocean side, creating a perfect feeding lane where baitfish get concentrated. The spot are thick in the back bay right now, and every outgoing tide is flushing them through that narrow throat. It's like a dinner bell for these big bass.

The fluke bite in the skinny water continues to improve as we move deeper into summer. I'm seeing consistent keepers in the 3 to 8-foot range, with fish pushing 5 to 6 pounds becoming more common. The technique that's been money is ultra-light presentations — 1/4 to 3/8-ounce bucktails tipped with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets, worked slow on the drift. The key is reading the bottom structure. These shallow flats have subtle contours that hold fish, and you need to feel every bump and depression with your jig.

Tuthill Point's been particularly productive on the incoming tide, especially that 6 to 10-foot edge that runs parallel to the shoreline. The fish are relating to the slight depth change, and they're aggressive. I'm seeing a lot of quality fish in that 20 to 24-inch range, with the occasional doormat mixed in. The bite window is typically the first two hours of the flood, when cooler water pushes in from the inlet and activates the fluke.

Porgy fishing remains solid throughout the bay, with the deeper holes around the marina channels producing steady action. Standard bottom rigs with clam or squid strips are doing the job, but I've been having better luck with small bucktails tipped with Gulp! sandworms. The porgies are hitting anything that moves, and you can load the cooler pretty quickly if you find a good school.

Weakfish are starting to show in better numbers, particularly around the inlet on the night tides. I'm picking up fish in the 2 to 4-pound range on the same live spot rigs I'm using for bass, just in slightly shallower water. The weakies are hitting about an hour after the bass bite peaks, usually in that 8 to 15-foot range where the current isn't quite as strong.

Looking ahead, this full moon cycle should really fire things up. The big tides are going to flush even more bait through the inlet system, and I expect the bass bite to get even more consistent. The key will be timing your trips with the tide — you want to be fishing that inlet drain right at sunset for the best shot at a trophy. Water temps are stabilizing in the mid-70s, which is perfect for keeping fish active through the evening hours.

The weekend should be prime time if you can handle the boat traffic. Get out early for the fluke bite, then position yourself for the evening bass run. This is some of the best inlet fishing I've seen in years.

reports.headline: Weakfish crash Fire Island surf as bay water hits prime temps
reports.subhead: Seven-pound tide-runner leads charge while fluke stack up on Captree drifts.
reports.body_markdown:
The water's telling a story this week, and it's one I haven't heard in years. A 26-inch, 7.3-pound weakfish hit the surf near Fire Island Inlet on a 9-inch Gravity Tackle Sand Eel — the kind of fish that makes you remember why we call them tide-runners. That's not a fluke catch, that's a signal. The weakfish are back in numbers we haven't seen since the early 2000s, and they're feeding hard in the transition zone where bay water meets ocean.

I've been running the inlet every morning this week, watching the bait move with the tides. The bunker schools are thick from Democrat Point to the Robert Moses bridges, and that's pulling everything up from the deep bay channels. Water temps in Great South Bay hit 68 degrees — a solid 4-degree spread from the ocean side — and that gradient is creating a feeding highway that's stacking fish on every tide change.

The fluke bite off Captree has been lights-out consistent. Laura Lee's been putting fares on keeper fish in 20 to 30 feet, working the edges where the channel drops off toward the inlet. The key has been matching the bait — those same sand eels the weakfish are crushing. Five-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift, are outproducing everything else three to one. The fish are holding tight to structure, so you need to feel that bucktail tick the bottom every few cranks.

What's really got me excited is the mixed bag coming over the rails. Sea bass limits are easy money right now — the Captree fleet's been boxing fish on every trip. Diamond jigs in hammered gold are deadly in 40 to 60 feet, but switch to clams when the bite slows and you'll pick up ling and porgies. I watched one angler pull three ling on clam after limiting out on sea bass with metal. The fish are stacked in layers, and you need to adjust your presentation to work through them.

The Robert Moses bridge has been a fluke magnet on the outgoing tide. That's where the bay empties hard, creating the kind of current break that holds bait and ambush predators. Fish the north side pilings with bucktails and soft plastics — 19-inchers are common, with enough keepers to make it worth the ride. The bite window is narrow though — first two hours of the ebb, then it shuts down until the flood starts pushing bait back through.

Night fishing has been producing some surprises. Bass are showing in the back bay on clam bellies, nothing huge but consistent slot fish that are feeding in the shallows after dark. The new moon we just passed stirred things up, and now with the waxing moon building toward full, expect the tidal flow to intensify. That means better bait movement and more aggressive feeding windows.

The surf has been clean and fishable, especially early morning before the boat traffic kicks up. Fire Island's ocean side is producing bass on bottle plugs and sand eel imitations, but you need to time it right — dawn patrol when the bait's moving through the cuts. The fish are there, but they're spooky in the clear water.

Looking ahead, this weekend's building toward a full moon on Friday means spring tides and serious water movement. I'm watching for the first real push of summer species — the water's warm enough now to pull weakfish, fluke, and bass into feeding mode simultaneously. That 68-degree bay water is the magic number, and we're holding steady there.

The inlet's been fishing like a different body of water since the spring tides started moving serious volume. Bait's everywhere, predators are following, and the bite windows are getting longer as the days stretch out. This is prime time fishing, the kind of week that reminds you why we live for summer on the South Shore.

reports.headline: Trophy bass crash Reynolds Channel as bunker schools stack thick in the inlet
reports.subhead: 48-inch cow taken on fresh bunker chunks while weakfish push back into the surf zone.
reports.body_markdown:
The inlet's been on fire this week, and I'm talking about the kind of fishing that makes you forget you've got bills to pay. A 48-inch, 42-pound cow bass came over the rail at Reynolds Channel off the back jetty at Atlantic Beach — fresh bunker chunks did the trick on what had to be one hell of a fight from shore. That's the kind of fish that reminds you why we do this.

The bunker schools are stacked thick from the inlet mouth all the way back to the Wantagh Bridge, and the bass know it. I've been watching the bait push in on the flood tide and get pinned against the channel edges where the current breaks. That's where you want to be — tight to structure with fresh chunks on fishfinder rigs. The fish are feeding heavy on the incoming water, especially the last two hours before high.

Weakfish are making their presence known too, which is something I haven't been able to say with a straight face in years. A 26-inch, 7-pound fish came out of the Fire Island surf on a 9-inch sand eel, but I'm seeing them push into our zone as well. The back bay water's been running warm — pushing 66 degrees in spots — and that temperature gradient between bay and ocean is creating the kind of conditions that stack bait and hold fish.

Fluke fishing's been solid but not spectacular. The Meadowbrook Bridge area continues to produce, with boats working the southeast side on the incoming tide. White bucktails with smelt have been the ticket — 15 to 17-inch fish are common, though keepers are still tough to come by. The key is getting your bait right to the bottom in that 20 to 30-foot zone where the current breaks over the structure.

Jones Beach surf has been producing at sunset, just like the old days. Diamond jigs with green tails cast past the break into the wash are connecting with bass sitting on the sandbar before the trough. It's a low-light bite — you need to be there as the sun drops and the fish move shallow. Two-ounce jigs seem to be the sweet spot, and don't overlook switching to SP Minnows once full dark sets in.

The inlet itself has been weedy — typical for this time of year when the water warms and everything starts growing. But don't let that discourage you. The fish are there, you just need to work around it. I've been having luck on the start of the outgoing tide when the current cleans things up a bit. Fluke are holding in the deeper holes, and you'll pick up the occasional keeper if you stay with it.

Birds have been working overtime on the small baitfish — sand eels mostly — from Point Lookout east toward the construction dock area. The action's been visual, but getting the fish to commit has been tougher. When you see the birds diving, get there fast and work the edges of the school rather than bombing right into the middle.

Looking ahead, we've got a new moon Friday which means spring tides and serious current. That's going to flush a lot of bait out of the back bays and could trigger the first real push of summer fish. I'll be watching the inlet drain at sunset — if the weakfish are really making a comeback, that's when we'll know for sure. The bunker are here, the water's warm, and the fish are feeding. This could be the week everything comes together.

reports.headline: Trophy bass crash Reynolds Channel as bunker schools pack the inlet
reports.subhead: 42-pound striper highlights explosive action from the jetties to the back bay bridges.
reports.body_markdown:
The inlet's been on fire this week, and I'm talking about the kind of fishing that makes you forget about everything else. A 42-pound bass came off the back jetty at Reynolds Channel on fresh bunker chunks — that's the kind of fish that reminds you why we do this. But that monster wasn't alone.

The bunker schools are thick from the inlet mouth all the way back to the Wantagh Bridge, and the bass are following them like a dinner bell. I've been watching this setup build for two weeks now, and it finally exploded. The key has been the outgoing tide — start of the drop is when these fish move. The inlet's been weedy, sure, but that's not stopping anybody who knows how to fish it.

Fluke action's been solid but not spectacular. The Meadowbrook Bridge area is holding fish, with boats stacking up on the southeast side during the incoming. Most of the action's been shorts in the 15-17 inch range, but there's enough keeper potential to make it worthwhile. White bucktails with smelt have been the ticket — hook the smelt behind the head and let it work in the current. The fish want that natural presentation.

What's really got my attention is the weakfish showing up. That 26-inch, 7-pound fish that came out of Fire Island Inlet tells me the comeback is real. I've been hearing whispers about weakies in the back bays, and with the bait concentrations we're seeing, it makes sense. These fish follow the same patterns as the bass — look for them on the moving water.

The sunset bite has been phenomenal at Jones Beach. Diamond jigs with green tails are working the sandbars just before the trough. The fish are sitting shallow at low light, and if you can get your jig past the break into that wash, you're in business. SP Minnows after dark are cleaning up for the guys who stay late.

Bait situation is excellent. Peanut bunker are everywhere, and the sand eels are thick in the surf zone. If you're fishing the inlet, fresh bunker chunks on fishfinder rigs are producing the biggest fish. For the fluke guys, squid and smelt combo is still the standard, but don't overlook sea robin strips — they're working better than they should.

Water's been clean despite all the boat traffic, and the temperature gradient between the bay and ocean is holding fish on both sides of the inlet. The birds have been working overtime on the small bait, which tells me the food chain is stacked up right.

Looking ahead, we've got a new moon coming Friday, which means spring tides and serious current. That's when the inlet really comes alive — the big tides flush everything out and concentrate the bait. I'm expecting the bass bite to get even better, especially on the evening outgoing. The fluke should spread out more as the stronger current gives them better feeding opportunities.

If you're planning to fish this weekend, get to the inlet early for the bass bite, then work the bridges and channels for fluke as the tide builds. The action's there — you just need to be in the right place when the water moves.

reports.headline: Bay water hits 69 as weakfish crash the party with keeper fluke
reports.subhead: Jamaica Bay's trifecta firing on all cylinders as temperatures climb and bait thins out.
reports.body_markdown:
The bay is alive right now, and I mean really alive. Water temps hit 69 degrees this week, which is telling us everything we need to know about what's happening out there. The stripers are starting their summer shuffle, moving deeper and getting pickier, but the silver lining is huge — the weakfish have moved in like they own the place.

I've been working the Marine Parkway Bridge area hard this week, and the action has been steady on the incoming tide. That 69-degree water is the magic number that flips the switch for weakies, and they're responding exactly like they should. I'm talking keeper fish to 19 inches, with some pushing over 20. The technique that's been money is simple: white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 1/2-ounce bucktails, worked slow on the drift. Don't overthink it — let the current do the work and just lift and drop.

The fluke bite has been the real surprise this week. I pulled a beautiful 25-inch doormat that went 5.5 pounds right off the bridge pilings on Monday morning. She hit a lugworm on a high-low rig during the first hour of the incoming. The key has been fishing tight to structure — those bridge pilings, the channel edges, anywhere the current creates an ambush point. The fish are holding in 15 to 20 feet, and they want that bait moving slow and steady.

What's interesting is how the bait situation is shaping up. The bunker schools that were thick in the bay through May are definitely thinning out. I'm still seeing pods here and there, especially around the Cross Bay Bridge area, but nothing like the acres we had a month ago. The good news is the spearing are everywhere, and that's what's keeping the weakfish happy. Northern kingfish are also showing up in decent numbers on clam baits, which tells me the bottom is warming up nicely.

The bass fishing has shifted gears completely. Those slot fish that were crushing everything in sight during the spring run are now scattered and selective. I'm still marking fish on the finder, but they're deeper and more spread out. The guys who are connecting are doing it on live eels at night, working the deeper holes around the inlet. The trolling bite with Mojos is still producing 32-inch fish, but you've got to cover water and stay patient.

Sea robins are absolutely everywhere right now — and I mean monster sea robins. I pulled one this week that was easily the biggest I've ever seen, thick as a football. They're hitting everything from bucktails to clam baits, and while they're not what we're targeting, they're a good sign that the bottom is active and holding bait.

The tide timing has been crucial this week. The incoming has been the producer, especially that first two hours when the water is really moving. The Marine Parkway Bridge creates a natural funnel that concentrates bait and predators, and that's where I've been focusing my efforts. Beach Channel Drive has also been consistent for shore fishermen working the outgoing tide with bunker chunks on fishfinder rigs.

Looking at the water conditions, that 69-degree reading is right where we want to be for summer fishing. It's warm enough to keep the weakfish active but not so hot that everything shuts down. The clarity has been good despite some recent rain, and the salinity feels right — that perfect mix of ocean water and bay nutrients that makes Jamaica Bay so productive.

The weekend should be prime time with the new moon approaching. Those spring tides are going to flush a lot of bait around, and I expect the weakfish bite to stay strong. The fluke should continue to be active in the deeper holes, especially if we can get some cooler nights to keep that water temperature stable. I'm planning to hit the inlet area hard on the outgoing tide — that's when the big fluke like to set up in the channel to ambush bait getting swept out of the bay.

For anyone looking to get in on this action, keep it simple. Bucktails with Gulp for the weakies, high-low rigs with fresh clams or lugworms for the fluke. Fish the structure, watch your tide timing, and don't be afraid to move if the bite slows down. This bay rewards the anglers who stay mobile and read the water.

reports.headline: Big bass crash Plum Gut as butterfish fuel feeding frenzy
reports.subhead: Overslot stripers hammer swim shads and spoons while blues wreck everything else.
reports.body_markdown:
The Race and Plum Gut are absolutely on fire right now. I'm talking about the kind of fishing that makes you forget about sleep, forget about everything except the next drift. Big migratory bass — the real Hudson River fish — have stacked up in the rips, and they're feeding like it's their last meal.

Here's what's working: Seven-inch Tsunami swim shads on three-way rigs are absolutely crushing the bucktails for size. I've been running head-to-head tests all week, and it's not even close. The swim shads are pulling overslot fish while the bucktails are getting schoolies. Set up with an 8-10 ounce cannonball on a foot of line below your three-way swivel, then run a 5-6 foot leader of 80-pound test to your lure. That heavy leader isn't just for abrasion — the stiffness keeps your presentation standing off the bottom in the screaming current.

The Gut's been the most consistent producer. Start your drift in 80 feet and ride it up over the rip to 40 feet, then back down. Current's running 2.5 to 3 mph on the stronger tides, so you're covering serious ground fast. Use that double-drop technique — hit bottom, crank twice, drop again, then pick up the slack. Keeps you tight to the structure where these fish are holding.

Butterfish are the key to this whole bite. They showed up early this year, and the bass are absolutely gorging on them. I'm also seeing squid mixed in, especially around Fishers Island and the outer edges of the rips. When you see that bait on the screen, get ready — the bass aren't far behind.

Topwater action has been insane during the slack periods. Yo-Zuri Hydro Pencils and X-Walks are getting crushed at first light when the current eases up. The fish are pushing bait to the surface, and you can see the explosions from a mile away. Switch to a 6-foot casting rod and work the edges of the rip — that's where the big ones are waiting.

But here's the problem: bluefish have moved in, and they're absolute tackle destroyers. I'm talking gorilla blues that'll snap 50-pound leader like it's nothing. If you're throwing expensive plugs, use wire or heavy fluorocarbon. These aren't the cocktail blues from the harbor — these are the real deal, 15-pound-plus fish that fight like they're twice that size.

Spoons are also producing, especially the 6-9 inch Tsunami models. Drop them into the current and let them work mid-column before they hit bottom. The bigger bass are often suspended, following the bait schools, and a spoon fluttering through that zone triggers vicious strikes.

The Race has been more hit-or-miss but when it's on, it's spectacular. The rip there gets absolutely evil on the big tides — we just had the full moon, so the current's been screaming. Only fish it if you know what you're doing. I've seen guys get their boats turned sideways in that rip, and it's not pretty.

Weather's been the limiting factor. We've had some nasty northeast blows that made it unfishable, but when you get those brief windows of calm, the fishing explodes. The bass seem to know when conditions are about to deteriorate, and they feed aggressively before the weather hits.

Looking ahead, we're moving into the new moon phase, which should settle the tides down and make the fishing more manageable. The butterfish should stick around through July, and as long as they do, these bass will keep feeding. Water temps are climbing into the mid-60s, which is perfect for this kind of action.

If you're planning to hit the eastern Sound this week, get out there early. The bite's been best on the first two hours of the tide change, whether it's flood or ebb. After that, the fish seem to settle deeper and get pickier. And bring plenty of terminal tackle — between the blues and the rocky bottom, you're going to lose some gear. But trust me, it's worth every rig you donate to see one of these 40-inch bass come tight on your line.

reports.headline: Swim shads crush bucktails as big bass stack in Plum Gut's screaming rip
reports.subhead: Seven-inch Tsunami shads producing overslot stripers while traditional bucktails get schoolies.
reports.body_markdown:
The rip is running like a freight train and the big bass are finally here. After weeks of schoolies and slot fish, the overslot stripers have moved into Plum Gut in numbers, and they're showing a clear preference for swim shads over bucktails.

I've been running head-to-head tests between seven-inch Tsunami swim shads and traditional Smiling Bill bucktails on the same three-way rigs, and the results are staggering. The shads are producing multiple overslot bass per tide while the bucktails are getting nothing but schoolies. Same drift, same depth, same current — the big fish want that soft plastic action.

The setup is critical in this screaming water. I'm running an 8 to 10-ounce cannonball on a three-way swivel, one foot below the main line, with a 5 to 6-foot leader of 80-pound test to the lure. That heavy leader isn't just for abrasion — the stiffness helps stand the bait off the bottom when you're drifting at 2.5 to 3 mph through the rip.

The bite window is tight. You've got maybe 90 minutes of fishable current before it gets too evil to present properly. I'm hitting the 80-foot mark on the east side and riding the contour as it rises to 40 feet across the main rip. The key is making preemptive cranks as the depth shallows — drag that rig on the rocks and you're done.

Double-drop technique is saving rigs out there. Drop to bottom, crank twice, then intentionally drop again to remove the belly that forms on the initial fall. The current's so strong it puts a bow in your line before you even feel bottom. Without that second drop, you're fishing 10 feet off the deck.

The Race is producing too, but it's a different game. Topwater action at first light with pencil poppers, then switching to three-way rigs when the sun gets up. The butterfish are thick, and that's what's drawing the Hudson River fish east. I'm seeing bass to 37 inches mixing with gorilla blues that'll wreck your expensive plugs in a heartbeat. Run wire leaders or stick to bucktails.

Water temperature hit 66 degrees this week in the eastern Sound — four degrees warmer than the ocean side. That thermal barrier is stacking bait on the flood tide and holding bass on the ebb. The gradient is most pronounced around Orient Point, where the warmer bay water meets the cooler ocean flow.

Bird life is the tell. When you see terns working over the rip, there's bait in the water column. That's when I switch from bottom rigs to 6-inch Tsunami spoons, letting the current suspend them mid-column before they hit bottom. The bigger bass are often feeding higher when there's active bait.

Fishers Island drops are holding blackfish for guys willing to bounce around in the chop. The 55-foot zone west of the island has been consistent for keepers to 19 inches, but you're dealing with wind against tide most days. Spot-lock technology is earning its keep out there.

Full moon Friday means spring tides and serious current. I'm watching for the first real push of weakfish on the big water moves. The Race and Plum Gut will be unfishable during peak flow, but the edges and eddies should stack fish. Plan your drifts for the hour before and after slack — that's when the big ones feed.

reports.headline: Bunker schools fire up bass and blues as Sound water hits prime summer temps
reports.subhead: Big bait pods from Norwalk to Port Jeff trigger feeding frenzies on the flood tide.
reports.body_markdown:
The Central Sound is absolutely alive right now, and it's all about the bunker. These adult menhaden have been stacking up from the Norwalk Islands clear across to Port Jefferson Harbor, and when they move, everything follows. I've been watching this build for two weeks, and it finally exploded this past weekend.

The bass bite has been exceptional on the flood tide, especially around the deeper structure. I'm talking 25 to 35 feet along the Connecticut shoreline drops and the edges near Middle Ground Light. The fish are keying on those bunker schools, and when you find the bait, you find the stripers. Live-lined bunker on a fishfinder rig with a 6/0 circle hook has been deadly — let that bait swim naturally in the current and hang on. I've seen fish to 40 inches taken this way, with most in that sweet 28 to 35-inch range.

What's really interesting is how the thermal structure is setting up. Water temps have climbed into the upper 60s in the harbors and bays, but the deeper water in the shipping channel is holding steady around 64 degrees. That temperature break is creating a perfect ambush zone where the cooler, oxygen-rich water meets the warmer surface layer. The bass are using this thermocline like a highway, following it east and west as they hunt.

Bluefish have joined the party in a big way. These aren't the snappers we'll see in July — these are legitimate choppers in the 3 to 8-pound class, and they're absolutely savage on the bunker schools. When you see the birds working, get there fast. Wire leaders are mandatory, and I've been having great success with 1-ounce white bucktails tipped with a strip of fresh bunker belly. Cast into the melee and retrieve fast — these blues want a bait that's trying to escape.

The fluke fishing has been solid but requires some patience. With all this bunker activity in the water column, the flatfish have been a bit scattered. Your best bet is to work the edges of the shipping channel during the outgoing tide, especially around the Stratford Shoal area. Four to 6-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets in white or chartreuse on 3/4-ounce bucktails are producing fish to 24 inches. The key is staying mobile — if you're not marking fish or getting bites within 20 minutes, move.

Porgies are thick on the deeper structure, and while they're not the glamour species, they're excellent table fare and great action for kids. The rocky areas off the Connecticut side in 30 to 45 feet have been loaded with scup in the 12 to 14-inch range. High-low rigs with size 4 hooks and small pieces of squid or clam are all you need.

The moon phase is working in our favor right now. We're coming off a new moon, which means the spring tides are flushing massive amounts of bait out of the harbors and estuaries. This is what's been concentrating those bunker schools and triggering the feeding response from the gamefish. The current has been running hard — sometimes too hard for effective fishing — but when it eases during the tide changes, that's when the magic happens.

Looking ahead, I expect this pattern to continue through the weekend and into next week. The weather looks cooperative, with light southwest winds and no major fronts approaching. The key will be timing your trips with the tide. The two hours before and after the tide change have been most productive, especially on the flood when all that bait gets pushed up against the structure.

One thing to watch for: as we move deeper into summer and water temps climb into the low 70s, expect the fish to go deeper during the heat of the day. Early morning and evening sessions will become increasingly important. The bass will still be there, but they'll be hugging that thermocline in 40 to 60 feet of water during the midday heat.

The action is only going to get better as we head toward the full moon next week. Those big tides will really get the bait moving, and I'm expecting some epic surface action when conditions align. Keep your eyes on the birds, your ears on the radio chatter, and be ready to run when the call comes in.

reports.headline: Bass blitz the Norwalk rocks as summer patterns lock in
reports.subhead: Stripers stack on structure while fluke move shallow in warming Sound waters.
reports.body_markdown:
The Central Sound is hitting its summer stride, and the fish are responding exactly how they should when water temps climb into the upper 60s and bait gets concentrated by the lunar cycle.

Striped bass are the story right now, and they're doing what bass do best — ambushing bait around structure when the current gets moving. The Norwalk Islands have been producing consistent action on the outgoing tide, particularly around the rocky points where bass set up to intercept spearing and small bunker getting swept out of the harbors. I'm seeing fish in the 28 to 35-inch range hitting white bucktails with Gulp trailers, worked slow along the bottom in 15 to 25 feet of water.

The key has been reading the current. These aren't random fish — they're positioned bass waiting for the tide to deliver food. I've been most successful on the last two hours of the ebb, when the flow really gets cooking and pushes bait off the structure. A 3/4-ounce white bucktail with a 5-inch Swimming Mullet, dragged just fast enough to keep contact with bottom, has been money.

Topwater action has been sporadic but explosive when it happens. Early morning around the rocky shorelines, pencil poppers in white or bone are drawing violent strikes from bass that have been feeding deep all night. The bite window is narrow — first light to about 7 AM — but when you hit it right, it's spectacular.

Fluke fishing has taken an interesting turn as water temperatures push toward 70. Instead of the typical deep-water summer pattern, I'm finding good numbers of fish in surprisingly shallow water — 18 to 30 feet over sandy bottom adjacent to structure. The theory makes sense: as surface temps climb, fluke are finding the thermal comfort zone in that mid-depth range where cooler water meets warmer, and bait gets concentrated.

Bucktail and Gulp combinations continue to dominate, but I'm seeing more success with chartreuse and pink than the usual white. A 1/2-ounce chartreuse bucktail with a 4-inch white Gulp grub, bounced slowly on the drift, has been producing fish to 22 inches. The bite has been best on the incoming tide when cleaner water pushes in from the east.

Porgies are thick around Middle Ground Light and the deeper structure off Stratford Shoal. These aren't the usual small harbor porgies — we're seeing fish in the 12 to 14-inch range that are actually worth keeping. High-low rigs with small hooks and pieces of clam or squid are all you need, but the key is finding the right depth. Most productive fishing has been in 35 to 50 feet, where the bigger porgies seem to hold.

Bait has been the underlying story driving all this action. Spearing are thick along the Connecticut shoreline, particularly in the deeper water adjacent to rocky structure. Bunker schools have been moving through the shipping channels, and when they stack up against the tide rips, everything feeds. I've been watching for bird activity — when the terns start working, there's usually something underneath worth casting to.

The new moon cycle we just passed through created some serious tidal movement, and that's when the fishing really turned on. Big spring tides mean fast current, and fast current means bait loses control and predators take advantage. I expect this pattern to continue through the weekend, especially with the moderate southwest winds keeping surface conditions manageable.

Looking ahead, I'm watching for the summer bluefish push that typically happens in early July. Water temps are climbing toward that magic 72-degree mark where blues really start to show in numbers. When they arrive, they'll likely follow the same bait concentrations that are holding bass right now — the Norwalk Islands, Stratford Shoal, and the deeper water off Charles Island.

The weekend forecast looks promising with light winds and building afternoon sea breezes. That's perfect for working the structure fishing, where you need boat control to stay positioned properly. I'll be focusing on the rocky areas during the outgoing tide, then switching to the fluke grounds on the flood when cleaner water moves in from the east.

reports.headline: Gator blues crash Western Sound as bass push deep in 70-degree water
reports.subhead: Big bluefish blitzing bunker while stripers retreat to structure in warming Sound
reports.body_markdown:
The Western Sound is telling two stories this week, and both of them are worth listening to. The first is about the gator blues that have moved in like they own the place, terrorizing bunker schools from the Throgs Neck Bridge to Matinecock Point. The second is about the bass that are getting pickier by the day as water temps climb toward 70 degrees.

I've been watching this pattern develop for three weeks now, and it's classic late June in the Sound. The big blues — and I'm talking 12 to 15-pound fish, not cocktails — are running the show during daylight hours. They're stacked up wherever the bunker are thick, and right now that's the deep water off Execution Rocks and the channel edges near Hart Island. These fish want big baits presented aggressively. Fresh bunker chunks on a fishfinder rig, or if you're trolling, large umbrella rigs with 9-inch shads are getting crushed.

The bass bite is a different animal entirely. With surface temps hitting 68 to 70 degrees in the back bays and shallows, the stripers have done what they always do — they've moved to structure and gone deep. The Stepping Stones area has been producing consistent fish in the 28 to 35-inch range, but you've got to work for them. Live eels fished tight to the rocks on the outgoing tide are still the ticket, especially after dark. During the day, it's all about finding the thermocline.

I've been marking fish consistently at 35 to 45 feet, right where the cooler water sits. The key is understanding that these fish aren't feeding aggressively like they were three weeks ago. They're relating to bait, but they're selective. Small live bunker on a circle hook, fished on a three-way rig to keep it just off bottom, has been my most consistent producer. The bite window is narrow — first two hours of the outgoing tide, when the cooler water from the deep Sound starts moving.

The fluke fishing has been the surprise story of the week. Little Neck Bay and the flats off Matinecock have been holding some quality fish, including several doormat-class fluke in the 6 to 8-pound range. The pattern is classic summer fluking: white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift. The key is finding the right depth — 25 to 30 feet where the channel edges meet the flats. The fish are holding right on that transition, ambushing bait that gets swept along by the current.

Porgies have moved in thick around any structure you can find. The pilings at the Throgs Neck Bridge, the rocks at Execution, even the old wrecks scattered throughout the Sound are holding good numbers of fish. Standard porgy rigs baited with clam or squid are all you need, but don't overlook the bigger fish. I've been seeing porgies to 3 pounds mixed in with the usual suspects.

The bait situation is interesting this year. We've got good numbers of bunker, but they're running larger than usual for June — more like fall-sized fish. The spearing are thick along the shorelines, especially in the protected coves and harbors. Sand eels are scattered but present, particularly around the deeper structure.

Looking at the lunar calendar, we're coming off a new moon, which means the tides are starting to build toward the full moon on July 3rd. That's going to mean stronger currents and better bait movement, which should fire up both the bass and blues. The key will be timing your trips to the tide changes — that's when the bait gets disoriented and the predators move in.

Water clarity has been excellent throughout most of the Sound, with visibility running 8 to 12 feet in most areas. The exception is the back bays and harbors, where runoff from recent rains has things a bit stirred up. That's actually been working in our favor for the fluke fishing — they seem to bite better when the water has a little color to it.

The weather pattern looks stable for the next week, with light winds and moderate temperatures. That should keep the water conditions consistent and make for comfortable fishing. The real story will be watching how the fish adjust as we move deeper into summer. The bass will continue to go deeper and get more selective, while the blues should remain aggressive as long as the bait stays thick.

For the coming week, I'm watching the full moon tides closely. The stronger currents should get the bait moving and trigger more aggressive feeding. The bass bite should improve, especially on the night tides, while the blues will likely spread out more as they follow the bunker schools. It's shaping up to be a classic summer pattern in the Western Sound — you just need to know where to look and when to be there.

reports.headline: Gator blues crash the Sound as bass trolling peaks at Execution Rocks
reports.subhead: Big stripers to 50 pounds on Mojos over the ledge while cocktail blues blitz butterfish in the shallows.
reports.body_markdown:
The Western Sound is firing on all cylinders right now, and I'm seeing the kind of fishing that makes you remember why you fell in love with these waters in the first place. Water temps have climbed past the magic 70-degree mark in most spots, and that's triggering the summer patterns I've been waiting for all season.

The big news is the bass trolling bite at Execution Rocks. I've been watching boats work the ledge structure there, and when the outgoing tide gets moving, those fish turn on like someone flipped a switch. The pattern is simple but deadly effective: large Mojos dragged over the drop-off in 35 to 50 feet of water. The key is timing it with moving water — the morning slack produces nothing, but once that ebb starts pulling, you're in business. I'm hearing about multiple 40-inch-plus fish coming over the rails, including one monster that went an estimated 50 pounds. That's the kind of fish that makes grown men weep.

The Stepping Stones area is producing similar results, especially on the flood tide when bait gets pushed against the structure. Bunker spoons in the 3 to 4-ounce range are working well here, particularly the chrome and blue patterns. The fish are staging deep during the day — 45 to 60 feet — but they'll come up to chase if you put the lure in their face.

Now here's where it gets interesting for the light tackle crowd: the bluefish invasion has begun in earnest. These aren't the cocktail blues we've been dealing with — I'm talking about legitimate gator blues in the 8 to 12-pound class that are absolutely demolishing baitfish in the shallows. Matinecock Point has been a hotbed, with schools of butterfish getting hammered in 15 to 25 feet of water. Small metal jigs — 1 to 2-ounce Hopkins and Ava diamonds — are all you need. Cast into the melee and hang on.

The fluke bite has been more challenging, but there are fish to be had if you know where to look. The grass beds between Oyster Bay and Lloyd's Neck are holding some decent fish, though you'll sort through plenty of shorts to find a keeper. The productive pattern has been 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets, worked slow on the drift. The fish are relating to the bottom structure, so you need to stay in contact. I'm seeing the best action on the incoming tide when the current pushes bait into the shallows.

Porgies have made their presence known around the rocky structure near Cold Spring Harbor. Standard porgy rigs baited with clam are producing steady action, with fish running 1 to 2 pounds. It's not glamorous fishing, but it's reliable, and these fish make excellent table fare.

The bait situation is what's really driving everything right now. Peanut bunker are thick in the harbors and bays, which is unusual for this time of year — normally we see adult bunker spawning in June, not the juveniles. But the fish don't care about our expectations. Spearing are also abundant along the shorelines, particularly around dock structures and marina areas.

Looking at the bigger picture, we're entering that sweet spot of summer fishing where multiple species are active simultaneously. The new moon on Friday is going to create some serious tidal movement, and I expect that to fire up both the bass trolling and the bluefish blitzing. The key is being flexible — if the trolling slows down, switch to casting metals for the blues. If the blues move off, try drifting for fluke.

One thing I'm keeping an eye on is the water temperature gradient between the Sound and the back bays. The harbors are running 4 to 5 degrees warmer than the main body of water, and that differential is creating some interesting fishing opportunities. Bass are using these cooler pockets as staging areas during the heat of the day, then moving shallow to feed at dawn and dusk.

For the week ahead, I'm watching the weather pattern closely. We've got stable conditions forecast, which should keep the fishing consistent. The full moon cycle is approaching, and that typically means big tides and active fish. I'd focus on the major structure — Execution Rocks, Stepping Stones, the Throgs Neck Bridge pilings — during the peak tidal flow periods. Early morning and late afternoon will be your best bets for surface activity.

The summer pattern is officially here, folks. Water's warm, bait's abundant, and the fish are feeding aggressively. This is what we wait all year for in the Western Sound.

reports.headline: Giants crash the canyon as 68-degree water stacks bait on the 100-fathom line
reports.subhead: Bluefin to 96 inches and yellowfin pushing 60 pounds light up the Hudson on jigs and stickbaits.
reports.body_markdown:
The Hudson Canyon is firing on all cylinders right now, and it's the kind of bite that reminds you why we make the long run out here. Water temps hit 68 degrees on the shelf this week — that's the magic number that brings everything together. The thermocline set up perfect at 45 feet, creating a conveyor belt of bait that's stacking bluefin and yellowfin from the Claw all the way down to the Dip.

Bluefin are the story right now. We're seeing giants — fish pushing triple digits — crashing bunker schools in spectacular fashion. These aren't the usual deep-water grinders. They're up top, feeding aggressive, and they want it loud and fast. The UVT stickbaits are absolutely deadly when you find them blowing up on bunker. Cast into the white water and hang on. I've been running 280-gram jigs with beefed-up hooks when they drop down to 75 feet after the surface feed dies. Work them slow through the water column — these fish are sitting just off the bottom, using that thermocline as a highway.

The yellowfin bite has been more consistent but requires more finesse. They're holding in 68-degree water along the canyon edge, and they're particular about presentation. Ballyhoo on the troll is producing fish to 60 pounds, but you need to match the bait size to what they're eating. The bunker schools are thick but small — peanuts mostly — so downsize your spread. Four-inch ballyhoo rigged on 8/0 hooks, pulled at 6.5 knots, has been the ticket.

Mahi are scattered but quality when you find them. The grass lines 15 miles southeast of the canyon mouth are holding decent fish. Feather rigs behind a teaser spread work, but don't overlook the old-school approach — a simple ballyhoo on a circle hook under a grass mat will get bit. The key is staying mobile. These fish are moving with the current, following the temperature breaks.

The bite timing has been crucial. Early morning — first light to 8 AM — is when the bluefin are most active on top. As the sun climbs, they sound, and that's when the jig bite turns on. The yellowfin seem less affected by light penetration, staying active through midday if you're on the right temperature water.

Current has been moderate but consistent, running northeast at about 1.2 knots along the canyon wall. That's perfect for holding bait against the structure without making boat control impossible. The new moon spring tides earlier this week flushed a lot of fresh bait out of the Hudson River system, and it's been stacking up where the current hits the canyon edge.

Weather looks cooperative for the next few days — light northwest winds shifting to southwest by the weekend. That should keep the surface conditions fishable and maintain the temperature structure we've been seeing. The 68-degree water is the key to this whole bite. It's warm enough to keep the tuna active but cool enough that they don't push deeper.

Looking ahead, I expect this pattern to hold through the weekend. The full moon Friday will bring bigger tides, which should push even more bait into the canyon system. If you're making the run, launch early — the best fishing has been happening before the fleet arrives. Bring heavy tackle and sharp hooks. These fish are not playing games.

reports.headline: Trophy bass crash Block Island as 68-degree water holds bait tight to the ledges
reports.subhead: Big stripers stacked on bucktails and flutter spoons as perfect water temps create feeding frenzy.
reports.body_markdown:
The water around Block Island hit that magic 68-degree mark this week, and the striped bass responded like someone rang the dinner bell. I've been fishing these waters for two decades, and when the temperature sits right in that sweet spot — not too warm, not too cool — the big girls move in and feed hard.

The Southwest Ledge has been absolutely loaded with quality fish. I'm talking 30 to 40-pound class stripers that are hitting bucktails like they haven't eaten in weeks. White and chartreuse 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with pork rind or 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets are producing the best action. The key is working them just off the bottom in 35 to 50 feet of water along the drop-off. Don't just cast and retrieve — let that bucktail flutter down, then work it back with sharp lifts and drops. These fish want action, not a steady swim.

Flutter spoons are absolutely deadly right now, especially when you mark fish suspended in the water column. I've been dropping 3-ounce chrome spoons right on top of marked schools and getting crushed on the fall. The fish are holding about 15 feet down over 40-foot bottom, probably following the bait that's getting pushed around by the current.

The North Rip has been producing some serious fish on the outgoing tide. The current has been moderate — not the screaming rips we sometimes get with the new moon — which makes presentation much more manageable. I've been anchoring uptide and letting live peanut bunker drift back on fishfinder rigs. The hits have been violent, and several fish have gone over the 40-inch mark.

What's really exciting is seeing the first bonito of the season showing up. They're small schools right now, but they're here, which means the water quality is prime. When bonito move into Block Island waters, it's always a good sign that the ecosystem is firing on all cylinders. The cool, oxygenated water that draws these pelagics is the same water that holds our trophy stripers.

The wind farm area has been surprisingly productive for sea bass, with some quality fish in the 3 to 5-pound range coming over the rails. High-low rigs with clam or squid strips are working well in 60 to 80 feet of water around the turbine bases. The structure is definitely concentrating baitfish, and the bass are taking advantage.

Porgies have been thick around the traditional spots — the rocky areas south of the island in 30 to 40 feet. Small hooks, light sinkers, and pieces of clam or sea worm are all you need. It's been a great way to fill the cooler when the stripers aren't cooperating.

The water clarity has been exceptional — that gin-clear blue that tells you everything is right with the world. Visibility is easily 20 feet, and you can see the bottom in 30 feet of water. This clarity, combined with the perfect temperature, is creating ideal hunting conditions for predators.

Tide timing has been crucial. The best action has been on the last two hours of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming. The moderate current is moving enough bait to get the fish active without making it impossible to fish effectively. Spring tides from the recent new moon have been flushing baitfish out of the protected areas and concentrating them along the ledges where the big bass are waiting.

Looking ahead, we're approaching the full moon on Friday, which should bring some serious tidal movement. I expect the fishing to get even better as those big tides push more bait around and get the fish really aggressive. The water temperature should hold steady in that perfect 68-degree range, and if the weather cooperates, this could be the week that produces some real monsters. Get out there and get tight to those ledges — the fish are here and they're hungry.

reports.headline: Jumbo blues crash Jersey inlets as bay water hits 68 degrees
reports.subhead: Raritan Bay stripers still thick on bunker while fluke fishing heats up from Shark River to Cape May.
reports.body_markdown:
The water's finally talking our language down here, and the fish are listening loud and clear. Bay temps hit 68 degrees this week — a solid four-degree jump from the ocean side — and that thermal gradient is stacking bait like you wouldn't believe. The bunker are thick from Sandy Hook to Shark River, and everything with teeth is having a field day.

Raritan Bay is absolutely loaded with stripers right now. I'm talking about fish from schoolies to solid 30-inchers crushing peanut bunker on the flood tide. The key is finding those temperature breaks where the warmer bay water meets the cooler ocean flow. Fish the edges with live bunker on a fishfinder rig, or throw 6-inch white Hogy soft plastics on 3/4-ounce jig heads. The bass are sitting in 15 to 20 feet, ambushing bait as it gets swept through the channel. Best action has been two hours before and after the tide change.

But here's the real story — the bluefish have returned in force, and I mean the jumbo choppers we haven't seen in years. Manasquan Inlet has been producing blues in the 8 to 12-pound class, fish that'll test your drag and your patience. They're hitting everything from metal jigs to fresh bunker chunks. I've been running 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 1-ounce bucktails, bouncing them through the inlet on the outgoing water. The blues are stacked up where the current rips around the jetties, waiting for bait to get flushed out of the back bay.

Fluke fishing has turned the corner too. Shark River has been consistent for keepers in the 18 to 22-inch range, with fish holding in the deeper holes on the incoming tide. The trick is working 5-inch white Gulp baits on 3/8-ounce jig heads, keeping them moving slow along the bottom. The fluke are feeding on the abundant spearing and small crabs that the warmer water has brought inshore. I've been finding the best action in 8 to 12 feet of water, especially around the marina docks where the structure holds bait.

Down at Barnegat, the inlet has been producing a mixed bag of blues, fluke, and even some early weakfish. The weakies are small — mostly 12 to 14-inchers — but they're a welcome sight after years of poor numbers. Pink Gulp on light jig heads has been the ticket, fished on the edges of the channel where the current slows.

The water clarity has been excellent despite some afternoon thunderstorms. That 68-degree reading in the bay is crucial — it's warm enough to fire up the baitfish but not so hot that it pushes the gamefish deep. The gradient between bay and ocean water is creating perfect ambush points at every inlet from Sandy Hook to Cape May.

Looking ahead, we're coming up on the new moon Friday, which means spring tides and serious current flow. That's going to flush even more bait out of the back bays and concentrate the predators at the inlet mouths. I'm expecting the bluefish bite to get even better as those big tides move more food around. The stripers should stay active as long as the bunker schools hold, and with water temps climbing toward 70, we might start seeing some early summer species like Spanish mackerel showing up in the mix.

This is prime time Jersey fishing — multiple species, aggressive fish, and conditions that are only going to get better. Get out there before the weekend crowds hit the water.

reports.headline: Sound shore bass stack up as water hits 68 degrees off Orient Point
reports.subhead: Plum Gut current is pulling bait through the rips while calm conditions make for perfect drifting.
reports.body_markdown:
Water's finally warming up proper out here on the Sound shore, and the bass are responding like they should. Been seeing 68 degrees steady from Mattituck east to Orient Point, which is that magic number that gets the stripers moving in earnest. The calm weather we've had — light northwest winds under 7 knots most days — has made for some real pleasant fishing, especially around the rips where you usually get your teeth rattled.

Best action's been coming off Orient Point where the current sweeps around the tip and sets up that beautiful edge. Been working the 25 to 35 foot range with bucktails and soft plastics, dragging them slow on the drift. White and chartreuse 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce heads are doing the damage, especially when you let them tick bottom on the downtide side of the rip. Had one morning last week where every drift through that sweet spot produced a keeper, most in the 28 to 32 inch range with a couple pushing 35.

The Plum Gut approach has been holding fish too, though you need to time it right with the current. That race gets nasty when it's really ripping, but on the slack and the first hour of the flood, it's been productive. Seeing a lot of bait getting pushed through there — mostly peanut bunker and some sand eels. The bass are sitting just outside the main current, picking off whatever gets swept past. Live peanuts on a fishfinder rig work, but honestly the artificials have been more consistent. Something about that steady retrieve that triggers them.

Porgy fishing's been solid too, especially around the rocky bottom off Horton Point. Nothing huge — mostly in the half-pound to pound range — but they're thick and eager. Small pieces of squid or clam on a high-low rig, fished on the anchor in 20 to 30 feet. The kids love it, and it makes for good table fare when the bass aren't cooperating.

Bluefish have been scattered but when you find them, they're aggressive. Had a school come through off Rocky Point two days back, all in the 3 to 5 pound range. They hit everything — spoons, poppers, even the bucktails meant for bass. Typical blues — here one minute, gone the next, but fun while it lasted.

What's interesting is how clean the water's been staying despite the calm conditions. Usually when the wind lays down this long, you get that green bloom, but the current through Plum Gut keeps things flushed. Visibility's been good, maybe 8 to 10 feet, which explains why the artificials are outfishing bait in a lot of spots.

The lunar cycle's working in our favor too. We're coming off the new moon, so the tides aren't extreme, but there's enough movement to keep bait active without making the current unmanageable. That's perfect for this kind of drift fishing where you need just enough push to work your lure but not so much that you can't control your presentation.

Looking ahead, the forecast shows more of the same — light winds, stable pressure, water temps holding steady or maybe creeping up another degree. That's good news because once we hit 70 degrees consistently, the weakfish usually start showing in numbers. Haven't seen many yet, just a few scattered fish mixed in with the bass, but I'm watching for them. The full moon's coming up next week, and that often coincides with the first real push of weaks through the eastern Sound.

If you're planning to fish this stretch, early morning's been best, especially that first hour after sunrise when the light's just starting to penetrate. The bass seem more aggressive then, probably because the baitfish are more active. Afternoon fishing's been decent too, but you need to work harder for your fish. And don't overlook the deeper water — some of the better bass have been coming from 40 feet or more, especially when the sun gets high.

reports.headline: Peconic porgies fire as bay water hits 72 degrees
reports.subhead: Jumbo scup stack around Shelter Island while weakfish show in numbers for first time this season.
reports.body_markdown:
The Peconic finally hit its stride this week as bay temperatures spiked to 72 degrees — a full 4 degrees warmer than the Sound side. That thermal gradient is doing exactly what it's supposed to do: stacking bait and firing up the porgy bite like I haven't seen since early May.

The jumbo scup are absolutely loaded around Shelter Island, particularly the deeper edges near the ferry run where the current keeps fresh water moving. I'm talking about legitimate 18-inch fish pushing 3 pounds, not the usual bay rats. The key has been anchoring in 25 to 30 feet on the flood tide with a steady chum slick of crushed clams. Simple high-low rigs with size 4 hooks and fresh clam strips are all you need, but the presentation matters — keep that bait moving just off bottom as the tide pushes through.

What's really got my attention is the weakfish showing up in numbers I haven't seen in years. The warming bay water has pulled them in from deeper water, and they're mixed right in with the porgies. I've been picking up 18 to 20-inch weaks consistently, with a few pushing 4 pounds. They're hitting the same clam baits as the porgies, but you'll know when you hook one — that head-shaking fight is unmistakable.

The striped bass bite has been more scattered but consistent for those willing to work for them. Early morning bucktailing around the deeper channels near Greenport has been producing slot fish in the 28 to 32-inch range. White and chartreuse 3/4-ounce bucktails with 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets are the ticket, worked slow on the drift during the last hour of the outgoing tide. The bass are relating to the thermocline that's set up around 20 feet — that's where the cooler Sound water meets the warmer bay water, and it's holding bait tight.

Three Mile Harbor has been a sleeper spot for fluke this week. The warming shallow water has pulled summer flounder into the back reaches where they're ambushing spearing and juvenile porgies. Bucktail and Gulp combinations in white and pink are working best, drifted along the channel edges in 12 to 18 feet. The fish aren't huge — mostly 16 to 19-inchers — but they're plentiful and aggressive.

The new moon we just passed really stirred things up with those big spring tides. The extra water movement flushed a lot of bait out of the back bays and concentrated it along the main channel edges. That's where I've been finding the most consistent action across all species.

Looking ahead, this weekend's weather should keep conditions stable with light winds and calm seas. The bay water should continue warming, which means the porgy bite will only get better. I'm expecting the weakfish numbers to increase as more fish move in from the Sound, and the early morning bass bite should remain solid as long as we keep getting that temperature differential between bay and Sound water.

The full moon coming up next week will bring another round of strong tides, which should really fire up the inlet fishing at Orient Point. That's when I'll be watching for the first real push of summer bluefish to show up in numbers.

reports.headline: Bass blitz fires the Point as 68-degree water stacks bait on the rips
reports.subhead: Eels after dark producing 40-pound class stripers while diamond jigs work the daylight hours.
reports.body_markdown:
The Point is absolutely on fire right now, and it's not just the summer crowds I'm talking about. Water temps hit 68 degrees this week — that magic number that flips the switch on everything from the lighthouse rocks to the deep rips off Shagwong. When the thermometer climbs into the upper 60s out here, the bait gets nervous and the bass get aggressive.

The night bite has been nothing short of spectacular. Live eels fished tight to the boulder fields are producing bass in the 30 to 40-pound class, with fish hitting hard in that golden hour right after sunset. The key is getting your eel down into the rocks where these big girls are ambushing sand eels and squid. I'm running a simple fishfinder rig with a 3/0 circle hook and just enough weight to tick bottom — usually 2 to 3 ounces depending on the current. The new moon we just passed stirred things up good, and now with the tides building back toward springs, the current is moving bait through the rips like a conveyor belt.

Daylight hours are producing too, but you need to work for it. Diamond jigs in the 3 to 4-ounce range are the ticket when the current is ripping. White and chartreuse are getting hit, but don't overlook the classic silver — sometimes simple is better when the water's clean like it's been. I'm seeing guys boat a couple dozen bass and blues mixed together, with the blues running thick in that 8 to 12-pound range. Those chunky cocktail blues are a great sign — means the bait chain is healthy and the big bass aren't far behind.

The south side has been the consistent producer, especially that drop-off in 30 to 40 feet where the bottom transitions from sand to rock. The water clarity has been exceptional, which means you can see the fish working, but it also means they can see you. Light leaders are critical — I'm dropping down to 30-pound fluorocarbon when the water's this clear, even though it means losing a few rigs to the rocks.

Fluke fishing has picked up considerably as the water warmed. The Viking Fleet and other party boats are seeing steady action with keepers mixed in among the usual shorts. White Gulp on bucktails is still the go-to, but I'm hearing good things about chartreuse when the current is really moving. The key spots are the edges where sand meets structure — those transition zones where fluke set up to ambush bait getting swept along by the tide.

Porgies are showing in decent numbers, though they're schooled up tight rather than spread out everywhere. When you find them, you find them good. Small hooks and small baits — clam bellies and sandworms on size 6 hooks are getting it done. The deeper water off the Point has been holding the better-grade fish.

What's really got me excited is the bait situation. Sand eels are thick, squid made a strong push through the area, and I'm seeing butterfish, shad, and mackerel all mixed in. That diversity tells me the ecosystem is healthy and the fishing should stay strong through the summer. The bunker are still scarce, which is actually a good thing — when there's no easy meal, the bass have to work the structure and that's where we can get at them.

Looking ahead, we're building toward full moon Friday, which means big tides and serious current. That's when the Point really comes alive. The spring tides will flush even more bait out of the back bays and estuaries, and with water temps climbing toward 70, we should see the summer pattern lock in solid. I'll be watching for the first real push of weakfish — they love these big moon tides and warm water. If you're planning a trip, focus on the tide changes, especially that last hour of outgoing when everything gets pushed through the rips. That's when the magic happens at Montauk Point.

reports.headline: Inlet blues crash the night bite as 68-degree water stacks bait on the flood
reports.subhead: Outgoing tides at Shinnecock producing slot bass to 28 inches while big bluefish hunt the rips.
reports.body_markdown:
The inlet's been electric after dark this week, and it's all about that 68-degree water pushing through on the flood tide. When bay water runs four degrees warmer than the ocean side, you get that thermal gradient that stacks bait against the jetties — and the predators follow.

Best action's been on the outgoing after midnight. I've been working the north jetty with 5-inch Yozuri Mag Darters in the traditional white-and-blue, letting the flat head wiggle in the current on a dead drift. That D-wood action is deadly when the water's moving — even on the pause, the current keeps the bait alive. Slot bass to 28 inches have been crushing it in the deep water off the tip, especially when the tide's really ripping.

The bluefish invasion started three nights ago. Big choppers — some pushing 15 pounds — are hunting the rips like wolves. They're scattered throughout the water column, so you need to adjust. When they're blitzing on top, I swing a 3/4-ounce bucktail with a white Zoom fork tail underneath the chaos. Pop-pop-pause retrieve gets the bass while the blues tear up the surface.

Crystal-clear water's made presentation critical. These fish can see everything in this gin-clear blue-green water we've got right now. I'm running 30-pound fluoro leaders even on my light tackle setup — that PC Fun Carbon rod handles it fine, and you need the insurance against those blue teeth. Lost too many Mag Darters early in the week before I wised up.

Bay fishing's been solid for mixed bags. The Ponquogue Bridge has been holding weakfish on the incoming tide — first real push I've seen this season. Small Deadly Dicks in silver work best, cast tight to the pilings and worked slow. Fluke are scattered through the deeper cuts, with the best action in 15 to 20 feet on the flood. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 1/2-ounce bucktails are producing keepers to 4 pounds.

What's driving this bite is simple physics. Ocean temps are sitting at 64 degrees while the bay's running 68 — that's a massive gradient for June. Add in these light northwest winds that have been holding for three days, and you get perfect conditions. The thermocline's setting up shallow, concentrating bait in the top 20 feet of water.

The new moon spring tides are flushing everything out of the back bay. Peanut bunker, spearing, even some sand eels are getting swept through the inlet on the ebb. I'm seeing bait balls stacked against the south jetty around 2 AM when the current's really screaming.

One thing I've noticed — boat traffic during prime time is killing schools. These big center consoles blasting through the inlet at sunset are scattering fish that took hours to set up. If you're serious about the night bite, wait until after 11 PM when the weekend warriors head home.

Looking ahead, this pattern should hold through the weekend. We're getting a full moon Friday, which means even bigger tides. That's when I expect the weakfish bite to really turn on — those big spring tides will flush more bait out of the Peconic system through the canal. I'll be watching the inlet drain at sunset for the first serious run of tiderunners.

Water temps should climb another degree or two this week if these light winds hold. Once bay water hits 70, the fluke bite in the deeper holes should explode. Until then, it's all about reading the current and being there when the bait moves.

reports.headline: Moriches bass bite fires as thermal layers stack bait in the inlet
reports.subhead: Trophy stripers hit live spot at night while fluke action heats up in skinny bay water.
reports.body_markdown:
The inlet's been absolutely electric this past week, and I can tell you exactly why. Water temps hit 68.2 degrees on the ocean side while the bay's running a solid 4 degrees warmer at 72 — that thermal gradient is creating a conveyor belt of bait through Moriches Inlet that's got the bass stacked like cordwood.

Night fishing has been the ticket for trophy stripers. I'm talking fish in the 35-inch class hitting live spot on fishfinder rigs, worked tight to the inlet's north jetty on the outgoing tide. The key is getting your bait down into that 8-to-12-foot channel where the cooler ocean water meets the warmer bay flow. That thermocline is holding massive schools of peanut bunker, and the bass are gorging themselves in the dark.

The bathymetry here tells the whole story. When that bay water dumps out on the ebb, it's carrying everything with it — grass shrimp, juvenile weakfish, sand eels — and funneling it right through the inlet's throat. I've been positioning at the inlet mouth just as the tide turns, watching my sonar light up with bait clouds at 15 feet. Drop a live spot into that chaos on a 6/0 circle hook with a 2-ounce egg sinker, and you're in business.

Fluke fishing has turned the corner in the bay's skinny water. We're seeing consistent action in 4 to 8 feet over the sand flats between Tuthill Point and the East Moriches channel. The secret is downsizing everything — 1/4-ounce bucktails with 3-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets, dragged painfully slow on the drift. These bay fluke are spooky in the shallow water, but when you dial in the presentation, you're looking at fish to 6 pounds.

The water clarity has been exceptional after last week's northwest winds cleaned out the bay. I'm seeing bottom in 6 feet, which means the fluke can see your rig from a mile away. Switch to 15-pound fluorocarbon leaders and keep your jig heads light. The fish are relating to the subtle depth changes — those 2-foot drops off the channel edges that most guys blow right over.

Cupsogue Beach has been producing solid bluefish action on the evening tide. The blues are running 3 to 8 pounds, crashing bait in the wash as the sun drops. Metal lips and small poppers are getting crushed in that last hour of light. The key is reading the water — look for the nervous bait dimpling the surface about 100 yards out, then work your way into casting range.

Weakfish are starting to show in better numbers around the inlet. I picked up three fish to 4 pounds this week on small bucktails tipped with Gulp, working the deeper holes on the bay side during slack water. The fish are holding in 12 to 15 feet, relating to the channel edges where the current creates those subtle eddies.

The lunar cycle is setting up perfectly for the coming week. We've got a new moon approaching, which means spring tides and serious current flow through the inlet. That's going to flush even more bait out of the back bay and concentrate the feeding fish in predictable spots. I'm planning to hit the inlet hard on the big outgoing tides, especially that 2-hour window before slack water when everything gets pushed through the channel.

Looking ahead, these northwest winds should keep the water clean and the temps stable. The bass bite should only get better as we move deeper into summer, and I'm expecting the first real push of weakfish to show up with the stronger tides. Keep your live wells stocked with spot and your light tackle rigged — this is shaping up to be one of those weeks where everything comes together.

reports.headline: Weakfish crash Fire Island surf as bay water hits 68 degrees
reports.subhead: Trophy tide-runners up to 7 pounds mixing with keeper fluke on the Captree drift.
reports.body_markdown:
The water's telling a story this week, and it's one I've been waiting all season to hear. Bay temperatures spiked to 68 degrees — a solid four-degree jump that's got bait stacked and predators feeding like it's September. When that thermal gradient sets up between the bay and ocean, magic happens at Fire Island Inlet, and we're seeing it now.

The headline catch came from the surf near the inlet — a 26-inch, 7.3-pound weakfish that fell for a 9-inch Gravity Tackle Sand Eel. That's not just a nice fish, that's a legitimate tide-runner, the kind of weakie that makes you remember why we chase these ghosts in the first place. The sand eel pattern is key here. With bay water warming faster than the ocean side, bait's getting flushed on every tide change, and the weakfish are staging right in the wash to ambush them.
