Out of Captree, the Laura Lee fleet's been putting keeper fluke on the deck consistently. The 30-foot zone off the Robert Moses bridges is producing doormat potential on the outgoing water. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails are the ticket — drag them slow on the drift, let the current do the work. The fish are holding tight to structure as that warmer bay water creates feeding lanes.

What's driving this bite is textbook Fire Island physics. We've got 68-degree bay water meeting 64-degree ocean water at the inlet mouth. That temperature break is a bait highway, and everything with fins knows it. The new moon we just passed means spring tides are flushing bunker and spearing out of the back bay like a conveyor belt. Bass are following, stacking on the ebb tide from the inlet jetties all the way to the Robert Moses span.

The Captree party fleet's been crushing mixed bags in the ocean — sea bass limits coming easy on diamond jigs and sabiki rigs, with ling cod and porgies filling out the coolers. But it's the inlet and bay mouth where the real action's happening. Clam bellies fished on fishfinder rigs are producing slot bass on the anchor, while casting Bass Assassins and soft plastics is connecting with the more aggressive fish.

Conditions are lining up perfectly. Light northwest winds at 5 knots, calm seas, and that high pressure system sitting over us means stable weather through the weekend. Water clarity's been excellent — you can see bottom in 15 feet, which tells you the spring flush is working.

The key zones right now are the inlet mouth on the outgoing tide, the Robert Moses bridges during the flood, and the surf from Democrat Point east to the lighthouse. For fluke, work the 25 to 35-foot contour with bucktails and Gulp. For bass and weakfish, focus on the inlet jetties and the channel edges where that temperature gradient is sharpest.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the full moon Friday, which means big water movement and serious feeding windows. That lunar pull is going to amplify everything we're seeing now — more bait movement, more aggressive fish, and better opportunities for trophy weakfish in the surf. The bay's warming trend should continue, potentially hitting 70 degrees by week's end, which will only intensify that thermal break at the inlet.

This is Fire Island fishing at its finest — when the bay becomes a bait factory and the inlet turns into a feeding frenzy. Get out there while the getting's good.

reports.headline: Weakfish crash Jones Inlet as bay water hits 68 degrees
reports.subhead: First real run of weakies in years coincides with perfect thermal gradient at the inlet mouth.
reports.body_markdown:
The water temperature hit that magic number this week — 68 degrees in the bay, 4 degrees warmer than the ocean side — and the weakfish responded like they've been waiting all season for this moment. I'm talking about real weakfish, not the scattered singles we've been picking at for the past few years. Schools of 3 to 6-pound fish are stacked up on the inlet's flood tide, and they're hungry.

The best action is happening right at the inlet mouth on the incoming water, especially the last two hours of flood. These fish are sitting in 12 to 18 feet, right where that warm bay water meets the cooler ocean flow. I've been working 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 1/2-ounce bucktails, keeping them just off the bottom on a slow retrieve. The key is feeling that thermal break — when your lure hits that cooler water, you know you're in the zone.

Fresh bunker chunks are also producing, especially fished on a fishfinder rig tight to the jetty rocks on the outgoing tide. The weakies are feeding heavily on the small bunker that have been thick in the bay all month. I watched one angler pull a 26-inch fish on a 9-inch sand eel imitation — these fish are keyed on longer baits right now.

The fluke bite has been solid but not spectacular. The Meadowbrook Bridge area is holding decent numbers, with most fish running 15 to 17 inches. White bucktails with squid strips or fresh smelt are the ticket, worked on the southeast side of the bridge structure. The incoming tide has been more productive than the outgoing, probably because it's pushing that warmer bay water over the structure and activating the bait.

Striped bass are showing in decent numbers around the inlet, especially at sunset. The fish are holding on the small sandbar just before the trough, and they're feeding on sand eels in the wash. A 2-ounce diamond jig with a green tail, cast past the break and worked back through the incoming water, has been the most consistent producer. After dark, switching to an SP Minnow has extended the bite.

The thermal gradient we're seeing right now is textbook for late June — bay water warming faster than the ocean, creating that conveyor belt effect that concentrates bait and draws in predators. With the new moon approaching Friday, we're looking at spring tides that should really flush the system and potentially trigger the first major weakfish run we've seen in years.

Bait has been exceptional. Peanut bunker are thick throughout the bay system, sand eels are showing in good numbers along the beach, and the squid have been consistent around the deeper structure. The birds have been working overtime on the small baitfish, which tells me the food chain is firing on all cylinders.

Looking ahead, this thermal setup should hold through the weekend. I'm watching for the full moon tides to really move some water and potentially push more weakfish into the system. The bass bite should continue to improve as we get deeper into the summer pattern, and the fluke fishing should pick up as the water continues to warm. This is shaping up to be the kind of week that reminds you why Jones Inlet has always been special — when conditions align, this place can produce like nowhere else on the South Shore.

reports.headline: Bay water hits 69 as weakfish crash the Jamaica Bay party with keeper fluke
reports.subhead: Trifecta fishing fires up as stripers move out and summer species settle in.
reports.body_markdown:
The bay hit 69 degrees this week and everything changed. I'm talking about a real shift — the kind that happens when water temps cross that magic threshold and the whole ecosystem flips the switch. The stripers that have been our bread and butter since April are starting to thin out, but don't cry about it. What's moving in is even better.

Weakfish are back in Jamaica Bay in numbers I haven't seen in years. Real weakfish, not the scattered singles we've been picking at. I'm talking keeper fish to 19 inches mixed with throwbacks, and they're hitting everything from bucktails to soft plastics to cut bait. The Marine Parkway Bridge area has been the hot zone, especially on the incoming tide when the cooler ocean water pushes bait up against the structure.

The fluke bite has absolutely exploded. Twenty-five-pound doormat? That happened this week right here in our backyard. The fish are staging in 8 to 15 feet of water along the channel edges, and they're not picky about presentation. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails are deadly when you drag them slow on the drift. But here's the thing — don't sleep on the hi-lo rig with lugworms. The old-school approach is putting fish in the boat when the fancy stuff fails.

What's really got me excited is the mixed bag action. You drop a line and you honestly don't know what's coming up. Keeper fluke, weakfish, sea robins the size of small dogs, and even some late-season stripers in the 24 to 28-inch range. That's the Jamaica Bay special right there — the kind of fishing that keeps you guessing and keeps it fun.

The bait situation tells the whole story. Bunker are still around but they're thinning out and spreading deeper into the bay system. The spearing are thick along the shorelines, especially around the Cross Bay Bridge pilings where the current creates eddies. Sand fleas are everywhere on the flats, which explains why the fluke bite has been so consistent.

Tide timing matters more now than it did a month ago. The outgoing has been producing the best weakfish action, especially that last two hours before low water when the bait gets funneled through the deeper cuts. For fluke, I'm seeing the best action on the incoming, particularly around the slack high when they settle on structure and ambush whatever drifts by.

The squid bite is absolutely insane right now. Sheepshead Bay has been the epicenter, but they're showing up in Jamaica Bay too, especially after dark around any structure with lights. Simple squid jigs worked vertically are all you need, and you can fill a cooler in an hour when you find them.

Water clarity has been decent despite some algae blooms earlier in the month. The 69-degree reading is about four degrees warmer than the ocean side of Rockaway Inlet, and that temperature gradient is creating a perfect setup. Bait gets pushed in on the flood, predators follow, and we get to intercept them.

Looking ahead, this full moon cycle should really fire things up. Spring tides mean stronger currents, which means better bait movement and more aggressive feeding. I'm watching for the first real push of porgies, which should happen any day now as the water continues to warm. The blackfish bite should also start to pick up around the deeper structure as we head into July.

If you haven't been out to Jamaica Bay lately, this is your week. The fishing is as good as it gets for this time of year, and with multiple species cooperating, you're almost guaranteed to bend a rod. Just remember — the bay is alive right now, so fish it like it is.

reports.headline: Race and Gut bass smash swim shads as 68-degree water stacks bait
reports.subhead: Big stripers crush butterfish and squid in the rips while bluefish wreck everything else.
reports.body_markdown:
The eastern Sound is absolutely on fire right now, and it's all about water temperature and bait positioning. We hit 68 degrees this week — that magic number that turns The Race and Plum Gut from decent fishing into a feeding frenzy. The thermocline is setting up perfectly at 45 feet, stacking butterfish and squid against the structure, and the bass are responding like they should.

I've been running three-way rigs with 8-ounce cannonballs and 80-pound leaders to keep the presentations clean in the screaming current. But here's the kicker — swim shads are absolutely destroying bucktails on size. I'm talking 7-inch Tsunami swim shads producing multiple overslot bass while the same bucktail that usually crushes them is only pulling slot fish. The bigger profile in that heavy current is triggering the gorilla bass that are keyed on the thick butterfish schools.

The Race has been the star performer. Water's running 3 to 4 knots on the big moon tides, and you need to time it right. I'm fishing the last two hours of the ebb when the rip stands up but isn't completely evil. The bass are stacked from 80 feet down to 40 feet across the main structure, and they're aggressive. Had seven bass to 37 inches yesterday morning, kept one slot fish and released the rest. The key is following that bottom contour and taking preemptive cranks as you drift from deep to shallow — lose contact with bottom in that current and you're done.

Plum Gut is producing similar action but with more boat pressure. The flood tide has been better there, especially the first hour when the current starts pushing but hasn't reached full scream. Same rig setup — heavy three-way with that stiff 80-pound leader to stand the bait off bottom. The bluefish have moved in too, and they're wrecking expensive lures. Use wire or heavy fluorocarbon if you're throwing plugs.

Bait situation is interesting. The butterfish showed up early this year, which is unusual, and they're thick in the 40 to 60-foot zone. Squid are scattered through the eastern Sound, particularly around Fishers Island and moving into the rips. The bass are feeding heavily on both, which explains why the bigger swim shads are outproducing traditional bucktails — they match the butterfish profile perfectly.

Current speed is critical. When it's ripping at 4-plus knots, the fishing shuts down. But in that 2 to 3-knot sweet spot, the bass feed aggressively. I'm using the double-drop method — hit bottom, crank twice, drop again to remove the belly, then work the bait. The Humminbird is showing fish marks consistently, and when you see them stacked on the screen, drop fast and get ready.

Weakfish are starting to show in the mix too. Nothing huge yet, but a few 16 to 18-inch fish are coming over the rail with the bass. They're hitting the same presentations, just lighter bites.

Sea bass action has been solid in the deeper structure around Fishers Island. The 55-foot drops are holding good numbers, though you're sorting through plenty of shorts to find keepers. Bucktails and jigs in the 3 to 6-ounce range are getting it done.

Looking ahead, we've got a new moon Friday which means spring tides and serious current. The Race will be unfishable at peak flow, but the edges and the slack periods should be dynamite. That new moon will also push more bait out of the back bays, and I expect the bass fishing to get even better. Water temps should hold in the mid to upper 60s, keeping that thermocline tight and the bait concentrated.

The eastern Sound is fishing as well as I've seen it in years. Get out there with heavy tackle, swim shads, and patience for the current. When it all comes together, you'll understand why we put up with the boat traffic and the challenging conditions.

reports.headline: Bass crash the Stratford Shoal rip as Sound water hits perfect 68 degrees
reports.subhead: New moon spring tides are flushing bait through the narrows and stacking stripers on the edges.
reports.body_markdown:
The Central Sound is firing right now, and it all comes down to that magic number: 68 degrees. The buoys are telling the story I've been waiting for all month — water temps have settled into that sweet spot where everything clicks. From the Norwalk Islands to Port Jeff, the thermometer is reading 68 to 68.2, and the fish are responding like clockwork.

I've been watching the Stratford Shoal rip closely this week, and it's become a striper magnet. The new moon on Friday is pushing serious water through the narrows, creating those current seams that concentrate bait and trigger feeding. White bucktails in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range are absolutely crushing it on the edges of the rip. Cast up-current, let it sink to the bottom, then work it back with slow lifts and drops. The bass are sitting in 25 to 35 feet, facing into the flow and ambushing anything that drifts down.

The key is positioning yourself correctly relative to the current. These spring tides are moving water fast — sometimes too fast for lighter jigs to maintain bottom contact. When the current's screaming, bump up to that 2-ounce bucktail and add a strip of silver Mylar for extra flash. The fish are eating on the fall, so keep that bottom contact and feel for the tick.

Across the Sound, the Middle Ground Light area has been producing steady action on fluke. The 4-foot drop from the shallow bar into 25 feet is holding fish, and they're responding to pink and white Gulp trailers on 3/4-ounce bucktails. The triangle method is working perfectly here — I'm rotating between three connected spots when one goes quiet. First drift tells you everything you need to know about whether fish are present.

What's really got me excited is the bait situation. Spearing are thick along the Connecticut shoreline, and I'm seeing good marks of bunker moving through the shipping channels. The larger bunker are pushing into deeper water as the Sound warms, which explains why the bass fishing has been so consistent in that 25 to 35-foot zone around structure.

The Norwalk Islands circuit is producing mixed bags of bass and blues on the rocky edges. Seven-inch white pencil poppers are working the early morning bite when the water's calm, but once the sun gets up, switch to bucktails and work the current breaks around the islands. The fish are holding tight to structure, so get your lures close to the rocks.

Port Jefferson Harbor has been a sleeper spot this week. The ferry terminal area in deeper water is holding fish, and the slightly green tint to the water tells me the bait is moving and the fish are paying attention. Live peanut bunker on fishfinder rigs are producing when worked tight to the pilings on the outgoing tide.

Looking at the conditions, this new moon period is setting up perfectly. These spring tides are going to flush massive amounts of bait out of the harbors and bays, creating feeding opportunities throughout the Sound. The strong currents can be challenging, but that's when the fish really get aggressive on the baitfish that lose control in the flow.

The weather pattern looks stable through the weekend with light winds, which means you can work the rips effectively without getting beat up. Water temps should hold steady in that productive 68-degree range, keeping the fish active and feeding.

For the week ahead, I'm watching for the tide changes around the full moon. These big water movements are going to concentrate bait and create those feeding windows where everything happens at once. Focus on the current edges, keep your bucktails in contact with the bottom, and be ready to move when the action shifts. The Central Sound is in prime time right now.

reports.headline: Gator blues crash the Sound as bass push deep on 70-degree water
reports.subhead: Big bluefish blitzing bait while stripers retreat to structure in warming Western Sound.
reports.body_markdown:
The Western Sound is telling two stories right now, and both of them are worth listening to. Water temps have climbed past the 68-degree mark — I'm seeing 68.2 at the nearshore buoys and pushing 70 in the back bays — and that's changing the game completely from what we had just two weeks ago.

The big news is the bluefish invasion. These aren't cocktail blues, either. I'm talking about legitimate gator blues, 8 to 14 pounds, that are absolutely demolishing bait schools from Throgs Neck to Matinecock Point. They showed up hard this past weekend and haven't let up. The pattern is classic mid-Sound structure fishing — they're holding on the deeper edges of the reefs and rockpiles, then charging up to crash whatever bait gets pushed their way by the tide.

Execution Rocks has been the epicenter. Fish the outgoing tide from two hours after high through the bottom of the ebb. The blues are staging in 35 to 45 feet on the south side of the rocks, then moving up to the 20-foot contour when the current really starts ripping. Large Mojos trolled at 3.5 knots are absolutely deadly — chartreuse and white, blue and white, anything with flash. If you want to cast, 2-ounce Crippled Herring or Deadly Dicks in bunker patterns will get crushed when you find the schools.

The Stepping Stones area is producing similar action, especially on the flood tide when bait gets funneled through the gap. I've been working the 25 to 35-foot zone with bucktails — 1-ounce white with chartreuse teasers — and the blues are absolutely slamming them. The key is matching the current speed. When it's really ripping, go heavier. When it slacks off, drop down to 3/4-ounce and work it slower.

Now, the striped bass story is more complicated. The warming water has pushed most of the fish deeper and tighter to structure. The schoolies that were all over the shallows in May are mostly gone, but the bigger fish — the 30 to 40-inch class — are still around if you know where to look. They've moved to the deeper channel edges and are much more selective about when they feed.

I had a charter out Sunday morning that perfectly illustrated this. We marked fish in 45 feet along the Matinecock drop-off, but they wouldn't touch anything we threw at them during the slack water. Once the outgoing tide started pulling and we had some current moving through, we connected on three fish between 32 and 38 inches. All came on live peanut bunker fished on fishfinder rigs, tight to the bottom.

The bunker situation is interesting. We don't have the massive schools you'd normally expect for late June, but there are pockets of adult bunker scattered throughout the Sound. The fish that are around are good-sized — 8 to 10 inches — and the bass are definitely keyed in on them. If you can find fresh bunker, either live-lined or chunked, you're in business.

Little Neck Bay and Manhasset Bay are both showing signs of the summer transition. Water temps in the back reaches are hitting 70 degrees, which is pushing the bass toward the mouths of the bays where they can find cooler, more oxygenated water. The grass shrimp hatch is in full swing, and that's drawing fluke into the shallower areas. I'm seeing decent fluke action on 3/4-ounce bucktails with white Gulp Swimming Mullets, especially around the channel edges where the grass beds drop into deeper water.

The porgy bite has been steady around any hard structure. Hart Island, the Throgs Neck Bridge pilings, even the dock lines in the harbors are holding fish. Standard high-low rigs with clam or sandworms are producing keeper-sized fish, though you'll have to sort through plenty of shorts.

Looking ahead, this new moon cycle should really get things moving. We're looking at spring tides through the weekend, which means big water movement and better feeding opportunities. The blues should continue their rampage as long as the bait holds, and I expect the bass fishing to improve as the stronger currents get them more active.

The key for the coming week is adjusting your tactics for the warmer water. Fish deeper, fish the current, and don't waste time in the back bays unless you're targeting fluke or porgies. The Sound is transitioning into its summer pattern, and the fish that are here are quality fish — you just have to work a little harder to find them.

reports.headline: Giant bluefin crash the Hudson as 68-degree water sets up the canyon edge
reports.subhead: Jigs and stickbaits producing trophy fish as thermocline stacks bait at 75 feet.
reports.body_markdown:
The Hudson Canyon is firing on all cylinders right now, and the water temperature readings tell the whole story. We're seeing 68.2 degrees at the 44025 buoy — that's the sweet spot that pulls bluefin up from the depths and concentrates them along the thermocline.

The action has been nothing short of spectacular. Giant bluefin are stacked at 75 feet, right where the temperature break sets up, and they're absolutely crushing jigs and stickbaits. I've been working the 100-fathom line hard, and the fish are responding to vertical presentations better than anything else. A 280-gram jig with a beefed-up hook has been money — bounce it off the bottom and work it slow through the water column. When they're tight to structure like this, that's where the heavy metal shines.

The stickbait bite has been equally impressive. When you see bunker getting pushed up by the current along the canyon wall, throw the biggest stickbait you've got. These fish are wanting it worked down and dirty — no finesse required. The UVT stickbaits have been producing fish that are damn near backflipping on the hookset.

What's really interesting is how the fish are positioning themselves. They're not showing on top like we sometimes see in the summer blitzes. Instead, they're hugging that thermocline at 75 feet, maybe 5 feet off the bottom in some spots. The 68-degree surface water is creating a perfect temperature gradient that's concentrating bait, and the bluefin are taking full advantage.

The trolling fleet has been getting their shots too, but the jig and stickbait guys are really cleaning up. There's something about working a lure vertically through that temperature break that these fish can't resist. I've been running 35 pounds of drag on the reel — these are serious fish that require serious pressure.

The Claw has been particularly productive, especially on the tide changes. That structure creates an upwelling that pushes bait right into the strike zone, and the bluefin are positioned perfectly to ambush anything that comes through. The current has been running clean at 2-3 knots — perfect for maintaining bottom contact with your jigs while still getting good action.

Looking at the broader picture, we've got light winds out of the northwest at 6 knots, and the sea state is nearly flat at 1 foot. These are ideal conditions for precision fishing, and it's showing in the catch rates. The barometric pressure is holding steady at 1012 millibars — no major weather systems to disrupt the bite.

The key has been reading the electronics and putting your lure right where the fish are marking. When you see those thick marks at 75 feet, that's your target zone. Don't waste time fishing water — get your jig down to where the fish are living and work it through their wheelhouse.

For the week ahead, I'm watching the moon phase closely. We're approaching a new moon, which typically means weaker tides but more stable conditions. The fish should continue to hold on that thermocline as long as the water temperature stays in this 68-degree range. If we see any significant warming, expect the fish to slide deeper, but right now they're positioned perfectly for the vertical bite.

The Texas Tower area has also been producing, particularly on the eastern edge where the current creates a natural feeding lane. The fish are using that structure to ambush bait, and a well-placed jig or stickbait in that zone has been getting crushed.

This is exactly the kind of fishing that makes the Hudson Canyon legendary. When conditions align like this — perfect water temperature, clean current, and concentrated bait — the fishing can be absolutely phenomenal. Get out there and get your shots while this bite lasts.

reports.headline: Trophy bass crash the Southwest Ledge as 68-degree water stacks bait
reports.subhead: Flutter spoons and bucktails producing keeper stripers to 40 inches in the thermal break.
reports.body_markdown:
The summer migration has officially arrived at Block Island, and the Southwest Ledge is firing like I haven't seen in years. Water temps hit 68 degrees this week — that magic number that pulls trophy bass from hundreds of miles away to our cool, oxygenated water. The thermal gradient between the 68-degree inshore water and the 63-degree offshore readings is creating a perfect feeding zone along the ledge structure.

I've been working the Southwest Ledge at first light, and the action has been consistent for keeper bass in the 28 to 40-inch range. Flutter spoons are absolutely deadly when you find fish marked on the finder. Drop them right into the schools and let them fall through the water column — the bass are hitting them on the flutter down, usually around 30 to 45 feet. White and chartreuse patterns are producing best, with the 3-ounce models getting down fast enough in the current.

Bucktails are also putting fish in the boat, especially when trolled along the structure breaks. I'm running 1-ounce white bucktails with 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets, keeping them just off the bottom in 35 to 50 feet of water. The key is that slow, steady retrieve that mimics the sand eels and peanut bunker that are thick along the ledge right now.

The North Rip has been producing as well, though the fish seem more spread out there. I pulled a solid 35-incher yesterday morning on a three-way rig with a 4-inch chartreuse grub, fishing the incoming tide as it swept bait up against the structure. The current was moderate — perfect for keeping your presentation in the zone without losing too much tackle to the bottom.

What's really encouraging is the size of these fish. These aren't schoolies — they're mature bass that have made the journey here for the summer feeding. The 68-degree water is holding massive schools of bait, from sand eels to juvenile scup, and the bass are taking full advantage. I'm seeing thick marks on the finder from 25 feet down to the bottom in 60 feet of water.

The bonito showed up this week too, which is always a good sign. First ones I've seen this season, hitting small metals and bucktails in the same areas where the bass are feeding. They're not thick yet, but their presence means the water quality is prime and more species will follow.

Tide timing has been crucial. The best action is coming on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing. The moderate current is keeping bait positioned along the structure without creating the washing machine effect you get during the big spring tides. We're coming off a new moon, so the tides are starting to build again — perfect timing for the weekend.

The wind has been cooperative this week, mostly light northwest to west at 5 to 7 knots. That's kept the seas manageable and allowed for precise boat positioning over the structure. The high pressure system sitting over us has created stable conditions, and the fish have responded accordingly.

Looking ahead, I'm watching for the full moon on Friday to really fire things up. Those big tides will flush more bait out of Narragansett Bay and concentrate it along our structure. The Southwest Ledge should be prime real estate, especially on the outgoing water when all that bay bait gets swept past the island. I'm planning to be there at sunset Friday — that's when the magic usually happens during the full moon cycle.

The water clarity has been excellent, gin-clear in most spots, which means lighter leaders and more natural presentations. I'm running 20-pound fluorocarbon leaders instead of my usual 30, and it's making a difference in the number of strikes. These bass have seen plenty of lures by now, so the subtle approach is paying off.

This is exactly what we wait for all year — prime summer conditions with trophy bass feeding aggressively in our backyard. The migration is in full swing, and Block Island is living up to its reputation as the striped bass capital of the East Coast.

reports.headline: Jumbo blues crash Jersey jetties as bay water hits 68 degrees
reports.subhead: Raritan Bay stripers still feeding on bunker while fluke action picks up in the inlets.
reports.body_markdown:
The water finally warmed up enough to flip the switch on our summer bite, and man, did it flip hard this week. Bay temps hit 68 degrees — a solid four-degree jump from the ocean side — and that thermal gradient is stacking bait like crazy on every flood tide. The result? Some of the best mixed-bag action I've seen in years.

The big story is jumbo bluefish returning to Monmouth County waters in force. These aren't your typical snapper blues — we're talking 8 to 12-pound choppers that'll test your drag and your wire leader. I've been finding them crashing bait off the jetties from Sandy Hook down to Manasquan, especially on the outgoing tide when bunker get flushed out of the bay. White metals and large spoons are absolutely crushing them, but you better have 40-pound wire because these fish are slicing through everything else.

The jetty bite has been phenomenal for mixed species. Small fluke are everywhere in the inlet mouths — mostly shorts, but there are some keepers mixed in if you work the deeper holes on the drift. Three-eighths-ounce jig heads with white Gulp Swimming Mullets are the ticket, dragged slow along the bottom on the last two hours of incoming water. The key is finding that sweet spot where the current creates an eddy behind the rocks.

Raritan Bay is still holding stripers, and the bunker schools are thick as thieves. These aren't the monster spring fish, but solid 24 to 32-inch bass that'll bend your rod and put up a real fight. Live bunker on a fishfinder rig is money, especially around the Raritan Bay Bridge pilings on the outgoing tide. The bass are using the current to ambush bait getting swept out of the shallows.

What's really got me excited is the water clarity. After weeks of dirty water from all that southwest wind, we finally got a few days of northwest breeze that cleaned things up. You can actually see bottom in 8 feet of water, which means the fluke are more aggressive and the bass are more willing to chase lures.

The thermocline is setting up beautifully offshore. Surface temps are running 68 to 70 degrees, but there's a sharp drop to 58-degree water at about 45 feet. That temperature break is holding bait, and where there's bait, there's fish. I'm hearing reports of thresher sharks working the nearshore waters, which makes sense with all this bait around.

Moon phase is working in our favor too. We're coming off a new moon, so the spring tides are really moving water through the inlets. That current is key for everything we're targeting — it positions the bait, triggers feeding, and gives us those defined bite windows.

Looking ahead, I'm watching the full moon on Friday. Those big tides are going to really flush the inlets, and I expect the first real push of weakfish to show up. The water temp is right, the bait is there, and those lunar tides should trigger some serious feeding. I'll be working the inlet mouths at sunset with bucktails and soft plastics, looking for that telltale weakfish bite.

The Cape May area is also starting to fire up. Water temps down south are running a few degrees warmer, and the fluke bite is more consistent. If you're willing to make the run, the back bays around Great Bay are holding some real doormats.

Bottom line: this is prime time Jersey fishing. The water's warm, the bait's thick, and the fish are feeding. Whether you're working the jetties for blues, drifting the inlets for fluke, or live-lining bunker for stripers in the bay, there's something biting. Just make sure your tackle is up to the task — these fish are healthy and hungry.

reports.headline: Sound shore bass turn on as water hits 68 — Plum Gut pushing bait west
reports.subhead: Schoolies thick from Mattituck to Rocky Point as thermal break stacks bunker on the flood.
reports.body_markdown:
Water hit 68 degrees this week and the Sound shore woke up. Been fishing these beaches sixty years and I can tell you — when that thermometer climbs past 67, the bass start moving serious. Saw it happen Tuesday morning, dead calm conditions with light northwest wind, and suddenly the schoolies were everywhere from Mattituck Inlet clear east to Rocky Point.

The action's been best on the flood tide, first two hours after the turn. Water's been clean, that pale green you want to see, and the bait's stacked thick along the drop-off. Mostly peanut bunker with some spearing mixed in. Bass are feeding aggressive — not the lazy spring picking we had in May. These fish want to eat.

Best fishing's been bucktails with white Gulp Swimming Mullets, 3/4-ounce heads in the 15 to 25-foot range. Drag them slow on the drift, let the current do the work. Had good luck with chartreuse too when the water's got a little color to it. The key's been staying mobile — fish a spot for twenty minutes, if nothing's happening, move on. They're schooled up but they're moving.

Horton Point's been producing steady bass in the 24 to 30-inch range. Nothing huge, but good action if you time it right. The rocky structure there holds bait on the slack water, and when the current picks up, the bass move in to feed. Been using fishfinder rigs with fresh bunker chunks, 3/0 circle hooks, fishing right on the bottom. The bite's been best hour before peak flood.

Plum Gut's been interesting this week. The Race is running hard with these spring tides — we're coming off the new moon — and it's pushing a lot of bait west into the Sound. Been seeing good marks on the fish finder along the Orient Point approach, but you need to know that water. Current runs six knots on the peak, and if you're not positioned right, you'll spend more time fighting the drift than fishing.

Porgy fishing's been solid too, especially around the oyster cages east of Rocky Point. Water's warm enough now that they're feeding regular. Small pieces of clam on high-low rigs, size 4 hooks, fish it on the anchor. Nothing fancy, but steady action. Seeing fish in the 12 to 14-inch range, good eating size.

Weakfish showed up this week for the first time since early May. Not thick, but they're around. Caught three Tuesday evening on small bucktails with pink Gulp, fishing the edges of the eelgrass beds on the outgoing tide. These are the early scouts — if the pattern holds, we should see more as the water warms another degree or two.

Bluefish have been scarce, which is fine by me. Rather have bass anyway. Saw a few small ones mixed in with the schoolies, but nothing worth targeting. They'll show up when they show up.

Looking ahead, we've got a full moon coming Friday, which means big tides all weekend. That's going to flush a lot of bait out of the bays and harbors, and the bass know it. I'm watching the inlet mouths at sunset — that's when the real action usually starts. Water temperature's climbing steady, should hit 70 by the weekend if this weather holds.

The northwest wind pattern we've had all week is breaking down. Forecast shows southwest winds picking up Thursday, which could dirty up the water some, but it might also push more bait inshore. Either way, the fish are here now, and they're feeding. Just need to be in the right place when the tide turns.

reports.headline: Peconic bass bite fires as bay water hits 72 degrees
reports.subhead: Slot stripers crash bucktails on the flood while porgies stack thick around Shelter Island.
reports.body_markdown:
The Peconic finally woke up this week. Bay water spiked to 72 degrees — a full 8 degrees warmer than the ocean side — and that thermal gradient is doing exactly what it should: stacking bait on the flood and holding bass on the ebb.

Slot stripers are hitting bucktails hard around the usual suspects. The flood tide through Plum Gut has been money, especially that last hour before slack. White and chartreuse 1-ounce bucktails tipped with 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets are getting crushed in 25 to 35 feet. The key is staying tight to the bottom on the drift — these fish are hugging structure as the current pushes bunker through the channel.

What's interesting is the bite timing. With the new moon behind us, we're seeing more consistent action through the tide cycle rather than those brief feeding windows we had during the spring tides. The bass seem more settled, less spooky. I'm marking good numbers of fish holding in 20 to 30 feet around the channel edges, and they're feeding aggressively when you put the right presentation in front of them.

The porgy bite around Shelter Island remains world-class, though it's shifted slightly deeper as the water warmed. The 35 to 45-foot drops are holding the biggest fish — true jumbos pushing 3 pounds. Clam chum is still king, but you need to be patient. Give it 20 minutes to work, then expect steady action for the next two hours. High-low rigs with size 2 hooks and fresh clam are all you need. The bite has been best on the last two hours of the outgoing, when the current slows and the fish can settle on the bottom.

Weakfish are showing in better numbers than we've seen in years. Three Mile Harbor and the deeper holes in Noyack Bay are producing fish to 4 pounds. The trick is finding the right depth — they're suspended in that 15 to 20-foot zone, right above the thermocline. Small bucktails with white or pink teasers, worked slowly through the water column, are getting bit. The early morning bite has been strongest, especially on the incoming tide when bait gets pushed into the back bays.

Fluke fishing picked up considerably as the bay water warmed. The channel edges between Shelter Island and Greenport are holding keeper fish to 6 pounds. Drift the 25 to 35-foot contours with white Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails. The key is covering water — these fish are scattered, but when you find them, they're hungry. Outgoing tide has been most productive, especially when the current creates that perfect drift speed.

Bait situation is excellent. Bunker schools are thick throughout the bay system, and the bass are keyed in on them. Sand eels are showing in good numbers around the deeper structure, which explains why the bucktail bite has been so consistent. Spearing are thick in the shallows, drawing weakfish and small blues into the back bays.

Looking ahead, this warming trend should continue the bass bite. With water temperatures now in the low 70s, we're entering that sweet spot where the Peconic really shines. The full moon on Friday will bring bigger tides — I'm watching for that evening drain through the inlet to fire up the first real weakfish push of the season. Those spring tides should also concentrate bait in the channels, setting up what could be an epic weekend for anyone willing to work the moving water.

The bay is fishing like it should in late June. Get out there.

reports.headline: Montauk bass bite fires as water temps hit 68 degrees at the Point
reports.subhead: Eels after dark producing 40-pound class stripers while diamond jigs work the rips.
reports.body_markdown:
The Point is absolutely on fire right now, and it's all about the water temperature finally hitting that magic 68-degree mark. After weeks of cooler water holding fish back, we've got the thermal conditions that make Montauk the striper capital of the world.

The big bass are here in numbers I haven't seen this early in the season for years. We're talking legitimate 40-pound class fish coming over the rail after sunset on live eels fished tight to the boulder fields. The technique is classic Montauk — fishfinder rig with a 6/0 circle hook, just enough weight to get down, and let that eel work in the current along the rocks. The key is fishing the last two hours of the outgoing tide when the water really starts to move.

Diamond jigs are absolutely crushing it in the rips during the day. Two to four-ounce AVA 007s in white or chartreuse, worked fast through the water column, are producing steady action with bass in the 20 to 30-pound range. The technique that's working is dropping to the bottom, then working the jig with sharp lifts about three feet off the deck. Don't let it hit bottom again — that's where you lose them.

The water clarity has been exceptional, which is why the bucktail bite has been so consistent. One-ounce white bucktails tipped with Uncle Josh pork rind or a 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet are working the structure perfectly. Fish them slow along the bottom, especially around the North Bar on the incoming tide.

What's really driving this bite is the bait situation. Sand eels are thick throughout the area, and that's what these bass are keyed in on. The squid that pushed through a few weeks back have settled into their summer pattern, but it's the sand eels that are keeping fish in the area. Bunker are still scarce, which is actually working in our favor — when bass don't have those big easy meals, they stay aggressive on smaller baits.

The fluke fishing has been a pleasant surprise. The south side drops in 30 to 40 feet are producing steady action with fish to six pounds. White Gulp on chartreuse bucktails, dragged slow on the drift, is the go-to rig. The key is fishing the edges where the current creates those little eddies — that's where the fluke are ambushing bait.

Porgies are showing up in good numbers around the rocky structure, though they're not everywhere like they used to be. Green crabs on high-low rigs in 20 to 35 feet are producing steady action, with some nice fish in the two-pound range.

The bluefish situation is interesting — we're seeing those chunky little cocktail blues in the one to two-pound range, which is always a great sign for the overall health of the fishery. They're hitting small metals and bucktails, and they're a blast on light tackle.

Conditions this week have been nearly perfect. Light winds, clean water, and that 68-degree temperature reading is exactly what we want to see. The new moon earlier this week spread fish out a bit, but now that we're building toward the full moon Friday, expect those big tides to really get things moving.

Looking ahead, this full moon is going to create some serious current flow. I'm watching for the inlet to really drain at sunset — that's when we might see the first real push of weakfish. The water temperature is right, the bait is there, and those big tides should trigger some serious feeding activity. If you're planning to fish the Point this weekend, focus on the last two hours of the outgoing tide with live eels, and don't overlook the incoming tide around the North Bar with bucktails. This is shaping up to be one of those classic Montauk summers.

reports.headline: Blues blitz the inlet as bay water hits 68 — night bass bite fires on the ebb
reports.subhead: Crystal clear conditions and perfect outgoing tides stack stripers on the south jetty after dark.
reports.body_markdown:
The inlet has been absolutely electric this week, and I'm talking about the kind of fishing that makes you forget about sleep. Water temps hit 68 degrees in the bay — a solid four-degree jump from the ocean side — and that thermal gradient is doing exactly what it should: stacking bait on the flood and holding bass on the ebb.

The bluefish showed up first, and when I say showed up, I mean they arrived like a freight train. We're talking 10 to 15-pound choppers crushing everything from 5-inch Mag Darters to bucktails with Zoom fork tails. The key has been fishing the incoming tide when the blues are blitzing, then switching tactics once they move through. I've been running 50-pound fluoro leaders — learned that lesson the hard way after losing three lures in one session.

But here's where it gets interesting for us night owls. Once the blues clear out and the tide turns, the stripers move in like clockwork. I'm talking about clean, fat bass in the 15 to 25-pound range holding tight to the south jetty structure on the outgoing water. The crystal-clear conditions we've had — that blue-green tropical look — means these fish are spooky as hell during daylight. But come sunset, it's a different story.

My go-to setup has been a 3/4-ounce white bucktail with a chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet trailer, worked with a pop-pop-pause retrieve right in the rip. You need to get on one side or the other of the structure to punch through that current — trying to fish straight down the middle is a waste of time. The fish are hitting far out in the wash, not tight to the rocks like you'd expect.

The Ponquogue Bridge has been producing weakfish on the night tides, especially around the new moon we just had. Those spring tides are flushing serious amounts of bait out of the back bay, and the weakies are stacked up waiting for the buffet. Peanut bunker on fishfinder rigs, fished tight to the pilings on the outgoing, has been money. Nothing huge — mostly 14 to 18-inchers — but consistent action if you can handle the boat traffic.

Fluke fishing in the bay proper has been solid, with keepers coming from the usual suspects: the channel edges in 15 to 20 feet, drifting white Gulp and chartreuse bucktails. The warmer bay water has these fish active and feeding, though you're still sorting through plenty of shorts to find the keepers.

What's really got my attention is how clean these inlet stripers are looking. No parasites, bright silver sides, thick shoulders — these are ocean fish that just moved in with the bait, not residents that have been sitting in the bay all season. That tells me we're in the early stages of what could be a serious summer run.

The weather pattern looks stable for the next week, with light winds and continued warm nights. That 68-degree bay water should hold, maybe even climb another degree or two, which will only improve the bait situation. I'm watching for the full moon Friday — those big tides always shake things up, and I've got a feeling we're about to see the first real push of weakfish through the inlet.

For the weekend warriors, focus on the last two hours of the outgoing tide, especially after 9 PM. The inlet gets busy during the day, but once the sun drops and the boat traffic dies down, it's a different world out there. Just remember to bring a good light and watch your footing on those jetty rocks — the fishing's been too good to risk a stupid accident.

reports.headline: Moriches Inlet fires as 68-degree water stacks bait on the flood
reports.subhead: Trophy stripers crash live spot at night while fluke fishing heats up in the skinny water.
reports.body_markdown:
The inlet's been absolutely electric this week, and the numbers tell the story. Water temps hit 68.2 degrees on the ocean side while the bay's running a solid 4 degrees warmer — that thermal gradient is what's been stacking bait on every flood tide and holding bass through the ebb. When you've got that kind of temperature differential, the inlet becomes a funnel, and right now it's funneling everything from peanut bunker to spot right into the waiting mouths of some serious stripers.

Night fishing has been the ticket for trophy bass. Live spot on fishfinder rigs, dropped tight to the inlet's north jetty on the incoming water, has been producing fish in the 30-pound class. The key is getting that bait down into the 15-foot hole that forms on the flood — that's where the big girls are sitting, waiting for the current to deliver dinner. I've been running 30-pound fluorocarbon leaders with 6/0 circle hooks, letting the spot swim naturally in the current. The bite window is tight — usually the hour before and after slack high — but when it happens, it's violent.

The inlet's bathymetry has shifted again after last month's nor'easter, and the new channel cut is holding fish differently than it did in May. The main flow now runs closer to the south side, which means the traditional north jetty spots aren't producing like they used to. Instead, I'm finding bass staged along the new drop-off that runs from the inlet mouth southeast toward the first channel marker. It's a subtle change — maybe 3 feet of depth difference — but it's enough to redirect the entire food chain.

Fluke fishing in the bay has turned the corner this week. The skinny water bite is on fire, with fish to 6 pounds coming from 6 to 10 feet of water along the channel edges. The secret has been downsizing everything — 1/4-ounce bucktails with 3-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets, dragged painfully slow on the drift. In water this shallow, presentation is everything. I'm using 15-pound braid straight to a 20-pound fluorocarbon leader, no swivel, no hardware that might spook fish in gin-clear water.

The Tuthill Point area has been particularly productive for doormat fluke. There's a subtle depression that runs parallel to the channel, about 200 yards east of the point, where the bottom drops from 8 to 12 feet. It's not much, but it's enough to hold bait and concentrate fish. I've been anchoring uptide and casting into the hole, letting the bucktail tick bottom as it swings in the current. The takes are subtle — often just a slight heaviness on the line — but the fish have been quality.

Bait has been the story this week. Massive schools of peanut bunker have moved into the bay, pushed by the warming water and spring tides. They're thick from the inlet all the way back to the Forge River, and everywhere you find bunker, you find bass. The fish are feeding aggressively, but they're also spooky. Approach these schools wrong — too fast, too loud — and they'll disappear like smoke.

Cupsogue Beach has been producing consistent action for surf casters working the dawn and dusk bites. Clam rigs fished in the wash have been taking keeper fluke, while fresh bunker chunks on fishfinder rigs are drawing bass after dark. The key has been reading the structure — there's a subtle bar that runs parallel to the beach about 80 yards out, and that's where the fish are staging.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the new moon on Friday, which means big spring tides and maximum current flow. That's when the inlet really comes alive. I'm expecting the bass bite to intensify as the stronger currents flush more bait out of the back bay. The fluke fishing should remain strong as long as water temps stay stable — any sudden warming could push fish deeper or scatter them entirely.

The weekend forecast shows light northwest winds and calm seas, perfect conditions for working the inlet at night or drifting the bay's skinny water for fluke. With bait this thick and water conditions this good, it's shaping up to be one of those magical late June periods when everything comes together in Moriches Bay.

reports.headline: Weakfish surge hits Jones Inlet as bay water climbs to 68 degrees
reports.subhead: Trophy weaks return to the inlet while fluke fishing stays steady on the drift.
reports.body_markdown:
The water's telling a story this week, and it's one I haven't heard in years. Bay temperatures hit 68 degrees — a solid four degrees warmer than the ocean side — and that thermal gradient is doing exactly what it's supposed to do. It's stacking bait on the flood tide and holding weakfish on the ebb, just like the old days.

I've been watching this setup develop all month. The inlet's been flushing clean with these new moon spring tides, and now we're seeing the payoff. Weakfish to 26 inches are showing in the surf at night, and I'm hearing about fish in the 6-pound class coming from the inlet mouth on the outgoing water. These aren't the schoolie weaks we've been getting used to — these are the real deal, the fish that made this inlet famous back when my father was teaching me to read the current.

The pattern's been consistent: hit the inlet on the start of the ebb with fresh bunker chunks or live peanuts on a fishfinder rig. The fish are holding in the deeper cuts where the current sweeps bait out of the bay. I've been working the north side of the channel, tight to the jetty rocks, and the takes are solid — none of that tentative pecking you get from schoolies.

Fluke fishing's been steady but not spectacular. The Meadowbrook drift is producing keeper-sized fish to 20 inches, but you're working for them. White bucktails with squid strips on the bottom, chartreuse teaser up top, and you need to stay mobile. The fish are scattered, not packed up like they'll be in July when the water really heats up.

What's interesting is the bait situation. The inlet's loaded with sand eels right now — thick clouds of them moving on every tide change. That's what's drawing the weakfish in from deeper water, and it's also why the striper bite has been hit-or-miss. When bass are keyed on sand eels, they get selective. Diamond jigs in the 2-ounce range with green tails are taking fish at sunset, but you need to work past the break and into the wash where the eels are getting tumbled.

The Wantagh Bridge area has been producing short fluke consistently, but most are running 15 to 17 inches. Still, it's good action for kids and light tackle. Smelt has been outfishing squid there — hook it behind the head and let it flutter on the drift.

Looking at the water conditions, we're sitting pretty for the next week. Ocean temps are holding in the mid-60s while the bay stays warm, and that temperature break is critical for keeping bait concentrated in the inlet. The southwest winds we've been getting are actually helping — they're pushing warmer surface water into the bay and creating that thermal layering that holds fish.

Full moon's coming Friday, which means big tides and serious water movement. I'm expecting the weakfish bite to really turn on during the evening ebb tides. The inlet will be draining hard, concentrating bait in the channel, and those big weaks will be there to ambush them. This could be the week we've been waiting for — the first real run of quality weakfish in years.

For the weekend warriors, focus on the inlet mouth from sunset through the first two hours of outgoing tide. Fresh bunker chunks on circle hooks, fished on the bottom in 15 to 25 feet. Don't overthink it — these fish want a big meal in moving water. And if you hook into something that feels heavy and fights deep, don't horse it. These weakfish have soft mouths, and we need every one of them to make it back to spawn again.

reports.headline: Bay water hits 69 degrees as weakfish crash the Marine Parkway drift
reports.subhead: Keeper fluke mixing with surprise weakies while bass stage for the summer exodus.
reports.body_markdown:
The bay hit 69 degrees this week, and that magic number flipped a switch. After weeks of chasing scattered bass around the flats, the real action shifted to the Marine Parkway Bridge area where keeper fluke are finally showing in numbers — and they brought friends.

I've been working the drift from the bridge pilings out to the channel edge, and the mix of species has been the best I've seen all season. Keeper fluke to 25 inches are hitting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, but here's the kicker — weakfish are back in the rotation. I'm talking keeper weakies, not the usual runts. The 19-inchers are taking the same rig on the drift, and I had one push 5 pounds that fought like it remembered what these waters used to be like.

The technique is classic drift fishing, but timing matters. I'm hitting the bridge area on the first three hours of incoming tide when the current is moving but not ripping. Too much water and the bucktails get swept away from the structure. Too little and the fish won't commit. That sweet spot when you can feel the jig tick bottom every few seconds — that's when they eat.

Bass are still around, but they're staging for the summer move. The bigger fish — 32 to 36 inches — are holding tight to the deeper channel edges, and they're getting picky. Live eels fished on the bottom during the flood tide are still producing, but the window is narrowing. These fish know summer's coming, and they're not wasting energy on marginal presentations.

The bunker situation is interesting. There's still bait in the bay, but it's thinning out and getting pushed around by the warming water. I'm seeing schools concentrated near the Cross Bay Bridge area on the outgoing, but they're not the thick clouds we had in May. The bass that are still feeding are keying on these scattered pods, so if you're trolling, work the edges where the bait shows on the finder.

Sea robins are everywhere — and I mean everywhere. Some of these things are pushing 2 pounds, which tells me the bottom is loaded with crabs and worms. That's good news for the fluke fishing, but it means you're going to sort through a lot of robins to find the flatfish. Fresh clam strips on a high-low rig will cut through the robin madness better than artificials.

Water clarity has been decent despite the warming trend. That 69-degree reading is about 4 degrees warmer than the ocean side of Rockaway Inlet, and that gradient is creating a thermal barrier that's holding bait and fish in the bay longer than usual. But it won't last. Once we hit consistent 70-plus readings, the bass exodus accelerates.

The weekend warriors have been hitting Breezy Point for cocktail blues and the occasional bass, but the real action is in the bay proper. Canarsie Pier has been producing fluke on the incoming tide, especially early morning before the boat traffic picks up. Standard bucktail and teaser rigs are working, but don't overlook a simple high-low with fresh bait.

Looking ahead, this full moon cycle should push some bigger tides through the inlet, and that usually means a flush of fresh bait and maybe some late-season bass activity. I'm watching for the first real push of summer porgies, which should show up once the water stabilizes in the low 70s. The weakfish bite could be a preview of better things — these fish have been scarce for years, so any sign of a comeback is worth paying attention to.

Fish the tides, watch the water temperature, and don't get locked into one species. This transition period between spring and summer is when Jamaica Bay shows its diversity, but you have to be ready to adapt when the fish tell you what they want.

reports.headline: Race and Gut firing on swim shads as 68-degree water stacks bait
reports.subhead: Big bass crushing butterfish in the rips while bluefish wreck everything else.
reports.body_markdown:
The eastern Sound is absolutely on fire right now, and it's all about reading the thermal breaks. Water temps hit 68 degrees this week — that magic number where everything clicks. The Race and Plum Gut are holding massive concentrations of bass, and they're not messing around with small offerings.

I've been running three-way rigs with 8-ounce cannonballs and 80-pound leaders, but here's the kicker: swim shads are absolutely destroying bucktails for size. Seven-inch Tsunami swim shads on the same three-way setup are pulling overslot fish while bucktails are getting the slot fish. It's not even close. The heavier leader material stands the bait off the bottom better in that screaming current, and the swim shad's profile is triggering the bigger fish.

The Gut's been producing on both flood and ebb, which tells you the bait is stacked thick. I'm seeing butterfish and squid getting hammered in 80 to 40 feet across the main rip. The key is following that bottom contour and taking preemptive cranks as you come up the mountain — these fish are sitting right on the structure, and you need to keep that bait dancing just off the rocks.

But here's your warning: the bluefish have arrived in force, and they're absolute savages. Big gator blues are cutting through everything — topwater plugs, expensive glide baits, you name it. Run wire leaders or kiss your tackle goodbye. I watched three guys lose bucktails in ten minutes before they figured it out.

The Race is producing similar action, especially on the slack tide periods when you can work topwater. Yo-Zuri Hydro Pencils and X-Walks are getting crushed at first light when the current eases up. Once the tide starts ripping, it's back to the three-way rigs and deep presentations.

What's driving this bite is the thermal structure. That 68-degree water is holding against cooler ocean water, creating a perfect feeding zone. The butterfish showed up early this year — usually don't see them thick until July — but they're here now and the bass are locked onto them.

Current's been running 2.5 to 3.5 mph through the Gut, which is perfect for drift fishing but brutal if you're not prepared. Double-drop your rigs to remove line belly, and don't fight the drift — let it carry you through the productive water and reset for another pass.

Fishers Island drops are also holding fish, particularly the deeper structure in 55 to 70 feet. Same three-way approach works, but the fish seem more spread out compared to the concentrated action at the main rips.

Looking ahead, we've got a new moon Friday which means spring tides and serious current. That's going to flush more bait out of the back bays and really fire up the inlet mouths. The thermal gradient should hold with this weather pattern, so expect the Race and Gut to stay hot. Just make sure you've got plenty of terminal tackle — between the structure and those bluefish, you're going to lose some gear.

reports.headline: Spring tides fire the Sound as bass crash bunker pods in 68-degree water
reports.subhead: New moon currents push bait against structure while fluke move shallow on warming bottom.
reports.body_markdown:
The new moon that peaked Friday delivered exactly what I expected — screaming currents that turned the Central Sound into a feeding machine. Water temps hit 68 degrees across my beat, from the Norwalk Islands to Port Jeff, and that magic number has everything switched on.

I've been watching the bunker schools thicken all week, and these spring tides are doing exactly what they're supposed to do — flushing bait out of the harbors and stacking it against the structure where bass wait. The Stratford Shoal rip has been producing consistent fish on the outgoing, especially that last two hours when the current really gets moving. White bucktails in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range are the ticket here — cast up-current, let them sink to the bottom, then work them back with slow lifts. The bass are hitting on the drop, classic ambush behavior when they're positioned on structure facing into the flow.

What's got me excited is how the bait is positioning. The spearing are thick along the Connecticut shoreline from Stamford to New Haven, and I'm seeing good marks on the fishfinder in 25 to 35 feet of water. This is where the fluke action has really turned on. The warming bottom — we're seeing 68 degrees in the shallows versus 64 in deeper water — is pulling flatfish up onto the edges where they're easier to target.

For fluke, I'm running 3/4-ounce white bucktails with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets, dragged slow on the drift. The key is reading the bottom first — use your electronics to find those drop-offs from 15 feet down to 30. That's where they're stacked. The Norwalk Islands have been particularly good, especially the channel edges on the north side where the depth breaks from shallow flats to deeper holes.

The current situation is textbook for this lunar phase. These big spring tides take time to get moving — sometimes an hour after the tide change before you feel real flow — but when they hit, they're screaming. That's when the baitfish lose control and the predators capitalize. I've been timing my trips for that sweet spot two hours into the outgoing when everything lines up.

Porgies are showing up as a bonus, especially around Middle Ground Light where the structure holds them in 30 to 40 feet. Small pieces of clam on high-low rigs are producing nice keepers mixed in with the usual shorts. The bigger porgies seem to move in when the current eases, so don't write off the slack periods entirely.

One pattern I'm tracking closely is how the thermal structure is setting up. That 4-degree gradient between shallow and deep water is creating edges that concentrate bait. The bass are using these temperature breaks like highways, following them as they hunt. When you find 68-degree water next to 64-degree water, that's where you want to focus your efforts.

Looking ahead, we're moving into the heart of summer fishing with water temps climbing toward the 70-degree mark. This should push the bigger bass deeper during the day, making early morning and evening the prime windows. The bunker schools will continue to thicken, and I'm expecting the first real bluefish push any day now. Keep an eye on the bird activity — when you see terns and gulls working, that's your cue to get there fast with topwater plugs or bucktails.

reports.headline: Execution Rocks fires as Western Sound bass hit 50 pounds on outgoing tides
reports.subhead: Trophy stripers stack on the ledges while bunker schools trigger feeding sprees from Throgs Neck to Matinecock.
reports.body_markdown:
The Western Sound is absolutely on fire right now, and I'm telling you this after 30 years of reading these waters — we're in the middle of something special. The bass bite has exploded over the past week, with fish pushing 50 pounds coming off the ledges at Execution Rocks and the Stepping Stones. Water temps have climbed to that magic 68-degree mark, and the bunker schools are finally where they should be for late June.

The standout story is happening at Execution Rocks on the outgoing tide. I've been watching boats work the ledge structure there, and when that water starts moving, it's lights out. The key is positioning yourself over the drop-off in 35 to 45 feet and working large Mojos or bunker spoons through the water column. The morning bite has been slow, but once that afternoon outgoing gets cranking, the bass turn on like someone flipped a switch. We're talking 40-inch-plus fish, with several pushing that magical 50-pound mark.

The technique that's been money is trolling large Mojos — 3 to 4 ounces — over the structure on the outgoing. Keep your speed around 2.5 knots and watch your fishfinder. When you mark fish staged on the ledge, that's when you want to be there. The bass are using that moving water to ambush bait getting swept off the rocks.

Bunker schools have finally moved into the sound proper, and that's changed everything. I'm seeing good concentrations from Matinecock Point all the way west to the Throgs Neck Bridge. The fish are following these schools, and when you find the bait, you find the bass. Live-lining peanut bunker on a fishfinder rig has been deadly, especially around the bridge pilings where the current breaks the schools apart.

The Stepping Stones area has been producing consistent action, particularly on the flood tide when bait gets pushed through the gap. Work the edges where the current creates that seam — that's where the bass set up to feed. Bucktails in the 1 to 2-ounce range tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullets have been taking fish in the 28 to 35-inch range consistently.

Fluke fishing has picked up significantly as bay temperatures climb past the 66-degree mark. The gradient between the cooler sound water and the warming bays is stacking bait on the flood and holding bass on the ebb. I've been finding good fluke action in 25 to 30 feet off the Matinecock area, particularly on white Gulp and chartreuse bucktails dragged slow on the drift.

Porgies have moved into their summer haunts around the rocky structure. The docks and pilings from Little Neck Bay to Hempstead Harbor are holding good numbers of keeper-sized fish. Standard porgy rigs baited with clam are producing, but I've been doing better with small pieces of squid on size 4 hooks.

The water clarity has been excellent, which means the fish can see your presentation clearly — but it also means they can see you. Light leaders are critical right now. I'm running 20-pound fluorocarbon for the bass and dropping down to 15-pound for the fluke.

Looking ahead, we're coming into the new moon on Friday, which means big spring tides and strong currents. That's going to flush even more bait out of the bays and concentrate the feeding. The bass bite should only get better as we move into the weekend. I'm watching for the inlet drains at sunset — that's when the first real push of weakfish typically shows up, and the conditions are setting up perfectly for it.

The Western Sound is fishing as well as I've seen it in years. The combination of proper water temperatures, abundant bait, and strong tidal movement is creating ideal conditions. Get out there while it lasts.

reports.headline: Fluke bite fires as bay water hits 68 degrees — jumbo blues crash the bunker schools
reports.subhead: Late June heat wave stacks bait in the inlets as summer patterns lock in from Sandy Hook to Cape May.
reports.body_markdown:
The water finally woke up this week, and so did the fish. Bay temps spiked to 68 degrees while the ocean side is holding steady at 64 — that 4-degree gradient is pure gold for anyone who knows how to read it. The thermocline set up perfect at 30 feet, and every inlet from Manasquan to Barnegat is stacking bait like a cafeteria line.

Fluke fishing exploded overnight. I'm talking keeper-class fish, not the dinks we've been picking at all month. The Dream Boat Challenge weigh-ins tell the story — 8.95-pound doormat came out of Jersey waters this week, and that's no fluke. The fish are following the sand eels, and those baitfish are concentrated where the temperature breaks are sharpest. One day you're on them, next day they've moved two miles down the beach. That's summer fluke fishing — you chase the bait, not the structure.

Best action is coming on 3/8-ounce jig heads with white Gulp Swimming Mullets, dragged slow on the drift. The key is staying in that 25-to-35-foot zone where the cooler bay water meets the warmer ocean push. Outgoing tide at dawn has been money — that's when the gradient is strongest and the bait gets flushed out of the back bays right into the waiting mouths.

Raritan Bay is absolutely loaded with stripers right now. The bunker schools are so thick you can smell them from shore, and everything with teeth is on them. Forty-inch-plus bass are common, and the bluefin are mixing in too. I'm not kidding — inshore bluefin in Raritan Bay in June. Find the bunker balls and you'll find the circus. Live peanuts on a fishfinder rig, or if you want to have some fun, throw metals at the breaking fish.

The bluefish showed up in force this week, especially along the Monmouth County beaches. These aren't the snappers — we're talking 5-to-7-pound choppers that'll test your drag and your wire leader. They're hitting everything from spoons to poppers, but the real action is on the jigs. One-and-a-half-ounce albie jigs in white or chartreuse, worked fast through the schools.

Manasquan Inlet has been spectacular for squid — yeah, squid in June. The cooler water we had earlier this spring pushed them inshore, and they're still hanging around the mid-range depths. Azori squid jigs are the ticket, and you're getting both bait-sized squid and jumbo calamari. The headboats are running dedicated squid trips, which tells you everything about how good this bite is.

Sea bass season is winding down — we go from 10-fish limits to 1-fish limits starting July 1, so get out there now if you want to fill the freezer. The Axel Carlson reef area has been producing limits of 14-inch-plus fish on clams and jigs. Drop and reel when they're stacked in the water column, but switch to bottom bouncing when they're tight to structure.

Looking ahead, this full moon Friday means spring tides and big water movement. That's going to flush even more bait out of the back bays and fire up the inlet fishing. The weakfish should start showing in the evening outgoing tides — they always follow the big moon phases. Water temps are climbing toward 70, which means the summer patterns are locking in hard. The fluke bite should only get better as more fish push out of the bays toward their offshore summer haunts.

The gradient is everything right now. Find where the bay water meets the ocean water, find where the bait is stacked, and you'll find the fish. It's that simple and that complicated. This is Jersey fishing at its finest — when the water warms up and the bait moves, everything else follows.

reports.headline: Weakfish crash Jamaica Bay as water hits 69 degrees and bunker schools thin
reports.subhead: Keeper weakies mixing with slot fluke and jumbo sea robins on the incoming tide.
reports.body_markdown:
The bay is alive right now, and I mean really alive. Water temps hit 69 degrees this week, and that magic number has flipped a switch. The weakfish have moved in hard — I'm talking keeper-sized fish up to 19 inches, with some pushing over two pounds. This is the Jamaica Bay special we've been waiting for: weakies, keeper fluke, and sea robins the size of small stripers all hitting on the same drift.

I've been working the incoming tide from the Marine Parkway Bridge wall back toward the deeper channels, and the action has been consistent. The weakfish are taking fresh clams and lugworms on simple fishfinder rigs, nothing fancy. Drop it down, let it sit, and when that rod tip starts dancing, set the hook. These fish are feeding aggressively in 12 to 18 feet of water, especially where the current creates those little eddies along the bridge pilings.

The fluke bite has stepped up too. I pulled a solid 25-inch doormat last week on a white bucktail tipped with Gulp, working it slow along the bottom on the drift. The key is staying patient with the retrieve — these bay fluke want that bait crawling, not racing. I'm seeing fish from 16 inches up to that keeper size, with most of the action happening on the first three hours of the incoming.

What's really interesting is how the bait situation has changed. The massive bunker schools that usually pack the bay this time of year are noticeably thinner. I'm still seeing pockets of them, especially near the Cross Bay Bridge on the outgoing, but nothing like the acres of bait we typically have by late June. That might actually be working in our favor — less bait means the fish are more willing to hit our offerings.

The sea robins deserve a mention because they're absolutely massive right now. I'm talking fish that would make you think you hooked a keeper fluke until you see those wing-like fins. They're hitting everything — clams, worms, even bucktails. While they're not target species, they're great indicators that the bottom is active and feeding.

Striped bass are still around but transitioning. The bigger fish are starting to move out as the water warms, but I'm still picking up slot fish in the 28 to 32-inch range, especially on live eels fished tight to structure on the outgoing tide. The Marine Parkway Bridge remains the go-to spot — fish the shadow line on the outgoing, work the pilings on the flood.

Weather has been cooperating with light northwest winds most mornings, keeping the bay relatively calm. That 69-degree water temp is right in the sweet spot for multiple species, and with the new moon approaching this weekend, I expect the tides to really start moving bait around.

Looking ahead, I'm watching for that water to push toward 70 degrees, which should bring even more weakfish into the bay. The full moon tides next week will flush a lot of water through the inlet, and that's when I expect to see the fluke fishing really turn on. If you're planning to hit the bay, focus on the incoming tide, bring plenty of clams and lugworms, and don't be surprised if you end up with the trifecta — weakies, fluke, and maybe a slot bass to round out the day.

reports.headline: Weakfish return to Jones Inlet as bay water hits 68 degrees
reports.subhead: First keeper weakies in years showing at the inlet mouth while fluke fishing picks up steam.
reports.body_markdown:
The water's telling a story this week, and it's one I haven't heard in a long time. Bay temperatures hit 68 degrees — a solid four degrees warmer than the ocean side — and that thermal gradient is doing exactly what it's supposed to do. It's stacking bait on the flood tide and holding predators on the ebb. More importantly, it's brought the first real weakfish bite to Jones Inlet in years.

I'm talking keeper weakfish, not the usual runts. Fish pushing 24 to 26 inches are showing at the inlet mouth on the last two hours of outgoing water. The pattern's simple: fresh bunker chunks on fishfinder rigs, fished tight to the jetty rocks where the current sweeps hard. These fish are feeding in the wash, right where the bay water dumps into the ocean and creates that perfect feeding lane.

The weakfish bite is early morning and late evening — classic low-light pattern. But here's what's interesting: they're not alone. I'm seeing stripers mixed in, good fish too, some pushing 40 inches. Both species are keyed on the same thing — peanut bunker getting flushed out of the bay system on the dropping water.

Fluke fishing's been solid throughout the inlet and back bay. The Meadowbrook Bridge area is holding steady with keeper-sized fish on the southeast side during incoming water. White bucktails with squid strips or fresh smelt are producing best, but you need to fish them right. Single hook on the bottom, teaser bucktail 18 inches up the leader. The key is keeping contact with bottom on the drift — these fish are hugging structure.
