Wantagh Bridge has been consistent for smaller fluke, mostly shorts but good action for kids. The north side's been better than the south, especially on the first three hours of incoming. Gulp Swimming Mullets on quarter-ounce jigheads are deadly here — white and chartreuse are the colors.

The real surprise has been the back bay action. Hempstead Bay's been producing bluefish in the 18 to 20-inch range, perfect eating size. They're chasing spearing and sand eels in the shallows, especially around the channel edges near Wantagh Park. Small diamond jigs with white or green tails cast to breaking fish are connecting.

Bait's been the story all week. The bay's loaded with peanut bunker, and I mean loaded. Every outgoing tide brings clouds of them through the inlet. Sand eels are thick too, especially on the ocean side of the jetties where the current creates that perfect feeding zone. The birds have been working overtime — terns diving constantly, which tells you the bait's staying high in the water column.

Weather's been cooperative with light southwest winds most days, but that's changing. We've got a front moving through this weekend that should stir things up. The good news is it's bringing northwest winds behind it, which typically cleans up the water and gets the fish feeding aggressively.

Moon phase is working in our favor too. We're coming off new moon, so the tides are still running strong but starting to moderate. That's perfect for inlet fishing — enough current to move bait but not so much that you can't control your drift.

Looking ahead, I'm watching for the weakfish bite to expand. If this thermal gradient holds and we keep getting good bait flushes, we could see the best weakfish fishing in a decade. The key will be hitting the inlet on the last two hours of outgoing water with fresh bunker. Don't overthink the rig — simple fishfinder with a 6/0 circle hook.

For fluke, the action should only get better as water temperatures stabilize. Focus on structure — bridges, channel edges, anywhere the current creates an ambush point. And don't ignore the back bays. With all this bait around, the blues and stripers are going to follow it wherever it goes.

reports.headline: Bay water hits 68 degrees as weakfish crash Fire Island surf and fluke stack deep
reports.subhead: Seven-pound weakfish from the inlet surf signals the return of the ghost fish to South Shore waters.
reports.body_markdown:
The water's telling a story this week, and it's one I've been waiting all season to hear. Bay temps finally cracked 68 degrees — a solid four degrees warmer than the ocean side of the inlet — and that thermal gradient is doing exactly what it's supposed to do. It's stacking bait on the flood, holding bass on the ebb, and bringing back a fish we haven't seen in real numbers for years.

A 26-inch, 7.3-pound weakfish came out of the Fire Island Inlet surf this week on a 9-inch Gravity Tackle Sand Eel. That's not just a nice fish — that's a statement fish. Weakfish don't show up by accident. They follow the bait, and when you see one this size in the surf, you know the ecosystem is starting to hum the way it should.

The fluke bite has been absolutely ridiculous. The Laura Lee boats out of Captree are putting keeper fluke in the box every trip, with fish to six pounds coming off the Robert Moses bridge drift in 30 feet of water. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails are the ticket — drag them slow on the outgoing tide when the current pushes bait against the structure. The key is staying patient with your drift speed. Too fast and you're pulling over their heads; too slow and you're not triggering strikes.

What's really got me excited is the sand eel bite. These little silver bullets are everywhere right now, and they're the reason everything else is working. The weakfish are on them, the fluke are gorging on them, and the bass are using them to stage for their summer patterns. When I see sand eels this thick in late June, I know we're in for a summer to remember.

The inlet itself has been fishing like a textbook. Outgoing water at sunset is producing bass to the mid-30s on everything from bottle plugs to soft plastics. The new moon spring tides we just had flushed a ton of bait out of the bay, and the bass are lined up in the channel waiting for the next push. Fish tight to the pilings on the ebb — that's where the current creates the ambush points they love.

Sea bass action has been lights-out on the party boats. The Captree Pride and Princess are coming back with boat limits regularly, and the fish are quality — plenty of keepers mixed with the shorts. Diamond jigs in gold are working, but don't sleep on the sabiki rigs when the bite gets finicky. Sometimes you need to match the bait size exactly, and those small hooks on the sabiki do the trick.

The ocean side has been producing mixed bags that would make any angler smile. Porgies, blackfish, ling, and even some early bonito are showing up on the deeper drifts. The water's clean, the bait's thick, and the fish are feeding aggressively. It's that perfect mid-summer window when everything comes together.

Looking ahead, we've got a full moon Friday, which means big spring tides and serious water movement. I'm watching the inlet drain at sunset for what could be the first real push of weakfish we've seen in years. That 68-degree bay water is going to meet the cooler ocean water, create some serious current breaks, and stack bait like a dinner bell. If you've been waiting for the right time to get out there, this is it.

reports.headline: Trophy bass crash Moriches Inlet as thermal layers stack bait on the flood
reports.subhead: Night sessions with live spot producing fish over 30 inches while fluke action heats up in skinny bay water hitting 68 degrees.
reports.body_markdown:
The inlet's been absolutely electric this past week, with trophy stripers staging in the deeper cuts where cooler ocean water meets the warming bay. Water temps hit 68 degrees inside the bay while the ocean side is running 4 degrees cooler — that thermal gradient is creating a perfect feeding zone right at the inlet mouth where bait gets compressed on every tide change.

Night fishing with live spot has been the ticket for the big bass. I'm talking fish pushing 30-plus inches coming out of the 15 to 20-foot channel edges on the flood tide. The key is positioning your boat in that sweet spot where the incoming water creates an eddy against the north jetty. Drop your spot on a fishfinder rig with a 6/0 circle hook, keep it moving just off bottom, and wait for that telltale thump. These fish are feeding aggressively in the dark, capitalizing on disoriented bait getting swept through the cut.

The daytime bite has been more technical but equally productive for those who understand the structure. The recent storms shifted sand around the inlet again, creating new drop-offs and filling in some of the traditional holes. I've been finding bass in 8 to 12 feet of water along the channel edges, particularly where the current creates that back-eddy near the coast guard station. Soft plastics — specifically 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails — have been deadly when worked slowly along these new contours.

Fluke fishing has turned the corner as bay temperatures climbed into the upper 60s. The skinny water bite in 3 to 8 feet has been exceptional, with doormat-class fish showing up in numbers I haven't seen in years. The pattern is classic Moriches: ultra-light presentations in water so shallow you can watch the fish attack your jig. I'm running 1/4-ounce bucktails with 3-inch Gulp grubs, dragging them painfully slow across the sandy bottom near Tuthill Point and the eastern flats.

What's driving this action is the perfect storm of conditions we've got right now. The new moon earlier this week created strong tidal flows that flushed massive amounts of bait out of the back bay creeks. Peanut bunker, spearing, and juvenile weakfish are stacked in the inlet, creating a feeding frenzy that's drawing predators from miles around. The light northwest winds have kept the water clean and allowed for precise boat positioning — critical when you're fishing these shallow bay areas.

Weakfish have also made their presence known, particularly on the outgoing tide around sunset. These fish are staging in the deeper pockets near Smith Point, hitting small bucktails tipped with Gulp. It's been years since we've seen this kind of consistent weakfish activity, and I suspect the cooler spring we had delayed their migration, concentrating more fish in our area than usual.

The bluefish bite has been solid but predictable — they're following the bunker schools and hitting anything that moves. Cupsogue Beach has been producing nice blues in the surf, particularly early morning and late evening when the bait moves into the wash. Simple setup: fish finder rig with fresh bunker chunks or a Hopkins spoon worked through the breaking waves.

Looking ahead, this full moon cycle should intensify everything we're seeing. The stronger tides will move more bait, and I expect the inlet to be absolutely loaded with feeding fish. The key will be timing your trips with the tide changes — that first hour of the flood and the last hour of the ebb have been magic. Water temperatures should continue climbing, which will push more fluke into the bay shallows and keep the bass bite strong through the night hours.

Pay attention to the wind direction over the next few days. Southwest winds will dirty up the bay water and push bait toward the inlet, while northwest winds will keep conditions clean for sight fishing in the shallows. Either way, this is prime time fishing in Moriches — the kind of action that reminds you why this inlet system is one of the most dynamic fisheries on Long Island.

reports.headline: Inlet blues crash the night shift as bay water hits 68 degrees
reports.subhead: Outgoing tides after midnight are producing doormat fluke and slot bass in crystal-clear water.
reports.body_markdown:
The night bite is absolutely on fire right now. Water temps hit 68 degrees in the bay this week — a solid 4-degree jump from the ocean side of the inlet — and that thermal gradient is stacking bait on every flood tide and holding predators on the ebb. I've been working the inlet from 11 PM to 3 AM, and it's been lights-out fishing.

The bluefish showed up in force Sunday night. Big choppers, 8 to 12 pounds, crashing bait in the rip on the outgoing. I'm throwing 5-inch Yozuri Mag Darters on 50-pound fluoro — you need the heavy leader or these blues will cut you off in seconds. The flat head on the Mag Darter gives it subtle action even in the strong current, and that D-wood drag is deadly when the water's moving. Pop-pop-pause retrieve, let the current work the bait on the drift.

What's really interesting is how clean this water is. Crystal clear, almost tropical-looking blue-green that you don't usually see until August. The stripers are visible 10 feet down, and they're spooky as hell. When the blues are blitzing on top, I'm swinging a 3/4-ounce bucktail with a white Zoom fork tail underneath the school. That's where the bass are — just under the chaos, picking off wounded bait.

Fluke fishing in the bay has been exceptional. The Ponquogue Bridge area is holding some real doormat potential. I'm drifting 30 feet of water with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, working the drop-offs where the channel cuts close to the bridge pilings. Outgoing water is key — that's when the current pushes bait off the flats and concentrates it in the deeper cuts. Had a 6-pounder Tuesday night that hit right at the tide change.

The weakfish are starting to show at the bridge too. Nothing huge yet, but 14 to 16-inch fish on the incoming tide after dark. Small Deadly Dicks and 1/4-ounce bucktails with pink teasers are getting bit. The fish are holding in 15 to 20 feet, right where the current breaks around the bridge structure.

Bait situation is solid. Peanut bunker are thick in the bay, especially around the canal entrance. Spearing are showing up in good numbers near the inlet mouth. If you're fishing bait, a simple fishfinder rig with fresh bunker chunks is producing both bass and blues. Fish it tight to the inlet jetties on the outgoing — that's where the current creates the ambush points.

One thing I'm watching closely is how the new moon spring tides are affecting the bite. We're getting big water movement, especially on the outgoing, and that's flushing a lot of bait out of the back bay areas. The inlet becomes a funnel, and everything has to pass through that narrow opening. Position yourself on the ocean side of the inlet around midnight, and you'll intercept fish following the bait.

The only downside has been boat traffic during the day. Big boats running through the inlet are scattering the schools, so the night bite has been much more consistent. Less pressure, better fishing.

Looking ahead, we've got a full moon Friday, which means even bigger tides. I'm expecting the inlet to really drain hard at sunset, and that should trigger the first serious run of weakfish we've seen this season. The bay-to-ocean temperature differential should hold for another week, so this pattern isn't going anywhere soon. Get out there after dark — the fish are feeding.

reports.headline: Trophy bass crash Block Island as 68-degree water draws summer migration
reports.subhead: Southwest Ledge producing 40-inch fish on bucktails while bonito arrive early at the rips.
reports.body_markdown:
The summer migration is officially on. Water temps hit 68 degrees around the island this week, and the bass responded exactly like they're supposed to — big fish moving in from deep water to feed in the cool, oxygenated currents that make Block Island the East Coast's premier striper destination.

The Southwest Ledge has been the star of the show. I'm talking legitimate trophy fish — bass pushing 40 inches coming up from the 60-foot contour on bucktails and flutter spoons. The key has been working the drop-off where the shallow ledge meets deep water. Fish are holding in that 45 to 60-foot zone, right where the thermocline sets up. White bucktails with pork rind trailers have been deadly, especially on the drift when you can keep contact with bottom but still work the lure through the water column.

What's making this bite special is the bait situation. The sand eels are thick and they're the right size — not the tiny stuff we see early season, but proper 4 to 5-inch baits that big bass can't ignore. I've been watching birds work over schools of them, and where you see that activity, you'll find fish underneath.

The North Rip has been producing too, but it's been more technical. The current has been ripping with these new moon tides, so you need to time it right. Hit it on the slack or just as the tide starts to move, and work flutter spoons vertically. I've seen fish to the mid-40-inch class come up from 80 feet of water when you drop a spoon right on their heads.

Here's what's interesting — we're seeing the first bonito of the season already. That's early, even for Block Island. Small schools are showing up at the rips, hitting anything that moves. If you're targeting them specifically, small metals and tiny poppers are the ticket, but honestly, they're so aggressive right now that they'll eat a bucktail meant for bass.

The fluke fishing has been solid but not spectacular. The 30 to 40-foot zone around the island is holding fish, with keepers coming on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and chartreuse bucktails. The bigger fish seem to prefer the outgoing tide when bait gets flushed off the shallow areas.

Porgies are everywhere if you want to fill the cooler. Any structure in 40 to 60 feet is loaded with them. Clam strips on small hooks, nothing fancy required.

What's driving all this activity is that perfect Block Island setup — 68-degree water that's clean and loaded with oxygen, strong tidal flow that concentrates bait, and structure that gives fish ambush points. The temperature gradient between the island's cool water and the warmer stuff offshore is creating an edge that's stacking everything from bait to bass.

Looking ahead, we're moving toward the full moon Friday, which means bigger tides and more current. That should fire up the rips even more and potentially draw more fish up from deep water. The bonito showing up this early tells me we might be in for an exceptional summer season. When the water conditions are this good this early, it usually means the migration is going to be strong and sustained.

If you're planning a trip, focus on the Southwest Ledge and North Rip. Work the tide changes, keep your bucktails in contact with bottom, and don't be surprised if you hook into the fish of a lifetime. This is what Block Island is all about.

reports.headline: Montauk bass bite fires as water hits 68 degrees — 40-pounders on eels after dark
reports.subhead: Diamond jigs and bucktails producing limits while big bass move into summer patterns on the rips.
reports.body_markdown:
The Point is absolutely on fire right now, and it's not just the summer crowds I'm talking about. Water temps finally cracked 68 degrees this week, and that magic number has flipped the switch on what might be the best bass fishing we've seen all season. The rips are loaded, the bait is thick, and the fish are cooperating in ways that remind you why Montauk earned its reputation as the striper capital of the world.

The action starts at first light with diamond jigs in the traditional spots. North Bar has been producing steady limits of bass in the 20 to 30-inch range, with enough overs mixed in to keep things interesting. The key is getting your 4 to 6-ounce diamonds down through the current and working them with that classic lift-and-drop retrieve. White and chartreuse are the go-to colors, but don't overlook silver when the sun gets high.

What's really got me excited is the after-dark bite on live eels. The big girls — and I'm talking legitimate 40-pounders — are moving in tight to the boulder fields as the sun drops. Fish a live eel on a fishfinder rig with just enough weight to get down, maybe 2 to 3 ounces depending on the current. Cast it out toward the rocks and let it work. The takes are violent, and these fish have shoulders that'll test your drag and your patience.

Bucktails are absolutely crushing it during the day, especially on the south side drops. A 1 to 2-ounce white or chartreuse bucktail tipped with a 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet has been the money combination. Work it slow on the drift, keeping contact with the bottom but not dragging. The fish are holding in that 25 to 35-foot range where the current creates the perfect ambush zone.

The bait situation is interesting this year. Sand eels are everywhere — thick clouds of them stacked against the structure — but the bunker schools that usually dominate this time of year are surprisingly scarce. That's actually working in our favor because it's concentrating the bass on the eels, and they're feeding aggressively. When you see the ospreys working, you know you're in the right neighborhood.

Shagwong Reef has been producing some beautiful fish on the incoming tide, particularly that first hour when the current really starts to move. The 68-degree water is holding right along the reef structure, creating a temperature break that's stacking bait and bass. It's classic Montauk fishing — read the water, find the current, and put your bait where the fish expect to find their next meal.

Fluke fishing has picked up considerably as well. The south side in 30 to 40 feet has been giving up some nice doormats, with fish to 6 pounds hitting white Gulp on bucktail heads. The key is fishing the edges where the current creates those subtle depth changes. A 3/4-ounce bucktail with a 6-inch Swimming Mullet, worked slow and steady, has been the ticket.

Porgies are around but scattered — not the wall-to-wall action we sometimes see. They're holding in specific spots, usually the deeper structure, and once you find them, the fishing can be fast. Small hooks, light tackle, and pieces of clam or squid will fill the cooler quickly.

The new moon earlier this week spread the fish out initially, but as we build toward the full moon this weekend, I expect the action to intensify. Those spring tides are going to flush more bait out of the back bays and really fire up the rips. The forecast shows light winds and manageable seas, perfect conditions for getting out to the productive water.

Looking ahead, I'm watching for the first real push of cocktail blues — those 1 to 2-pounders that signal the summer pattern is fully established. They're starting to show in small numbers, which is always a good sign. When they arrive in force, it usually means the bass fishing is about to get even better as the food chain stacks up.

This is prime time at the Point. Water temps are perfect, bait is abundant, and the fish are in their summer feeding mode. Whether you're jigging the rips at dawn or soaking eels in the boulder fields after dark, Montauk is delivering the kind of fishing that built its legend.

reports.headline: Bay bass bite fires as Peconic hits 72 degrees, porgies stack deep at Shelter Island
reports.subhead: Early flood tides producing slot stripers on bucktails while jumbo scup fill coolers in 30 feet.
reports.body_markdown:
The Peconic finally hit its summer stride this week, with bay temperatures spiking to 72 degrees — a full 8 degrees warmer than the ocean side. That thermal gradient is doing exactly what it should: stacking bait on the flood tides and holding bass through the ebb.

The striper bite has been lights-out at first light, especially around the deeper channels between Shelter Island and Greenport. I've been working 3/4-ounce white bucktails with 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets, keeping them just off bottom on the drift. The key is hitting that last 90 minutes of the flood tide right at sunrise — that's when the bass are most aggressive. Slot fish from 28 to 34 inches have been the norm, with most fish coming from 15 to 25 feet of water.

What's really interesting is how the new moon spring tides are setting up the bite. The stronger current is flushing massive amounts of peanut bunker and spearing out of the back bays, creating feeding opportunities that weren't there during the neap tide cycle two weeks ago. I'm seeing bass following these bait schools right into the shallows, especially around the Jessup Neck area where the channel drops from 8 feet to 30 feet in a boat length.

The porgy fishing remains world-class, though you need to adjust your thinking from the May patterns. The big scup have moved deeper as water temperatures climbed, settling into 25 to 35 feet around the traditional Shelter Island haunts. Clam chum is still king, but I'm finding the bite more selective now. Fresh clam strips on size 4 hooks are outproducing everything else, and you need to keep that chum line steady — these fish are educated.

Weakfish are making their presence known in a big way. The 68-degree water has triggered their summer feeding pattern, and I'm finding them mixed in with the porgies during the day, then moving shallow at dusk. Chartreuse Gulp on light jigheads has been deadly, especially in 12 to 18 feet as the sun drops. Several fish over 20 inches have shown up this week, including a few pushing 4 pounds.

The bluefish situation is typical for late June — they're here, but you have to work for them. Small cocktail blues are scattered throughout the bay, with better fish showing up around the bird activity near Noyack and Three Mile Harbor. Wire leaders are mandatory, and small spoons or Deadly Dicks are producing better than soft plastics.

Looking ahead, this full moon cycle should really fire things up. The spring tides will push more bait around, and with water temperatures holding steady in the low 70s, all species should remain active. I'm particularly excited about the weakfish potential — this is prime time for the bigger fish to show up in numbers.

The weather pattern looks stable through the weekend, with light winds and calm seas. That means you can fish the deeper structure around Shelter Island without fighting the drift, and the shallow water bite should be accessible for smaller boats.

One tactical note: don't overlook the night bite. With these warm water temperatures, bass are feeding aggressively after dark, especially around the lighted docks in Sag Harbor and Greenport. Live eels or large soft plastics worked slowly along the pilings have been producing some of the best fish of the week.

reports.headline: Bass push through Plum Gut as Sound water hits 68 degrees
reports.subhead: Incoming tide at Orient Point producing keeper stripers on bunker chunks and eels.
reports.body_markdown:
Water's finally warming up proper out here on the North Fork sound shore, and the bass are starting to move like they mean it. Hit 68 degrees this week according to the buoys, and that's the magic number that gets these fish thinking about summer patterns instead of just wandering around looking confused.

Been working the Orient Point area pretty steady, and the incoming tide is where you want to be. Not the flood — the incoming. There's a difference, and it matters more than most people think. That push of cooler water coming through Plum Gut carries bait, and the bass know it. They're setting up along the drop-off about a quarter mile west of the point, waiting for whatever the current brings them.

Chunked bunker is producing the most consistent action. Fresh stuff, not the frozen bricks from last fall. Cut your chunks palm-sized, hook them through the back, and fish them on a fishfinder rig with enough weight to hold bottom in the current. I've been using 6-ounce pyramids, sometimes 8 when the water really starts moving. The fish aren't huge — mostly schoolies in the 24 to 28-inch range — but there's been a few keepers mixed in, including one that went close to 35 inches on Tuesday morning.

Eels are working too, especially after dark. Live ones if you can get them, but the rigged eels from the tackle shop will do. Fish them the same way as the bunker chunks, but use a lighter weight. These bass are eating the eels on the drop, not picking them up off the bottom, so you want that bait to move natural in the current.

The porgy bite has been steady but not spectacular. Rocky Point area, anywhere you can find structure in 25 to 35 feet of water. Small hooks, size 6 or 8, with pieces of clam or sandworm. Nothing fancy about it — just drop down, feel for bottom, and wait for the tug. The fish are running small this year, mostly shorts, but there's enough keepers to make it worthwhile if you're looking to put something in the cooler.

Bluefish showed up in numbers this past weekend, which surprised me a little. Usually don't see them this thick until July, but the warm water must have pulled them up from wherever they spend the early season. They're hitting everything — spoons, poppers, chunks, doesn't matter. The problem is they're mixed in with the bass, so if you're targeting stripers, you're going to catch blues whether you want them or not.

Mattituck Inlet has been quiet for fluke, which is disappointing but not unexpected. The water in there is still a little cool, and the bait hasn't really moved in yet. Give it another week or two of this weather, and things should pick up. The few fluke that are around are small — nothing worth keeping.

Weakfish have been showing sporadically in the deeper water off Horton Point. Not a steady bite, but when they're there, they're there in numbers. Pink and white bucktails with a strip of squid, bounced along the bottom in 40 to 50 feet. The trick is finding them — they move around a lot, and what worked yesterday might not work today.

Looking ahead, we've got a new moon coming this weekend, which should really get the water moving through Plum Gut. That's when I expect to see the best bass fishing of the season so far. The spring tides will flush a lot of bait out of the bays and harbors, and the bass will be waiting for it. Plan on fishing the incoming tide, especially the last two hours before high water.

Water temperature should hold steady or maybe climb another degree or two if this weather pattern continues. That's good news for everything except maybe the blackfish, which seem to disappear when the water gets much over 70. But for bass, blues, and weakfish, we're right in the sweet spot now.

One thing to watch — the wind has been light all week, which makes for easy fishing but not necessarily the best fishing. A little chop on the water helps break up the light and makes the fish less spooky. If we get some southwest wind this weekend, that could really turn things on.

reports.headline: Plum Gut bass crash butterfish schools as 68-degree water triggers feeding frenzy
reports.subhead: Trophy stripers stack in the rips while swim shads outproduce bucktails on big fish.
reports.body_markdown:
The water hit 68 degrees this week and everything changed. After weeks of scratching for fish, Plum Gut exploded with bass feeding on thick schools of butterfish that moved in with the warming water. I've been hammering them on the flood and ebb, with fish to 37 inches coming over the rail on every other drift.

The key has been matching the current to the presentation. When the tide screams at 3 knots, I'm running heavy — 8 to 10-ounce cannonballs on three-way rigs with 80-pound leaders. That thick mono stands the lure off the bottom and prevents constant hang-ups on the rocky terrain. The surprise has been how much better swim shads are producing over bucktails for the bigger fish. Seven-inch Tsunami swim shads in white are absolutely crushing it, pulling overslot bass while the bucktails are getting the slot fish.

The Race has been equally productive but more dangerous. The new moon spring tides are pushing serious current through there — I clocked 4 knots on the sounder yesterday. The rip stands up like a wall when the wind goes against it, but when conditions settle, the bass are stacked on the edges feeding on squid and butterfish. Topwater action has been spectacular at first light before the current gets nasty.

Orient Point has been the sleeper spot. The temperature gradient between the Sound and the ocean side is holding bait tight to the structure. I'm finding 68-degree water on the Sound side while the ocean drops to 64 — that 4-degree difference is creating a feeding zone that's been loaded with slot bass. Three-way rigs with eels after dark have been deadly, especially around the deeper structure off the point.

The bluefish showed up in force this week and they're wrecking tackle. These aren't the small snappers — we're talking gorilla blues to 15 pounds that are cutting through 50-pound leaders like they're nothing. Switch to wire or heavy fluorocarbon if you want to keep your expensive plugs. The blues are mixed in with the bass schools, so you never know what's going to hit.

Fishers Island has been producing steady blackfish action for those willing to make the run. The 20-foot drops on the west side are holding keeper tog, with green crabs on jig heads getting the nod over fiddlers. The bite has been best on the flood tide when the current pushes bait against the structure.

Bait situation is interesting — the butterfish showed up earlier than usual, probably pushed in by the rapid temperature rise. Squid are scattered but present around the deeper rips. Bunker are around but not in the massive schools we usually see. The bass seem keyed in on the butterfish, which explains why the swim shads are so effective.

Looking ahead, this full moon Friday is going to push some serious water through the rips. The spring tides will flush bait out of the back bays and stack it in the current breaks. I'm planning to hit the Gut on the ebb when the ferry traffic dies down and the current creates those perfect feeding lanes. If the wind stays light, the topwater bite at The Race could be epic at sunset when the tide turns.

Water temps should hold steady in the high 60s, which keeps the bass aggressive and the bait active. This is prime time fishing — the kind of conditions that make you remember why you put up with all the blown-out days and slow tides. Get out there while it lasts.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Bluefin blitz hits Poor Man's as 68-degree water stacks bait on the shelf
reports.subhead: Spencer and Lindenkohl firing on the troll while Norfolk holds yellowfin in the deep.
reports.body_markdown:
The southern canyons are absolutely on fire right now, and I'm telling you — this is the kind of week that makes you remember why we run these long miles offshore. Poor Man's Canyon has been the star of the show, with bluefin tuna crashing the shelf edge in 68-degree water that's been holding steady for three days running.

I made the run to Poor Man's Sunday morning and found the magic at the 30-fathom line where that beautiful temperature break sets up. Water temp jumped from 64 degrees inshore to 68 at the shelf, and that 4-degree gradient is stacking bait like you wouldn't believe. We're talking thick marks of sand eels and squid getting pushed up against that thermal wall, and the bluefin are taking full advantage. Fish are running 75 to 110 inches, with most of the action coming on the troll at 6 knots.

The hot setup has been cedar plugs and small feathers — nothing fancy, just classic canyon trolling. Pink and white cedar plugs on the long riggers, chartreuse feathers on the short corners. Key is staying in that temperature break and watching your fishfinder for the bait clouds. When you see those thick red marks at 40 to 60 feet, that's where you want to be.

Spencer Canyon has been producing consistent yellowfin action, especially on the northeast wall where the current sweeps up from the deep. Water's running 72 degrees on the surface with a sharp thermocline at 80 feet. The yellowfin are holding right in that temperature gradient, and they're hungry. Chunking with butterfish has been deadly — cut the butterfish into 3-inch strips, hook them through the head on a 7/0 circle hook, and let them flutter down on a 6-foot fluorocarbon leader. The bite has been best on the incoming tide when that current really starts moving.

Lindenkohl has been the sleeper this week. Not getting the press that Poor Man's is getting, but the guys who know are finding white marlin and mahi in the 100 to 200-fathom range. Water temperature is perfect at 74 degrees, and there's a beautiful weed line running north-south along the western edge. Live ballyhoo under the kites has been the ticket for the white marlin, while the mahi are crushing anything that moves — ballyhoo, cedar plugs, even small poppers when they're really fired up.

Norfolk Canyon has been the deep-water play for serious yellowfin. You need to run out to the 200-fathom line where the water drops to 70 degrees and the current really rips. It's a longer run from Cape May — we're talking 65 miles — but the payoff is there. Yellowfin to 80 pounds are holding in the deep water, and they're not spooky like the fish on the shelf. Chunking with squid and butterfish has been producing, but you need to get your baits down to 100 feet where the fish are holding.

The moon phase is working in our favor right now. We're coming off the new moon, so the tides aren't extreme, but there's enough current to keep the bait moving and the fish active. The real key has been timing your arrival at the canyons for the start of the incoming tide. That's when the current starts pushing bait up the canyon walls, and that's when the tuna turn on.

Weather has been cooperative with light northwest winds and 1 to 2-foot seas. Visibility has been excellent — you can see the color changes from miles away, which makes finding that temperature break so much easier. The high pressure system sitting over us should keep conditions stable through the weekend.

Looking ahead, I'm watching the water temperatures closely. That 68-degree water at Poor Man's is the sweet spot for bluefin, and if it holds through the week, we should see continued action. The full moon is coming up next week, which means bigger tides and more current — that could really fire up the bite at Spencer and Lindenkohl where current is king.

If you're planning a trip, don't overthink the tackle. Medium-heavy trolling rods, 50-pound test, and a good selection of cedar plugs and feathers will get the job done. For chunking, bring plenty of butterfish and squid, and don't forget the circle hooks. The fish are there, the conditions are right, and the southern canyons are fishing as good as I've seen them in years.

reports.headline: Sound bass chase bunker deep as new moon stirs the middle grounds
reports.subhead: Spring tides push bait off the ledges while fluke move shallow on the warming flats.
reports.body_markdown:
The new moon hit Friday and it's doing exactly what I expected — stirring up the middle Sound like a cocktail shaker. Water temps are sitting pretty at 68 degrees across most of my beat, but here's what's got my attention: there's a solid thermal break setting up between the shallow Connecticut flats and the deeper channels.

Striped bass are stacked along the 30 to 45-foot contours from the Stratford Shoal east to Middle Ground Light. The spring tides are flushing bunker out of the harbors and these fish are positioned perfectly to ambush them. I'm seeing consistent action on white bucktails in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range, worked slow along the bottom with the current. The key is reading the tide — fish are hitting hardest during the first two hours of the ebb when that bait gets swept off the ledges.

What's interesting is how the fish are behaving differently depending on depth. In 25 to 35 feet, they're aggressive on topwater at dawn — pencil poppers and SP Minnows are producing solid fish in the 28 to 34-inch range. But once the sun gets up, they're dropping to the thermocline and you need to get down to them with bucktails or live eels on fishfinder rigs.

The Norwalk Islands have been particularly productive, especially the rocky drops on the back sides where current creates natural ambush points. I'm finding the best action on the outgoing tide when bait gets pushed through the channels between the islands. A 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce jighead has been deadly, especially when you let it sweep naturally with the flow.

Fluke fishing has taken an interesting turn with the warming water. They're moving up onto the flats in 15 to 20 feet, particularly around Port Jefferson Harbor and the shoals off Charles Island. The warmer water — we're seeing 72 degrees in the shallows versus 68 in the deeper water — is concentrating bait and the fluke are following. Pink and white Gulp on light bucktails are outproducing everything else, but you need to match your weight to the current. In the lighter flows, a 1/2-ounce head keeps you in the strike zone without hanging bottom.

The current situation is textbook for this lunar phase. We're seeing 3 to 4-knot flows during peak tide changes, which is perfect for moving bait but challenging for presentation. The trick is positioning yourself up-current from structure and letting your offering drift naturally through the strike zone. Don't fight the tide — work with it.

Porgies are thick around any hard bottom in 25 to 40 feet, and they're running large. These aren't the usual dinner-plate fish — I'm seeing plenty of 12 to 14-inchers that are worth keeping. Small pieces of clam or squid on a high-low rig will fill the cooler quickly if you need backup dinner plans.

Looking ahead, this new moon cycle should keep the action strong through the weekend. The big tides are going to continue moving bait, and with water temps holding steady in the upper 60s, the fish should stay active. I'm particularly watching for the first real push of weakfish — the conditions are setting up perfectly for them to move through the western Sound in the next week or two.

The key to success right now is mobility. Don't sit on a dead spot hoping fish will show up. Use your electronics to find the bait, watch for bird activity, and be ready to move when the action shifts. The fish are here — you just need to think like they do and position yourself where the current is doing the work for you.

reports.headline: Yellowfin blitz fires Hydrographer as bluefin migration finally arrives
reports.subhead: Eastern canyons come alive with late-season tuna push and white marlin mixed in.
reports.body_markdown:
The eastern canyons finally woke up this week, and it happened fast. After weeks of waiting for the migration to materialize, yellowfin tuna crashed Hydrographer Canyon in numbers we haven't seen since early May. Water temps hit that magic 68-degree mark at the shelf break, and everything changed overnight.

Hydrographer has been the star performer, with yellowfin from 40 to 80 pounds taking spreader bars and cedar plugs in 100 to 200 fathoms. The bite's been best on the northwest corner where the 100-fathom curve makes that hard turn. We're seeing fish scattered from the 30-line all the way out to the 200, but the consistent action is happening where that warm 68-degree water meets the cooler upwelling along the canyon wall.

The technique that's been money is running a five-rod spread with medium ballyhoo on the riggers and a mix of cedar plugs and small feathers on the flat lines. Keep your speed between 6.5 and 7.5 knots — any faster and you're pulling the baits away from the fish. The yellowfin are aggressive but spooky. Once you hook up, get the other lines in fast or you'll tangle the whole spread.

What's really got me excited is the bluefin showing up in force. These aren't the resident fish we've been picking at all spring — this is the real migration finally arriving from the south. Fish from 60 to 200 pounds are mixed in with the yellowfin, and they're taking the same baits. The difference is in the fight. When a bluefin grabs that ballyhoo, you know it immediately. They go deep and stay deep, while the yellowfin make those screaming surface runs.

Veatch Canyon has been producing too, though not with the same consistency as Hydrographer. The northeast corner has been holding white marlin in good numbers — fish from 50 to 70 pounds that are absolutely crushing live mackerel on circle hooks. The marlin bite has been best during the afternoon hours when the sun gets high and warms that surface layer. We're fishing the mackerel on 30-pound fluorocarbon leaders, about 50 feet back from a 12-ounce egg sinker.

The mahi situation is interesting. We're not seeing the massive schools yet, but there are quality fish scattered throughout both canyons. Most are in the 15 to 25-pound range, with a few pushing 30. They're taking small ballyhoo and squid strips fished under the birds. When you find working birds over deep water, it's worth checking out — half the time there are mahi underneath picking up the scraps.

Water conditions have been near perfect. That 68-degree reading at the shelf break is exactly what we want to see this time of year. The gradient is sharp — you can watch your surface temp climb from 64 degrees in 50 fathoms to 68 degrees in 100 fathoms, then drop back to 65 degrees out in the deep water. That thermal structure is what's holding bait and concentrating fish.

The full moon this Friday is going to shake things up. These big tides always trigger movement, and with water temps where they are, I expect the bite to get even better. The strong currents will position bait differently along the canyon walls, and the tuna will follow. Plan your trips around the tide changes — the hour before and after slack water has been producing the most consistent action.

Looking ahead, I'm watching Oceanographer Canyon closely. It's been quiet compared to Hydrographer and Veatch, but the water temps are climbing there too. Once that canyon hits 68 degrees, it usually explodes with yellowfin. The run from Montauk is longer, but when Oceanographer fires, it's worth every gallon of fuel.

The season that started slow is finally hitting its stride. Water temps are climbing, bait is thick, and the migration is in full swing. If you've been waiting for the right time to make the run east, this is it.

reports.headline: Yellowfin blitz fires at the Wilmington as Gulf Stream eddy locks in 72-degree water
reports.subhead: Temperature break at 100 fathoms stacking bait and holding tuna through the tide changes.
reports.body_markdown:
The Wilmington Canyon is fishing like a different ocean this week. A warm-core eddy has spun off the Gulf Stream and parked itself right over our favorite 100-fathom corner, creating the kind of temperature break that makes yellowfin tuna lose their minds. We're seeing a solid 8-degree gradient from the 64-degree inshore water to 72-degree blue water at the shelf edge, and that thermal wall is stacking bait like a dinner bell.

Yellowfin are the story right now. We're marking fish from 40 to 80 pounds consistently, with a few pushing the century mark. The bite has been most reliable on the northwest corner where the canyon wall drops from 60 to 200 fathoms. That's where the eddy circulation is tightest and the bait gets compressed against the structure. I've been running a spread of cedar plugs and ballyhoo on the troll — pink and white Bombers in the short riggers, natural ballyhoo on circle hooks in the long outriggers. The key is staying in that 68 to 72-degree water and watching for the temperature jumps on the fish finder.

When we mark a good show of bait, we've been stopping to chunk. Fresh butterfish and squid are getting crushed, but the real magic happens with live peanut bunker when you can find them. Fish them on 8/0 circles with just enough weight to get down 20 feet in the current. The yellowfin are feeding aggressively in the top 40 feet of water, especially during the morning and evening hours when the bait pushes up.

Mahi mahi are mixed in with the tuna action, mostly smaller fish in the 10 to 20-pound range, but they're eager and make for good action on lighter tackle. They're hitting the same cedar plugs that are working for yellowfin, plus any floating debris or weed lines you can find in that warm water. I've been keeping a few spinning rods rigged with bucktail jigs for when we find them busting bait on top.

The wahoo bite has been more scattered but worth mentioning. We've picked up a few nice fish to 40 pounds trolling the deeper edges where the canyon drops to 300 fathoms. High-speed trolling with Ilander lures and ballyhoo combos has been the ticket — purple and black, pink and white. You need to cover water to find them, but when you hook up, it's game on.

White marlin are starting to show in better numbers as we get deeper into summer. We've raised a handful this week, mostly on the troll in that same 100-fathom zone where the yellowfin are concentrated. The standard spread of small ballyhoo and sea witches is working, but you need to stay alert for the subtle bites. These fish are notorious for short-striking, so keep those hooks sharp and your drag settings honest.

The current has been running moderate to strong on the flood tide, which is actually helping the fishing. It's keeping the bait tight to the structure and giving our presentations good action. The new moon spring tides this week are creating some serious water movement, but that's exactly what we want to see. It's stirring up the food chain and keeping the predators active.

Looking at the water temperature readings, that warm eddy is holding steady. The 44069 buoy is showing 72.3 degrees, which is exactly what we're seeing on the surface at the canyon. The gradient is sharp and well-defined — you can literally see the color change when you cross from green inshore water to that deep blue Gulf Stream influence. That's your target zone.

Weather has been cooperative with light winds and manageable seas. The forecast shows more of the same through the weekend, which should keep this bite going strong. When conditions are this stable, the fish settle into predictable patterns, and that's exactly what we're seeing.

For the week ahead, I'm expecting this yellowfin action to continue as long as that eddy stays parked over the canyon. The full moon is coming up next week, which typically fires up the night bite for bluefin tuna. I'll be watching for those bigger fish to move in as the lunar phase changes. The temperature structure looks stable, so plan your trips accordingly and bring plenty of ice.

reports.headline: Washington Canyon fires early as 68-degree water stacks bait on the walls
reports.subhead: Yellowfin and bluefin both showing in the upper water column as June heat kicks the season into gear.
reports.body_markdown:
The Washington is coming alive exactly when it should — three weeks ahead of the other canyons, just like clockwork. That 68-degree water showing up on the buoys tells the whole story. We've got legitimate temperature separation now, and the fish are responding.

Yellowfin are the story this week. Schools of 40 to 60-pounders have been working the northeast wall in 80 to 120 fathoms, and they're not being shy about it. The key has been finding the temperature break where that warm Gulf Stream water meets the cooler shelf water. When you see that 4-degree jump on the fish finder — from 64 to 68 — that's where you want to be.

The bite's been best on the troll, running a spread of cedar plugs and small feathers at 7 to 8 knots. Blue and white cedar plugs on the long riggers, pink and white feathers on the short ones. The fish have been coming up from 60 feet, so keep those baits in the top 40 feet of water. When you mark them, don't be afraid to circle back — these schools are holding tight to structure.

Bluefin are mixed in with the yellowfin, mostly smaller fish in the 40 to 70-inch range, but there's been some bigger fish showing. The northeast corner of the canyon, where it bends toward the 100-fathom line, has been holding the better grade of fish. Same trolling spread works, but when you see the bluefin, switch to chunk bait. Fresh butterfish chunks on 8/0 circles, fished on 50-pound fluorocarbon leaders about 30 feet down.

The mahi bite has been sporadic but worth watching. Small schools of schoolies — 5 to 15 pounds — have been under the scattered weed lines on the southeast wall. They're hitting small ballyhoo on the troll and 3-inch Hogy soft baits when you stop to chunk. The water's still a touch cool for a consistent mahi bite, but it's building.

What's really got my attention is the bait situation. There's been good marks of squid along the 50-fathom line, and that's what's drawing everything in. The yellowfin especially have been gorging on squid, and when you clean them, that's all you see. This early squid concentration usually means the canyon's going to fish well through July.

The water conditions have been nearly perfect — light northwest winds all week, seas under 2 feet, and that beautiful blue water pushed right up against the shelf. Visibility's been 100 feet plus, and the current's been manageable at 1 to 1.5 knots on the wall.

One thing to watch: the temperature gradient is still pretty tight. You can go from 64-degree water to 68-degree water in less than a mile, especially along the northeast wall. That's where the fish are stacking, but it also means you need to pay attention to your electronics. The fish aren't spread out — they're concentrated in specific temperature pockets.

Looking ahead, this weekend's new moon is going to stir things up. The increased tidal flow should push more bait up from the deep water and spread the fish out along more of the wall structure. I'm expecting the bite to get even better, especially if this weather pattern holds.

The Washington always fishes early, and this year's no different. While everyone else is still waiting for their canyons to turn on, we're already into fish. That's the beauty of this piece of water — it sits in just the right spot to catch that first push of warm water, and the fish know it. If you're thinking about making the run, now's the time. The season's here.

reports.headline: Giant bluefin stack at 100 fathoms as 68-degree water holds bait tight
reports.subhead: Jigging and stickbaits producing fish to 96 inches on the thermocline break.
reports.body_markdown:
The Hudson Canyon is firing on all cylinders right now, with giant bluefin tuna stacked along the 100-fathom line in numbers I haven't seen since early May. Water temps hit 68.2 degrees at the canyon edge this week, creating a perfect thermocline break that's holding massive schools of bunker and sand eels — and the giants are feeding hard.

The action has been split between two distinct bites. Early morning brings explosive topwater feeds when the bunker push up against the canyon wall. These fish want big stickbaits worked aggressively through the white water. I'm talking 8-inch to 10-inch sticks, cast right into the chaos and retrieved with sharp jerks. The takes are violent — fish launching completely out of the water before the hook sets.

But here's where it gets interesting: when those surface feeds shut down around 9 AM, the fish don't disappear. They drop to the thermocline, typically 65 to 80 feet down, and that's where the jigging bite takes over. I've been running 280-gram jigs with beefed-up hooks, bouncing them right off the bottom and working them slowly through the water column. The key is finding that temperature break — the fish are sitting right on it, sometimes just 5 feet off the deck.

The 68-degree surface water we're seeing is crucial. It's creating a distinct thermal layer that's concentrating bait, and when you find that edge on your fish finder, you'll mark fish. I've been working the area from the Claw south to the Dip, focusing on the 600 to 700-foot depths where the canyon wall creates natural upwelling.

Tackle is critical for these fish. I'm running 50-80 pound class rods with quality lever-drag reels spooled with 65-pound braid to 80-pound fluorocarbon leaders. Don't cheap out on the terminal tackle — these fish will test every connection. Start your drag at 35 pounds and be ready to back it off when they make their runs.

The bite timing has been predictable: first light for the surface action, then the jig bite from 9 AM through early afternoon. Tide changes seem to trigger feeding, especially the flood tide pushing bait up the canyon walls. With the new moon approaching Friday, expect bigger tidal swings and more aggressive feeding windows.

Looking ahead, this 68-degree water should hold through the weekend if we don't get any major weather. The thermal structure is stable, and the bait is thick from the Texas Tower north to the 100-fathom line. I'm expecting the topwater bite to continue strong, especially with calm conditions forecast. The key will be getting there early — first boat on the water gets first crack at the surface feeds before the fleet arrives and pressures the fish down.

reports.headline: Gator blues crash the Sound as bass bite turns technical in 68-degree water
reports.subhead: Big stripers still feeding on outgoing tides, but you need to match the hatch as water warms.
reports.body_markdown:
The Western Sound is in full summer mode now, and if you're still fishing like it's May, you're going home empty-handed. Water temps hit 68 degrees this week — that magic number where everything changes. The bass are still here, but they've gone selective, and the blues have moved in with an attitude.

I've been watching this transition for three decades, and it's happening right on schedule. The big stripers are still feeding, but they're keyed in on specific tide stages and structure. Execution Rocks has been the star performer on the outgoing water, especially that last two hours when the current really starts ripping over the ledge. The fish are staging deep — 35 to 45 feet — and you need to get down to them.

Trolling large Mojos has been the ticket for the oversized fish. I'm talking 8 to 10-inch baits, pulled slow over the structure. The morning bite has been soft, but when that afternoon outgoing tide kicks in and the water starts moving, it's lights out. Had reports of multiple 40-inch-plus fish this week, including one monster that went every bit of 50 pounds. That's Western Sound fishing at its finest.

But here's what's got me excited — the blues have arrived, and they're not the cocktail-size fish we usually see early. These are legitimate gator blues, 10 to 15 pounds, and they're absolutely crushing baitfish in the shipping channel. I've been seeing them blitzing on butterfish and spearing from Matinecock Point all the way west to the Throgs Neck. When you find them feeding on top, throw anything metal — diamond jigs, Kastmasters, even a simple bucktail with a white teaser.

The fluke bite has been steady but not spectacular. The fish are scattered from Eaton's Neck to Lloyd Harbor, mostly in that 20 to 30-foot range. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails have been producing the most consistent action. The key is working the grass edges where the sand eels are staging. I'm seeing plenty of shorts, but the keepers are there if you put in the time.

Porgies have made their appearance around the rocky structure, especially near the Stepping Stones and around the bridge pilings. Standard porgy rigs with clam have been working, but don't overlook the dock fishing opportunities. The fish are moving shallow in the early morning hours, and you can pick them on light tackle right from the bulkheads.

Here's what the conditions are telling me: that 68-degree water temp is the dividing line. Below that, the bass feed aggressively throughout the water column. Above it, they go deep and get picky. The thermal structure is setting up with cooler water on the bottom, and that's where the big fish are holding. The new moon we just had pushed a lot of bait around, but now we're heading into the full moon cycle, and that means big tides and moving water.

The squid bite has been phenomenal in the back bays — some of the best I've seen in years. They're thick around the dock lights at night, and if you like calamari or need bait for the big bass, get out there with a squid jig. The action has been consistent from Little Neck Bay all the way out to Hempstead Harbor.

Looking ahead, this full moon Friday is going to create some serious tidal movement. I'm watching for the inlet drains at sunset — that's when the weakfish typically show up for their first real push of the season. The water's warm enough now, and with all this bait around, conditions are perfect for them to move in.

The key to success right now is adapting to the conditions. The easy fishing of spring is over. You need to match your tactics to the thermal structure, work the moving water, and be ready to switch between species as opportunities present themselves. The Sound is alive with fish — you just need to fish smarter, not harder.

reports.headline: Washington Canyon fires early as 68-degree water brings first yellowfin push
reports.subhead: Warm eddies along the northeast wall are holding bait and drawing tunas up from the deep.
reports.body_markdown:
The canyon is waking up ahead of schedule this year, and I'm not complaining. Water temps hit 68 degrees on the northeast wall this week — a solid four degrees warmer than I usually see in late June — and the yellowfin are responding like it's mid-July. The thermal gradient between the 68-degree eddy water and the 64-degree surrounding ocean is creating a perfect setup along the 100-fathom line, stacking bait and drawing fish up from the depths.

I've been working the northeast wall hard this week, focusing on the 39°05' to 39°08' latitude range where the warm water is holding strongest. The key has been finding the temperature breaks — that sharp transition from 64 to 68 degrees where the yellowfin are feeding. Chunk baits are producing best, with fresh butterfish and squid on 8/0 circle hooks getting consistent bites in the 30 to 60-pound class. The fish are coming up aggressive in that warm water, so don't be afraid to use 80-pound fluorocarbon leaders.

The northeast wall has always been my go-to early in the season because of how it interacts with the Gulf Stream, but this year's setup is exceptional. That 68-degree water isn't just sitting there — it's moving, creating feeding lanes along the canyon edge. I'm seeing the best action from the 50-fathom line out to about 120 fathoms, with fish scattered throughout the water column but concentrating where the thermocline sets up around 80 feet.

Trolling has been productive too, especially in the morning hours when the yellowfin are pushing bait to the surface. Cedar plugs and small feathers in blue-white combinations are getting strikes, but the real money has been on the chunk. Set up on the drift where you're marking bait, get a good chum slick going, and be patient. These fish are feeding, but they're still spooky in the clear water.

The bluefin situation is interesting this week. I'm seeing scattered fish in the 40 to 80-inch range mixed in with the yellowfin, but they're being more selective. Fresh mackerel chunks on lighter tackle — 50-pound class — has been the ticket for the bluefin. They seem to prefer the slightly cooler water on the edges of those warm eddies, so don't ignore the 64 to 66-degree zones.

Bait has been the story this week. The canyon is loaded with squid, and there's a good showing of butterfish along the wall. I'm also seeing scattered schools of small blueback herring, which explains why some of the yellowfin are coming up so aggressive. When you find the bait concentrations, especially where they're stacked against the temperature breaks, that's where you want to set up.

The weather pattern has been cooperating, with light northwest winds keeping the seas manageable. That 68-degree water I keep talking about isn't going anywhere soon — the high pressure system that's been sitting over us is keeping the Gulf Stream influence strong along the canyon edge.

Looking ahead to the weekend and into next week, I expect this bite to continue building. The new moon is Thursday, which should bring stronger currents and better bait movement along the wall. If this warm water holds — and I think it will — we could see the first real mahi push of the season. I'm already seeing scattered dolphin in the 72-degree water further offshore, and it won't take much for them to move into the canyon proper.

The key right now is being flexible with your approach. The fish are there, but they're not always in the same spot or at the same depth. Work the temperature breaks, follow the bait, and don't get locked into one technique. This early-season bite in Washington is setting up to be something special — the kind of June fishing that makes you forget about the long winter months. Get out there while the getting's good.

reports.headline: Yellowfin blitz fires at the break as Gulf Stream eddy spins up warm water
reports.subhead: 72-degree water at the canyon edge is stacking bait and firing up the best tuna bite in weeks.
reports.body_markdown:
The Gulf Stream finally decided to cooperate this week, spinning off a beautiful warm eddy that's sitting right on the 100-fathom line and lighting up the yellowfin bite like I haven't seen since early May. Water temps jumped from the mid-60s to a solid 72 degrees at the break, and that 8-degree gradient is acting like a magnet for everything with fins.

I've been running the same pattern for three days straight — trolling the temperature break from the northeast corner down to the southern wall, working that sweet spot where the 72-degree blue water meets the cooler inshore stuff. The yellowfin are stacked up in that transition zone, and they're not being picky. Cedar plugs in natural and pink have been absolute money, especially the smaller 6-inch models pulled on the long riggers. The key is keeping your speed right around 7.5 knots and watching your fishfinder for that thermocline at 45 feet.

Tuesday morning was the standout trip. Hit the break at first light and had three yellowfin in the boat before 8 AM, all fish in the 40 to 60-pound class. The bite window was tight — maybe two hours of steady action — but when they turned on, it was game over. Ballyhoo on the flat lines produced the biggest fish, a beautiful 58-pounder that took a perfectly rigged bally behind a pink and white Islander. The wahoo showed up around 10 AM, typical pattern for this time of year. Lost two good fish to cutoffs before I switched to wire, then boated a nice 35-pounder on a blue and white Yo-Zuri Bonita.

The chunking bite has been solid too, especially on the evening trips. Once the trolling bite dies off around noon, I've been anchoring up on the 30-fathom line and putting out a slick. Fresh butterfish chunks on 8/0 circles have been the ticket, fished on 50-pound fluorocarbon leaders about 15 feet under the surface. The yellowfin come up in the slick just as the sun starts to drop, and they're aggressive. Had one evening where we put six fish in the boat in 90 minutes, all on chunks.

What's really got me excited is the bait situation. The water's been thick with juvenile mahi, those little chickens in the 2 to 5-pound range, and where you find baby mahi, the big pelagics aren't far behind. I'm seeing scattered weed lines holding decent fish too — nothing huge, but schoolies in the 8 to 12-pound class that are perfect for the dinner table. Small feathers and spoons worked through the weed have been producing steady action.

The bluefin situation is interesting. I'm marking fish on the bottom machine in 80 to 120 feet of water, but they're being stubborn. Had one morning where we raised three fish on the troll but couldn't get a hookup. They're there, just not feeding aggressively yet. I suspect once this new moon cycle kicks in and we get some stronger tidal movement, those fish are going to turn on.

Conditions have been about as good as you can ask for — light winds, 1-foot seas, and that gorgeous blue water pushed right up against the shelf. The ride out has been a pleasure, and with fuel prices where they are, that 90-minute run to the break doesn't hurt the wallet as much when you're burning minimal fuel in calm conditions.

Looking ahead to this weekend, I'm watching the weather closely. We've got a weak front approaching that might stir things up a bit, but nothing that should shut down the bite. If anything, a little wind might help concentrate the bait even tighter against that temperature break. The new moon is Friday, which should start pulling some stronger currents through the canyon and potentially fire up those bluefin that have been playing hard to get.

My game plan for the coming week is simple — keep working that temperature break while it's there, because these eddies don't last forever. When the Gulf Stream shifts, and it will, that 72-degree water could disappear as quickly as it showed up. Until then, I'm making hay while the sun shines and putting clients on some of the best yellowfin action we've seen all season.

reports.headline: Canyon bluefin stack deep as 68-degree water holds at the 100-fathom line
reports.subhead: Jigging and stickbaits producing giants in 75 feet of water while trollers work the edges.
reports.body_markdown:
The Hudson Canyon is firing on all cylinders this week, with bluefin tuna stacked in impressive numbers along the 100-fathom line where 68-degree water has settled in and held steady. The temperature gradient we're seeing — 68.2 degrees at the canyon head dropping to the low 60s on the shelf — is creating the kind of thermal barrier that concentrates bait and keeps these fish locked in position.

I've been working the Claw and the Dip hard this past week, and the pattern is clear: these bluefin are holding tight to structure in 75 to 85 feet of water, feeding on bunker schools that are getting pushed up against the thermocline. The fish aren't showing on top like we saw in May during those white-water feeds, but they're absolutely there if you know how to reach them.

Jigging has been the standout technique. I'm dropping 280-gram jigs with beefed-up hooks right to the bottom, then working them slow through the water column. The key is keeping that jig within five feet of the bottom where these fish are holding. On the drift, I'm bouncing them off the deck and bringing them up methodically — no fast retrieves, just steady pumps that mimic wounded bait.

Stickbaits are also producing when you can mark fish on the sounder. The UVT stickbaits in particular have been deadly when worked through schools that are showing 75 feet down. Cast them out and let them sink into the zone, then work them with long, slow sweeps. When these fish are locked on bunker, they want that presentation that looks like a crippled baitfish falling through the column.

The trolling bite has been more selective, but boats working the canyon edges are picking up quality fish on spreader bars and ballyhoo rigs. The key is staying in that 68-degree water and working the temperature breaks where the warm canyon water meets the cooler shelf water. I'm seeing the best action on the incoming tide when current is pushing bait up against the canyon walls.

What's interesting this week is how concentrated the fish are. Instead of scattered pods across miles of water, they're stacked in specific areas where the bottom structure and temperature combine perfectly. The Texas Tower area has been particularly productive, especially on the northeast corner where an eddy has been holding warmer water.

The lunar phase is working in our favor too. We're coming off the new moon, so these spring tides are creating strong current flow that's keeping bait active and fish feeding aggressively. The tide changes have been producing the best action — that switch from slack to moving water seems to trigger feeding windows that last 45 minutes to an hour.

Gear-wise, don't go light. These are legitimate giants we're dealing with, and the rocky bottom of the canyon means you need tackle that can handle both the fish and the structure. I'm running 80-pound braid to 100-pound fluorocarbon leaders, and even then I'm losing some to the rocks. Heavy jig rods in the 50-80 pound class are essential — this isn't the place for finesse gear.

Looking ahead, the weather pattern is setting up perfectly for the weekend. Light northwest winds and calm seas should make the run comfortable, and more importantly, the water temperature is holding steady. That 68-degree mark seems to be the magic number this season, and as long as we maintain that thermal structure, these fish should stay put.

The yellowfin haven't shown up in numbers yet, but I'm expecting them to move in as we get deeper into summer and the water warms another degree or two. For now, it's all about the bluefin, and they're as thick as I've seen them in the canyon in years. If you're making the run, bring plenty of jigs and be prepared to work for them — but when you connect, these fish are worth every minute of the fight.

reports.headline: Raritan Bay bass blitz fires as 68-degree water stacks bunker on the flood
reports.subhead: Inlet fluke bite picking up steam while squid invasion keeps headboats busy from Manasquan south.
reports.body_markdown:
The water finally hit that magic number — 68 degrees in the bay this week — and it's like somebody flipped a switch. The stripers that have been playing hard to get all spring are suddenly everywhere, and I mean everywhere. From the Raritan Bay flats to the back channels behind Sandy Hook, bass are stacked up on bunker schools like it's April all over again.

I've been watching this setup build for two weeks. The bay water climbed from 64 to 68 while the ocean side stayed stuck at 63, and that 5-degree gradient is pure gold. Every flood tide pushes warm bay water out through the inlets, and the bass are riding that thermal highway like a conveyor belt. The bunker know it too — they're thick as thieves from the Shrewsbury rocks all the way down to the Manasquan inlet mouth.

The bite's been best on the moving water, especially that first hour of flood when the warm bay water starts mixing with the cooler ocean stuff. I'm throwing 6-inch white Hogy soft baits on 3/4-ounce jig heads, working them slow through the current breaks. The fish want that bait moving just fast enough to look alive but not so fast they have to work for it. These aren't the aggressive spring fish — they're summer lazy, picking off easy meals.

Down at Manasquan, the inlet's been producing solid keeper fluke on the outgoing tide. The key is getting your bucktail down to the bottom before the current grabs it. I'm using 1-ounce chartreuse bucktails with 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets, bouncing them along the channel edges where the current slows down. The fish are holding in 15 to 20 feet, right where the inlet channel starts to widen into the bay.

But here's the real story nobody's talking about — the squid. They're everywhere from Shark River south, and it's not just bait-sized stuff. The headboats out of Manasquan are running dedicated squid trips and guys are coming back with coolers full of jumbo calamari. The cool water we've had all spring kept them inshore longer than usual, and now they're concentrated in the 30 to 50-foot range. Azori squid jigs in pink and white are absolutely crushing them.

The sea bass bite is still on fire before the regulations change next week. We can keep 10 fish over 12.5 inches until June 30, then it drops to one fish through August. The Axel Carlson reef area has been producing limits in under two hours, with most fish running 14 to 16 inches. Drop a clam rig in 40 feet and hang on — these fish are aggressive and hungry.

Weakfish are starting to show up in the back bays, especially around the Barnegat Bay flats on the evening tides. They're small — mostly 12 to 14 inches — but they're there. Pink Deadly Dick jigs worked slow over the grass beds have been getting bites, though you need to be patient. These fish spook easy in the shallow water.

The porgies are thick around any structure in 20 to 40 feet. High-low rigs with small hooks and clam pieces are the ticket. The fish are running decent size — plenty of 10 to 12-inchers mixed in with the usual pan-sized stuff.

Looking ahead, this new moon cycle should keep the tides moving strong through the weekend. The bay water's still warming — I wouldn't be surprised to see 70 degrees by next week — and that should keep the bass bite going strong. The fluke are definitely moving in from the ocean as the water warms, so the inlet fishing should only get better.

The squid bite might be the sleeper story of the summer. With water temperatures staying cooler than normal, they could stick around inshore well into July. That's rare for this area, but I've seen stranger things happen when the ocean doesn't follow the script.

If you're planning to get out this week, focus on the moving water during the day and the back bay flats in the evening. The bass are there, the fluke are coming, and the squid are a bonus most people aren't even thinking about. Just remember — the sea bass regulations change July 1, so if you want a full bag, get out there before the weekend.

reports.headline: Bay water hits 69 as weakfish crash the party with keeper fluke and sea robins
reports.subhead: Jamaica Bay's trifecta firing on bucktails and clams as stripers start their summer shuffle.
reports.body_markdown:
The bay is alive right now, and I mean really alive. Water temps hit 69 degrees this week, and that magic number has flipped the switch on everything from the Marine Parkway Bridge to the back channels near Cross Bay. We're seeing the classic Jamaica Bay summer transition — stripers moving out to cooler ocean water while the warm-water crew moves in to fill the void.

The big story is weakfish. Real weakfish, not the rumors we've been chasing for years. I'm talking keeper-sized fish to 19 inches mixed in with shorts, hitting bucktails and fresh clams on the incoming tide. The best action has been around the bridge pilings and the deeper holes near the inlet, where that 69-degree bay water meets the slightly cooler ocean flow. These fish are staging up just like they used to, and it's bringing back memories of the old days when weakies were a regular part of the Jamaica Bay mix.

Fluke fishing has turned the corner too. The warming water has them active and feeding, with keepers showing up on white Gulp Swimming Mullets dragged slow on 3/4-ounce bucktails. The key is working the edges where the bay channels drop into deeper water — 12 to 18 feet seems to be the sweet spot. I'm seeing fish to 25 inches, with most keepers running 19 to 22 inches. The outgoing tide has been most productive, especially that first hour when the current really starts to rip.

What's really got me excited is the sea robin explosion. I know, I know — most people curse these guys, but when you're seeing monster sea robins like we are now, it means the bottom is loaded with crabs and worms. That's bait, and where there's bait, bigger fish follow. Plus, these sea robins are eating machines on light tackle, and the big ones make decent table fare if you know how to clean them.

The stripers haven't disappeared completely, but they're definitely thinning out as the water warms. The fish that are still around are mostly smaller slot fish in the 28 to 32-inch range, and they're getting pickier about when they feed. Early morning and late evening are your best shots, especially around the bridge structure where there's still some current and shade.

Bait-wise, fresh clams are absolutely crushing it right now. The weakfish and fluke both love them, and even the sea robins can't resist. I'm running simple fishfinder rigs with 2/0 hooks, keeping the sinker just heavy enough to hold bottom in the current. For the fluke, I'm sticking with that bucktail-and-Gulp combo that's been money all season — white or chartreuse Gulp on a white or pink bucktail head.

The bunker situation is interesting. We're not seeing the massive schools we usually get this time of year, which has some guys worried. But there's still plenty of bait around — spearing, sand eels, and small crabs are thick in the shallows. The lack of big bunker schools might actually be helping the fluke bite, forcing them to focus on smaller, easier targets.

Looking ahead, this warming trend should continue to push more summer species into the bay. I'm expecting porgies to show up in numbers any day now, and the first blackfish of the season shouldn't be far behind as they move into their summer haunts around the bridge pilings and rocky structure.

The new moon this weekend means spring tides and strong currents — perfect for flushing fresh bait through the system and getting fish moving. I'll be focusing on the inlet area where that tidal flow is strongest, especially on the outgoing when everything gets pushed toward the ocean. That's when the big fluke like to set up and ambush whatever comes their way.

reports.headline: Inlet bass blitz fires at sunset as bay water hits 68 degrees
reports.subhead: Trophy stripers crash the jetties on bunker chunks while fluke action heats up on the drift.
