Fish the bunker pods that are left at first light, fish the outgoing in the inlets through the middle of the day, and start paying attention to Cape May again — that southern end of the state is already running on summer time while the rest of us are still chasing the last of the spring fish.

reports.headline: Peconic porgy grind continues as bay warms past the 60-degree threshold
reports.subhead: Estuary thermal stratification between inside bay water and Plum Gut keeps scup pinned to chum lines while weakfish numbers slowly build.
reports.body_markdown:
The analyst desk came in thin this morning — no live buoy pull from the Peconic stations, and the SST package on file dates back to June 3 rather than today. That puts us reasoning from the last known thermal picture and the trajectory of the past two weeks. As of the most recent published imagery, inside-bay water from Noyack through Little Peconic and up into Southold Bay was running solidly into the low-to-mid 60s, with Gardiners and the approaches to Plum Gut and Orient lagging behind by six to ten degrees — the same inside/outside split that has defined this corner of the world since the bass first showed. Wind has been manageable, the bay glassed off through much of last week, and there is no indication the thermocline between the shallow bay basins and the deeper, tide-flushed water off Orient has closed yet.

What that means for the beat is straightforward. The porgies are locked into the warmer inside water — Jessup's, the Greenlawns, the Middle Grounds, the drops off the south side of Shelter Island — and they are responding to chum and tide stage more than to location alone. The bass that are in the system are still relating to the cold edge: Plum Gut, the rips off Orient, the deeper water where bay outflow meets Block Island Sound water in the upper 50s. Weakfish, which historically key on a 60-degree threshold in this estuary, are just beginning to register in respectable numbers, and that is consistent with the bay finally settling into their preferred range over the last ten days. Fluke are filling into the channels but the class is still mixed-heavy on shorts.

The porgy bite this spring has been a notch off the historic May standard — fewer of the easy, anchor-anywhere-and-load-the-box days that this bay is famous for. The fish are present in good size, with plenty of 16- to 19-inch jumbos pushing three pounds in the mix, but they are demanding the right ingredients: a working chum slick of clam, a clean drift or anchor set on a defined edge, and the flood tide doing the work. Drop on the wrong piece of bottom or get there during slack and you will sit. Spots near Shelter Island and the Jessup's complex have been the most reliable producers, while the Greenlawns and Middle Grounds have been streaky — boats sitting on top of marks without converting.

Weakfish have moved from a single-stray-per-trip oddity in mid-May to a legitimate secondary target by month's end, with keeper-class fish to four pounds turning up on porgy drifts and on dedicated drifts over the traditional weakfish bottom inside the bay. The pattern matches the thermal arc — these fish do not commit to the Peconics until the bottom water settles above 60, and we are there. On the bass side, the Plum Gut and Orient story has been a grind-it-out proposition, with slot-class fish available to those willing to work the tide and accept that the inside bay water is still six to ten degrees warmer than the Gut itself. As that gap closes through June, the bass will redistribute.

Looking ahead three to five days, the controlling variable is whether the inside bay pushes through 65 degrees and whether the Gut catches up into the upper 50s. If the warming trend holds and we get the light southwest pattern that has been dominating, the weakfish bite should consolidate into something a reasonable angler can plan a trip around rather than stumble into. The porgies will continue to demand chum discipline but should hold their size class through the moon. Fluke drifts in the deeper channels between Shelter Island and Noyack will start to convert better as the bait — spearing and small bunker — finishes pushing into the bay. Bass in the Gut become a window play: first and last light, hard outgoing, and likely shifting from the cold edge toward the bay proper as the thermal gradient relaxes.

The bay is doing what the bay does in early June — running a touch behind a classic year on the porgy front, building toward a real weakfish window, and holding bass on the cold edge until the thermal door opens. I would be fishing Jessup's on the flood with clam chum, prospecting weakfish on the tide changes, and saving the Orient and Plum Gut bass mission for a dawn outgoing rather than a midday run. The fish are here. The water is telling you which ones and where.

reports.headline: Montauk runs on faith as buoy feed stalls and SST package lags 48 hours
reports.subhead: With no live Montauk station readings in today's analyst sweep, the Point's early-June pattern has to be inferred from the last clean thermal frames and seasonal mechanism.
reports.body_markdown:
The honest lead this morning is that the data desk is thin. The oceanographic analyst published no live conditions for the Point today — no Montauk tide station reading, no fresh buoy package, and the SST catalog tops out at the June 3 frame with a small gap before that. Block Island Sound and the rip line east of the Lighthouse are, for the purposes of this report, being read off three-day-old thermal imagery and the seasonal clock. That clock says early June: inshore water around the Point should be climbing through the mid-to-upper 50s on the south side, with the colder Block Island Sound flank a few degrees behind, and the first real thermal wedge of the season setting up between the rips and the deeper water off North Bar. Until the SST pipeline catches up and a working buoy reading lands, treat any specific temperature number you hear at the dock with appropriate suspicion, mine included.

What the seasonal mechanism predicts for this beat is straightforward. Early June at Montauk is the window when the resident slot-class bass stack up tight to the boulder fields and the first wave of larger fish — the post-spawn migrants working east out of the Race and down from Block — start ghosting through on the stronger tides. The fluke fleet has been finding its rhythm on the south side drops for a couple of weeks now, and porgies have settled onto the hard bottom in Fort Pond Bay and along the north side. Blackfish closed out their spring window and the boats have largely moved on. Without a fresh wind reading I'd assume what the calendar usually delivers: a southwest sea breeze building through the afternoon and laying down overnight, which keeps the south side fishable in the morning and pushes the bite to the lee of the Lighthouse and into the Sound by late day.

On the bass side, the pattern that should be holding is a dropping-tide bite at the Lighthouse rip and along the Shagwong stretch, with bucktails and soft plastics outproducing bait for anyone who can hold bottom in current. Turtle Cove and the pocket east of False Bar are the places to walk if you're working the surf, especially the last two hours of the ebb into the slack. Most of what's coming over the rail right now is slot-class — 28 to 31 — with the occasional fish over 40 inches hitting the deck on the live eel guys working the boulders at night. North Bar is still more of a swing-through than a residence, but the bait push that typically arrives with the first sustained run of 60-degree water should start anchoring fish there within the week.

The fluke story south of the Point is the steadier read. Drift speeds have been workable, the keeper ratio is what it tends to be in early June — heavy on shorts, a respectable handful of doormats mixed in for crews who keep the bait clean and the drift honest. The productive depths have been the 40 to 60 foot drops off the south side, and the bigger fish are still tied to structure transitions, not to flat sand. Porgy fishing in Fort Pond Bay and on the Sound side hard bottom is in the early-season jumbo phase before the smaller resident class crowds the rail.

Look-ahead is where the missing data hurts. Without a current buoy plot I can't pin a wind shift to a tide window with any confidence. What I can say with the seasonal mechanism is this: the next stretch of light southwest air and a clean overnight tide cycle will be the trigger for the boulder fields east of the Lighthouse to fire on overslot fish, and the new moon working toward us later this month will tighten the rip bite considerably. If sand eels are stacking on the south side the way the bait scouts suggested through May, the fluke drift should hold its quality through the next week regardless of what the wind does. The thing to watch is surface temperature crossing 60 on the south side — when that happens the bigger bass start committing to the daytime program at the Point, and the night eel window opens up properly.

I'll have a cleaner report when the buoy feed and the SST package are both current. Until then, fish the tide, fish the structure, and don't overthink it — the Point rewards anglers who show up and read the water in front of them.

reports.headline: Shinnecock runs on memory as live buoy feed goes dark heading into the new moon
reports.subhead: With current SST and tide telemetry unavailable, early-June climatology and a building outgoing put the inlet night bite back in charge.
reports.body_markdown:
The analyst desk came up short this morning. There are no live buoy temperatures, no current tide station readings, and no fresh SST imagery past the June 3 package in the catalog — the pipeline gap is real and worth stating up front rather than dressing up. What we have to work with is the seasonal envelope: early June on the South Shore typically puts Shinnecock Bay surface temps in the mid-60s, with ocean water outside the inlet running three to six degrees cooler depending on wind history. That inside-outside delta is the single most important variable on this beat right now, and absent a hard number from the buoy, the working assumption is that the bay has continued its springtime warm-up while the ocean side is still lagging. New moon arrives June 14, so we're nine days out from peak tidal range, but the spring build is already underway.

What that means, mechanically, is that the inlet is doing exactly what it does every June — acting as a thermal and biological pump. Warmer bay water flushing out on the drop pulls bait with it, and the colder, denser ocean water pushing in on the flood stacks bass on the structure inside the jetty tips and along the rock piles on the west side. With the moon building toward new, outgoing tides through the back half of the night are going to run hard and long. That is striped bass water, and it is the dominant story on this beat until something changes. Slot fish should be the bread and butter on bucktails and soft plastics worked deep in the rip; the bigger class of fish — the overslot resident bass that hang on the inlet through June — will eat a live eel drifted through the same seams after midnight.

The Ponquogue Bridge has been the secondary node, and this is the window when weakfish typically reestablish on the south-side pilings on the last of the incoming and first of the dropping. Water temperature drives that bite as much as anything, and if the bay is sitting where it should be for the calendar, the tiderunners are in the system. Small soft plastics on light jigheads, fished tight to the pilings and let to swing in the current, is the technique that matches what the water is doing. Bluefish have been knocking around the bay in pulses — they will show up on the flats off Tiana on a warm afternoon and disappear by sunset, which is consistent with fish following bait pods rather than holding structure.

Fluke are the question mark. The drift in the channels between the inlet and the Ponquogue Bridge — eight to eighteen feet of water over sand and broken shell — should be producing keepers by now, but the class of fish this early tends to skew short, and you have to work through them. The deeper holes on the east side of the channel, twenty to twenty-five feet, are where the better fish stage before they push up onto the flats later in the month. Bucktail-and-teaser with a strip of squid or a Gulp trailer remains the rig that sorts size from numbers. The Shinnecock Canal, assuming the locks are running on their normal cycle, is the back door to the Peconic and will see its own porgy push any day if it hasn't already.

Looking three to five days out, the controlling factor is the moon. Each night between now and June 14 the outgoing gets a little stronger and a little later, and the back-tide window — that hour on either side of slack low — becomes the high-percentage shot inside the inlet. I'd be watching for any south or southwest wind event that pushes ocean water up against the beach and compresses the thermal gradient at the inlet mouth; that is the setup that triggers a real bass blitz on the outside, with fish hitting the wash at Tiana on the dropping tide. If the SST pipeline comes back online and shows a sharp front setting up off the inlet, that changes the conversation for the bigger fish.

Until the data comes back, the move is conservative and pattern-based: fish the outgoing at the inlet through the dark hours, work the bridge on the tide turn, and treat the bay drift as a daylight operation. The fish are where the calendar says they should be. The instruments are just catching up.

reports.headline: Moriches Inlet runs on stale intel as June bait window opens on the flood
reports.subhead: With the analyst pipeline quiet and the most recent SST package dated June 3, the inlet's tidal mechanics are doing the work the data isn't.
reports.body_markdown:
The oceanographic desk is thin this morning. The Dr. Fish analyst run came in without live buoy temperatures, without a fresh tide-station readout, and with the SST catalog topping out at the June 3 package — two days stale on a stretch of coast where bay water can swing four degrees in 48 hours under a sun-and-southwest pattern. No Moriches-adjacent buoy figure is in hand to publish honestly, so I won't fabricate one. What we do know is structural: the late-May through June 3 imagery showed the standard early-June setup, with bay water running notably warmer than the nearshore Atlantic and a sharp thermal lip stacking right at the throat of Moriches Inlet on every outgoing push. That gradient is the engine of this beat right now, and it doesn't need a new buoy reading to keep turning.

What the gradient means in practice: the inlet is fishing as a thermal door. Warmer bay water dumping out on the ebb pulls bait — primarily spearing and the first real push of peanut bunker staging in the back — over the bar and into the cooler ocean wash, and bass set up on the ocean side of the east and west jetties to ambush them. On the flood, the cooler ocean water sliding back into the bowl is firing the flats inside Cupsogue and the channel edges off Tuthill Point for fluke that want a temperature break from the increasingly warm shallow bay. This is a textbook early-June split: bass on the outside of the inlet on the drop, fluke on the inside flats and channel slopes on the rise. Slot-class linesiders are the realistic target on bucktails and soft plastics worked through the rip; the overslot fish are still mostly a dusk-to-dawn proposition with live or chunked bunker on the ocean-side beach drop at Cupsogue.

On-the-ground signal out of the bay over the last week and a half points to a fluke fishery that is finally finding its rhythm after a slow, cool start. Skinny-water drifts in three to ten feet — the East-West Channel, the slip gut, the edges off the Coast Guard station — have been producing a steady pick of shorts with a workable ratio of keepers mixed in, and the better fish have been coming off the cooler side of the tide rather than the heat of the afternoon. The pattern is classic Moriches: tiny jigs, light braid, a teaser ahead of a Gulp, and a trolling motor or a quiet drift sock to slow the boat down when the southwest builds. Bigger fish to the five- and six-pound class are around for anglers willing to grind the edges instead of camping on the obvious humps.

The surf side at Cupsogue has been the quieter story but the more interesting one. The recent storm cycle has continued to nudge sand around the east end of the inlet, and the bowl that formed late last season is still holding fish on the dropping tide an hour before and after low. Bluefish in the four-to-eight-pound class have been the dominant predator on metal at first light, with bass mixed in on darters and bucktails after dark. Weakfish — which had a real showing in the back bay last June around Tuthill and the mouth of the Forge — are worth probing on small soft plastics and pink shad bodies on the last of the outgoing through the deeper holes.

The next three to five days hinge on wind. Anything sustained out of the southwest above 15 will stack warm surface water against the north shore of the bay, push the thermocline down on the flats, and shut the daytime fluke bite off until the tide flips. A clocking northwest or a clean morning calm is the window — fish it hard at the inlet on the last two hours of the ebb. The moon is building toward fuller phases, which will sharpen the tidal velocity through the inlet throat and concentrate bait on the edges of the rips; that's the mechanism to watch, not the calendar. If the SST pipeline catches up and confirms the offshore wash is still sitting in the high 50s while the bay pushes past 65, expect the bass bite at the mouth to peak right at that thermal seam.

The data is thinner than I'd like to publish on, and I've flagged that honestly. But the inlet doesn't care about pipeline status. It runs on bathymetry, tide, and temperature differential, and all three are lined up for a productive week for anglers who fish the right side of the tide on the right side of the bar.

reports.headline: Bay warms ahead of ocean as June bait push lights up Fire Island Inlet
reports.subhead: With live oceanographic feeds thin this cycle, the controlling variable remains the estuary-to-ocean thermal gradient driving bass and fluke onto inlet structure.
reports.body_markdown:
The analyst desk is running lean this morning — no fresh buoy temperature readings came across the wire for Fire Island Inlet, and the published SST package is three days stale, dated June 3. Tide station feeds from Kings Point, Montauk, Battery, Bridgeport and Sandy Hook were carried over from the prior day rather than refreshed, and the offshore thermal imagery for June 4 and June 5 has not landed in the catalog. So this report leans on the physics of the calendar rather than a real-time number on a screen. Early June on the South Shore means one thing: the Great South Bay is running materially warmer than the nearshore ocean, the inlet is a thermal chimney, and every tide cycle is moving a wedge of warm bay water out into a cooler Atlantic on the ebb and dragging cleaner ocean water back in on the flood. That gradient is the engine right now.

For this beat, that means the inlet itself is the headline structure, not the open beach and not the back-bay flats yet. The Robert Moses bridge abutments, the sod banks at Sore Thumb, the channel edge off Democrat Point, and the rips on the outside of the inlet are all stacking bait against current seams. Bunker have been pushing into the bay on the flood for two weeks, and squid are still in the mix on the ocean side. The slot-class striper bite is the dominant signature — fish in that 28–31 inch window staging on moving water — with a meaningful population of overs mixed in around the bigger bait balls. Fluke have set up at the bridges and along the Sore Thumb-to-buoy 11 drift in 18 to 28 feet, with the better keeper ratio coming from the ocean-side drops rather than the inside flats, which are still throwing back too many shorts.

The Captree night bite has been the most consistent producer on the beat over the last three weeks. The pattern that has emerged is a clear shift away from clam baits — which have been getting overrun by dogfish on anchor — and toward soft plastics worked on the drift through the bridge lights and along the channel edges. Paddletails and jerk-shad style baits on a half-ounce to one-ounce head, fished on the down-current side of structure, have been pulling slot fish and a steady mix of overs after dark. Daytime, the bridges are giving up fluke on bucktail-and-Gulp combos, with the pool fish on the open boats coming from drifts that work the channel slope rather than sitting on the flat.

On the surf side, Democrat Point through the Robert Moses fields is the spot to walk at first light and last light. The wash is still cool, so the bigger bass are moving in tight to the bar on the low-light windows and pulling off when the sun gets up. Bucktails and small metal-lip swimmers in the dropping tide have been the higher-percentage approach over big plugs — the bait being eaten right now is on the smaller side, sand eels and spearing more than full-size bunker once you're outside the inlet mouth. Bluefish have been a sporadic presence, not a wall yet, and that's consistent with ocean temps still lagging the bay.

Looking three to five days out, the watch items are wind direction and the continued climb in bay temperature. A sustained southwest flow will push the warm bay surface layer out the inlet on the ebb and set up a sharp front just outside Democrat Point — that's where I'd be watching for the first real surface blitz of the season if it holds. Any meaningful east wind will stand the inlet up and scramble the drift for the open boats, pushing the fleet inside to the bridges. The new moon mid-month will tighten the tide windows and concentrate the bite into shorter, harder pulses, especially on the outgoing through the inlet between two and four hours down. If the ocean catches up to the bay by even two or three degrees this week, expect weakfish reports to firm up around the Patchogue and Sayville channels, where the warming flats meet deeper water.

The bay is ahead of the ocean, the inlet is doing the work, and the fish are using the gradient exactly the way they're supposed to in early June. Fish the moving water, fish the edges, and don't overthink the bait — match what's actually swimming, work the seams, and let the tide tell you when to be where.

reports.headline: Jones Inlet sits in a data fog as early-June bait stacks build inside the bay
reports.subhead: With buoy and SST feeds running thin, the read is on bait position and tide stage — bunker pods inside the inlet are the controlling variable.
reports.body_markdown:
The analyst desk is running with a partial deck this morning. No live buoy temperatures came through the Dr. Fish pipeline overnight, the most recent published SST package is two days stale out of June 3, and the tide station feeds that normally anchor a Jones Inlet read — Sandy Hook to the west, Montauk to the east — are not refreshed in today's brief. That means the report has to lean on what the water was doing 48 to 72 hours ago and on what early June around Jones Inlet typically delivers when the bay has had a stretch of settled weather behind it. The June 3 SST imagery, before the gap, showed the South Shore inshore band running warmer than the open Atlantic by a meaningful margin — the classic estuary-thermal setup where Hempstead Bay acts as a shallow solar panel and the inlet throat becomes the exchange valve twice a day. Bunker, both adult and peanut class, have been visible from the Wantagh Bridge south to the inlet mouth for the past two weeks, and that bait position is the single most useful piece of information on the board today.

What that means for the beat is straightforward. When the inside water is several degrees warmer than the ocean and bunker are stacked in the bay, the bass behavior splits cleanly by tide. On the outgoing, the predators set up on the ocean side of the inlet — the west bar off Jones Beach, the rip line off Point Lookout, and the deeper slot just outside the green can — and ambush bait getting swept out. On the incoming, the bite migrates inside, with fish pushing up the channel edges past the Coast Guard station and into the deeper holes behind Short Beach. Early June in this water column is a slot-and-overslot story, not a schoolie story; the fish working bunker right now are the post-spawn migrants from the Hudson and Raritan, and they are hungry, lean, and aggressive on big profiles.

The on-the-ground intelligence supports that picture. Bunker schools have been holding under birds inside the inlet on the morning incoming, and the reports of bass on big paddle-tail soft plastics in white — the bigger the better — match what the water column is asking for. Diamond jigging has been notably soft compared to plastics and big swimmers, which tells you the fish are keyed on full-bodied bait, not sand eels. Snag-and-drop with live bunker, when you can find a tight pod, is the high-percentage play at first light around the inlet markers. The fluke fleet has started to settle into the Meadowbrook Bridge southeast corner and the channel edges between the second and third Wantagh, with most of the action still on the short side of the slot — squid and smelt combos on white bucktails are doing the work, and a teaser dressed small is outproducing a bare hook.

Weakfish chatter is quiet but the water is right for them. The deeper holes in the Sloop Channel and the cuts north of the Loop Parkway bridge are worth a slow drift with pink or chartreuse plastics on a light jig as the sun drops. Bluefish are scattered — the snapper class is still building in the back, but legitimate cocktail blues to three or four pounds have been mixed in with the bass on the bunker schools, and any wire leader work near a visible pod will tell you quickly which predator is in charge that morning.

The next three to five days hinge on wind. If the forecast holds light southwest through the weekend, the inlet water will continue to warm and stratify, the bunker will stay put, and the morning incoming will be the window. A hard northeast or a frontal passage flips that — it pushes bait out of the bay, dirties the inlet, and shifts the bite to the ocean side of Jones Beach for a day or two before the system resets. With the SST pipeline behind schedule, I would not commit to a long offshore run on speculation; the inshore engine is firing and the bait is in front of you. Watch the bird work at the inlet mouth on the last two hours of the flood, and watch what the bunker pods do when the tide turns — that is the tell.

The inlet is fishing the way early June is supposed to fish when the bay warms before the ocean does. Big plastics, live bunker when you can get them, and a willingness to move with the bait rather than camp on a number. The data feed will catch up. The fish will not wait for it.

reports.headline: Jamaica Bay sits in early-June transition as analyst pipeline runs dark
reports.subhead: With no live buoy or SST data in today's analyst feed, the bay's thermal lag versus the ocean remains the controlling variable for bass, fluke and weakfish positioning.
reports.body_markdown:
The oceanographic desk came in thin this morning. The Dr. Fish analyst run is carrying no live buoy readings, no current tide-station data, and the SST package hasn't refreshed since June 3 — the most recent thermal imagery in the catalog is two days stale, and we have no verified surface temperature to attach to Ambrose, Rockaway, or the inside stations. That is the honest top of the report. What we can say with confidence, based on the early-June climatology of this estuary and the June 1–3 SST frames that did publish, is that the bay's interior is running meaningfully warmer than the inlet and the open ocean off Breezy. By the first week of June the back bay flats — the broad shallows behind Canarsie Pier, the marsh edges south of the Cross Bay Bridge — are typically pushing into the mid-60s while the inlet itself and the surf along Rockaway are still in the high 50s to low 60s. That thermal gradient is the engine right now.

What that gradient means for this beat is straightforward. Bait — bunker, spearing, the first real push of sand eels along the ocean side — stacks on the temperature break, and the bass stage on the structure that sits across it. The Marine Parkway Bridge is the obvious one: warmer water dumping out of the bay on the back half of the ebb, colder ocean water pressing in on the flood, and bridge abutments creating the eddy lines that hold fish on both sides of the swing. This is a slot-class window. The big April and early-May overslot bass that ate chunked bunker on the flats are largely gone or going; what's left and what's arriving is the 28-to-36-inch class working the bridge, the inlet rips off Breezy, and the deeper holes inside the bay on moving water. Fluke have opened up and the bay floor is warm enough — the channel edges from the Marine Parkway east toward the airport flats are the early-season play, drifting bucktail-and-teaser rigs in 12 to 22 feet on the last of the incoming.

On-the-ground intelligence supports the staging picture. The chunk bite that defined April in the back of the bay has clearly tapered, and the conversation has shifted to bucktails, soft plastics, and the first serious fluke drifts of the season. Weakfish are in the mix again — the bay has quietly held a real spring weakfish class the last couple of years, and the pattern of mixed bass, weaks, and short fluke on the same incoming tide drifts in 10 to 15 feet is exactly the early-June signature this estuary throws when the interior warms ahead of the ocean. The surf side is the laggard. Rockaway Beach from B 32nd east through the numbered streets is still a morning-and-dusk proposition with bunker schools nosing along the bar but no consistent daytime blitz yet; the water out front simply isn't warm enough to hold bait through the heat of the day.

Looking three to five days out, the variables to watch are wind direction and the moon. Any sustained southwest pushes bunker tight to the Rockaway beachfront and stacks them against the west jetty at Breezy on the outgoing, which is when the inlet turns on for shore casters working bucktails and soldiers off the rocks. A flip to onshore east winds will scour the surf, color up the inlet, and push the action inside the bay onto the bridge and the deeper channel edges. The bay interior will continue to warm faster than the ocean for at least another week, which means the thermal gradient at the inlet sharpens before it dulls — and sharper gradients hold more bait and more fish. I'd be watching the Marine Parkway on the last two hours of the outgoing into the bottom of the tide, particularly on the dawn slot, and I'd be running fluke drifts on the flood through the middle of the day.

Without a live SST refresh and without buoy numbers in hand, this is a report built on structure, season, and what the water has to be doing given the calendar. When the pipeline catches up I'll have hard numbers on the inlet-versus-interior break and we can sharpen the bridge call. Until then, fish the moving water, fish the edges, and respect that the bay is two weeks ahead of the ocean right now.

reports.headline: Race and Gut wait on data as June bass class settles into slot-fish pattern
reports.subhead: Buoy and tide feeds offline for the run, but seasonal thermal range and bait stage point to a classic early-June rip bite on the ebb.
reports.body_markdown:
The oceanographic desk came up thin this morning. The Dr. Fish analyst run published no live conditions, no current buoy readings, and no tide station numbers — Kings Point, Montauk, Bridgeport and New London are all dark in today's package. The most recent published SST imagery in the catalog is dated June 3, two days stale, and no June 4 or June 5 thermal frames have cleared the pipeline. That means there is no verified water-temperature figure to anchor this report against, and the eddy and front structure off the east end has to be inferred from the early-June climatology rather than read off a chart. What we can say with confidence: the Sound is in its early-June warming ramp, which in this zone historically means surface temps in the upper 50s to low 60s through the Race and Gut, with the outside water off Fishers and Plum running a tick cooler than the inside Gardiners and Peconic system. Bunker have been around the east end for weeks, sand eels are stacked on the harder bottom out toward Valiant Rock, and squid are still in the mix on the moon tides.

For the beat, that thermal window is the sweet spot. Bass are fully transitioned out of the spring staging mode and into rip-feeding posture. The Race and Plum Gut are the two engines driving the zone right now, and both fish the ebb harder than the flood at this stage of June — the ebb pulls colder, bait-loaded water out of Gardiners Bay through the Gut and dumps it into the temperature break at the west end of the Race, which is where the predator class sets up. Expect a slot-heavy box with a real shot at overs on the bigger moon tides, and bluefish moving in and shredding tails the second the bass window closes. Fluke are on the sand edges off Orient and the north side of Gardiners, and porgies are thick on any hard bottom from Mattituck east.

The Gut bite has been running a classic pattern — three-way rigs with bucktails down deep on the heavy current, then switching to surface presentations when the birds start working and fish push bait to the top. A six-foot casting rod with a small pencil popper has been a real weapon at the back end of the ebb when the rip lays down and fish come up on scattered bait. Drift discipline matters more than lure choice. The boats putting fish on ice are the ones managing their drift line on the down-current side of the rip and not getting swept into the standing water. Power-drifting through the slack into the early ebb has produced quality fish for guys willing to bump in and out of gear instead of just setting up for the screaming current.

Out at the Race, the boat traffic is going to be the limiting factor on weekends. Setting a clean drift through a fleet of 30 boats is harder than catching the fish. The bigger biomass is on the CT side near Valiant, and the bluefish presence is heavy enough that bucktail attrition is real — bring twice what you think you need. Soft plastics on a heavy jighead have been outproducing bucktails for guys who can keep them in the strike zone, particularly when the bass are keyed on sand eels rather than squid. Fishers Island rock structure is starting to fish for the wader crowd on the night tides, and the surf line from Orient State Park east is worth a 3 a.m. shot on a moving tide with a big swimmer.

Looking ahead three to five days, the controlling variable is going to be wind direction relative to tide. A sustained southwest will pile bait against the north-facing shorelines and prop up the daytime bite at the Gut. A northeast blow shuts the Race down for small boats and pushes the action inside to Plum Gut and the bay drops. The next significant moon push is the driver — when current velocity ramps, the overslot class moves in on the rips and the night bite on the Fishers rocks gets serious. I want updated SST imagery and a live read on the New London buoy before I commit to calling a thermal break location, but the seasonal mechanics are lined up.

Fish the ebb, manage your drift, and do not waste a clean weather window waiting for perfect intel. The water is ready.

reports.headline: Central Sound waits on data as June bait window opens between Stratford Shoal and the Norwalk Islands
reports.subhead: With the analyst pipeline thin on live buoy figures, seasonal thermal structure and bait timing point to a developing slot bass and porgy bite mid-Sound.
reports.body_markdown:
The honest lead this morning is that the oceanographic desk is running short. The Dr. Fish analyst package landed without live buoy readings, the SST chart catalog tops out at June 3, and tide station figures from Kings Point and Bridgeport are a day stale. That means no hard Fahrenheit number to hang on Execution Rocks, Stratford Shoal, or New Haven this dateline, and I'm not going to invent one. What we do have is the seasonal envelope — early June, post-Memorial-Day, sun angle climbing fast, freshwater pulses out of the Housatonic and the Connecticut River still cooling the north shore of the basin while the shallow south-shore bays of the Sound (Oyster, Huntington, Northport, Port Jeff inside) warm faster on each flood. That cross-basin thermal gradient is the controlling variable right now, even if I can't put a decimal on it.

For the Central Sound beat that translates to a very specific picture. The inside harbors are running ahead of the main basin, which means the bunker schools that wintered offshore are now staged along the mouths — Pier-to-Pier off Port Jefferson, the Asharoken shoreline, the Norwalk Islands chain — and bass are working the thermal edge where warm harbor water spills out on the ebb. Mid-Sound structure like Stratford Shoal and Middle Ground Light is the next tier; the water there is still cooler and is fishing more like mid-May than June, which favors a slower presentation. Slot bass (28–31 inches) should be the dominant class on the edges, with overslot fish keying on the bunker pods closer to the harbor mouths. Porgies have arrived on the Connecticut side rockpiles in the 25–40 foot band and that bite is the most reliable thing in the zone right now.

On the ground, the signal out of the Port Jefferson side has been a steady porgy pick on the CT shoreline drops between roughly 30 and 40 feet, with sea bass still mostly shorts and the occasional keeper mixed in — the keeper-to-short ratio that defined last summer's central Sound sea bass picture has not yet flipped, and won't until bottom temps climb another few degrees. The bass story is more about location than volume: fish are being found, but they're concentrated on bait, and boats running and gunning between the Norwalk Islands and Eatons Neck are doing better than anyone parked on a single piece. Soft plastics on a quarter to three-eighths jighead are out-producing bucktails in the harbor mouths during the low-light windows, while bigger profile swimbaits and live bunker matter on the open-water bunker pods.

The Stratford Shoal rip is in its transitional phase. Bass are there but the bait sign is inconsistent, and without a clean SST front to point at I'd treat the Shoal as a tide-stage play rather than an all-day destination — work the last two hours of the ebb into the first of the flood, fish the down-current side of the bathymetry, and move on if you don't mark bait inside thirty minutes. Blackfish season is closed in New York Sound waters in early June, so the rockpile crowd has shifted to porgies and sea bass culling, and that's where the central CT shoreline drops between Stamford and New Haven earn their keep.

Looking three to five days out, the move to watch is wind. A sustained south or southwest breeze stacks warm surface water against the north shore of Long Island and pushes the thermal break north, which historically lights up the Norwalk Islands and the Charles Island stretch first. A northerly knockdown does the opposite and resets the bass back toward the LI side harbor mouths. The new moon arrives next week, which sharpens the tidal range and will make Stratford Shoal and the Middle Ground fish noticeably better on the bigger ebbs. If the SST pipeline catches back up in the next 48 hours I'll have a real number to attach to all of this; until then, fish the mechanism.

The central Sound is doing exactly what early June is supposed to do — warming unevenly, concentrating bait at the thermal seams, and rewarding anglers who move with the tide rather than camping. Slot bass on the harbor-mouth edges, porgies on the CT rockpiles, and a Stratford Shoal program that's still finding its rhythm. That's the read, data gaps and all.

reports.headline: Western Sound settles into early-June slot pattern as bunker stack the mid-Sound rockpiles
reports.subhead: With the analyst's live buoy feed dark today, June 3 SST imagery and bait-class signals point to a structure-and-tide game from Execution Rocks to Matinecock.
reports.body_markdown:
The primary oceanographic feed came in thin this morning — the analyst flagged no live tide-station or buoy readings in today's package, and the most recent published SST imagery in the catalog is dated June 3. That's a two-day gap on the satellite side and a full blackout on Kings Point real-time numbers, so the read on the Western Sound has to lean on the trajectory the data was already on: a Sound that crossed the 60-degree threshold in the second half of May, surface temperatures climbing into the low-to-mid 60s on the June 3 chart inside the Throgs Neck-to-Execution line, and a soft thermal gradient between the warmer harbor water of Little Neck, Manhasset and Hempstead and the cooler, better-flushed mid-Sound. Wind has been manageable, seas inside Execution are running tight, and there is no evidence of a fresh upwelling event to scramble the pattern.

That thermal setup is exactly where the Western Sound wants to be in early June. Bait is the controlling variable now, not temperature — adult bunker have set up on the mid-Sound rockpiles and along the deeper edges off Matinecock Point, and the resident slot-class bass have stopped chasing and started camping. The fishery this week is a structure game on moving water: Execution Rocks on the back half of the outgoing, the Stepping Stones light on the first two hours of the flood, and the deep edge off Matinecock whenever the tide is actually doing something. Overslot fish are around but they are the exception; the meat of the class is 28 to 33 inches, and that is what trolled mojos, three-way bunker spoons, and snag-and-drop livies are connecting with.

The on-the-water intelligence over the past ten days reinforces it. The trolling crowd working the mid-Sound has been into slot fish on mojos and spoons with almost no shorts mixed in, which tells you the year-class structure here is mature and the bait is large — peanut-sized profiles showing in the bays back that up, and it is unusual to see that size class this early. Jigging marked fish near the harbor mouths and lighthouses has produced as well, including egg-laden females still holding roe, which means the spawning push out of the western tributaries is not fully unwound yet and you still have post-spawn fish refueling hard on whatever they can corner against structure.

The fluke side of the beat is honest but not generous. The Oyster Bay-to-Lloyd Neck drift and the ground off the CSH light have been producing shorts with the occasional measurable fish, and the lack of dense bait pods on the sand has kept the bite from turning on. Drifts have been short and the better fish have come on jigs tipped with Gulp rather than on classic bucktail-and-strip presentations — a sign the fish are sitting tighter to structure than to open sand, which is consistent with water that is still organizing thermally. Porgies are setting up on the harder bottom from Hart Island east and the blackfish window is closed, so the bottom rotation right now is fluke on the edges and scup on the rocks.

Looking three to five days out, the move to watch is the next stretch of southwest wind. A sustained southwest will push warmer surface water up against the North Shore, tighten the bunker schools against Matinecock and the Bayville shoreline, and concentrate the bass on the upcurrent side of every prominent rockpile. If the analyst pipeline catches up and the next SST package shows the inside water pressing into the upper 60s while the mid-Sound stays in the low 60s, expect the dawn topwater window at Stepping Stones and along the Hart Island edge to sharpen considerably. A hard northeast would do the opposite — knock the surface temp back, scatter the bunker, and force a return to deeper presentations on the troll.

For now the playbook is straightforward. Fish moving water on hard structure, match the adult-bunker profile, and accept that the class of fish in front of you is slot and low-overslot rather than trophy. The Western Sound is doing in early June exactly what a healthy Western Sound is supposed to do, and the next satellite pass and a live Kings Point reading will tell us whether the next leg of the run is already staged behind it.

reports.headline: Sandy Hook at 63 degrees turns Raritan Bay into the engine room of the spring run
reports.subhead: A four-to-six degree thermal gap between the back of the bay and the open Bight is concentrating bunker and bass inside the rips.
reports.body_markdown:
The Sandy Hook tide gauge (NOAA 8531680) is reading 63.1°F this morning, while buoy 44025 out in the New York Bight is sitting at 57.0°F and the Harbor Entrance buoy 44065 is at 57.4°F under a northwest wind of 11.7 knots gusting to 15.6, pressure 1016 hPa and holding. Block Island (44097) is at 56.1°F with a short, choppy 2.6-foot sea on a three-second period — leftover wind slop, not clean groundswell. The picture from Ambrose south to Barnegat is a classic late-May setup: the open ocean is still locked in the mid-to-upper 50s while the back of Raritan, the Shrewsbury and Navesink, Shark River, and the Barnegat back bays are pushing into the low 60s by mid-afternoon. The offshore SST package is two days stale (latest run 5/27), so I'm leaning on the in-situ tide-gauge temps and the buoy network, which tell the same story anyway.

What that thermal gap means for this beat is simple and it's the whole game right now: bait and bass are sitting inside the warm envelope, and the predators only slide out to the ocean side on the tide stages that flush warm water through the inlets. Raritan Bay is the obvious star at 63°F — that's bunker temperature, that's the temperature that holds the big resident and migratory cows that have been chewing through the western bay for the last two weeks. Down the coast, Manasquan and Barnegat inlets become outflow funnels on the drop, with the bay water two to four degrees warmer than the ocean it's dumping into, and that delta sets up a hard scent and temperature seam that fish will stack on. Cape May rips are the southern bookend of the same mechanism. Open surf on the straight beaches — Island Beach, Long Beach Island front, the Hook's north end — is the weakest play in the lineup until that ocean climbs another three to five degrees.

In Raritan, the bite remains a bunker game. Snag-and-drop on the western flats from the Reach Channel west toward the Conaskonk and around the Romer Shoal edges has been producing the overslot and trophy class, with the better grade of fish — 36 to 44 inches — keying on live or fresh-cut bunker fished on the moving water rather than the slack. The morning outgoing has been more consistent than the flood for the larger class. Bluefish, including chopper-grade fish, have been mixed in heavily enough that wire or heavy fluoro is not optional if you want your plugs back. The Hook rips on the ebb, particularly the north tip down through the False Hook, are holding fish on the swing as bait gets pulled out of the bay.

South of the Manasquan, the inlet game has tilted toward soft plastics and bucktails worked on the outgoing through the last two hours of the drop. Shark River has fluke in the channel and back by the train bridge with the warm-water flats producing better than the ocean side — the ocean fluke bite needs another warming cycle before it lights up off the Axel Carlson and the Klondike. Barnegat Inlet is fishing similarly: bass on the outflow seam, fluke staging on the bayside flats where the sun has the mud up into the low 60s by afternoon. Weakfish reports out of the Mullica and Great Bay back are consistent with what the thermal data would predict — small tides, warm flats, pink and chartreuse plastics on a light jig. Cape May rips and the Delaware Bay side are still holding fish that haven't moved north yet, which is normal for the calendar.

Looking out three to five days, the northwest flow knocks the ocean down by tomorrow afternoon and the next push of warmth into the back bays accelerates with light winds and sun in the forecast window. Watch for the Sandy Hook gauge to push 65°F by the weekend — that's the threshold where the bunker schools start sliding out of the bay and stretching down the Monmouth beaches, and that's when the Hook surf and the Long Branch-to-Deal stretch turns on for real. New moon is approaching, which means bigger tidal exchanges and stronger outflow plumes at every inlet from Shark River to Little Egg. If an east wind shows up later in the week, the ocean shuts down again and everything collapses back inside — plan accordingly.

The season is exactly where it should be on the calendar, maybe a hair ahead inside. Raritan is in its peak window right now and that window does not stay open forever. Fish the bunker, fish the moving water, and do not waste a tide standing on a cold ocean beach when the bay is six degrees warmer two miles behind you.

reports.headline: Bay thermal engine carries the Jamaica Bay bite while the ocean side stays sloppy
reports.subhead: A 6-degree delta between NY Bight at 57°F and the back-bay flats is stacking bass, weakfish and fluke on inlet structure and marsh drains.
reports.body_markdown:
The numbers tell the whole story this week. Buoy 44025 in the NY Bight is sitting at 57.0°F with a 2.3-foot southeast swell at a 9-second period, and 44065 at the Harbor Entrance is reading 57.4°F with a 12-knot northwest breeze gusting to 15. Sandy Hook, the closest comparable inside reading to our beat, is up to 63.1°F. That is a six-degree thermal wall between the open coast and the protected bay water, and it is the single most important fact on the Rockaway peninsula right now. The offshore SST package is two days stale (latest available is 5/27) and buoys 44039 and 44040 are offline, so I am reasoning off in-situ buoy and tide-gauge water temps rather than satellite imagery — but the structure is unambiguous.

For Jamaica Bay specifically, that delta means the engine is running inside the inlet, not outside it. Bass, weakfish, and fluke that would otherwise be spreading along the Rockaway beachfront are compressed into the warmer envelope behind Breezy Point. The Marine Parkway Bridge is the choke point where that warm bay water dumps on the ebb, and it is doing exactly what it does every late May — stacking bass on the down-current side of the pilings on the back half of the outgoing. Slot and overslot class fish are the dominant size structure regionally right now, with very few schoolies in the mix, which matches what the migration timing should be producing here. The Rockaway oceanfront is not dead, but with a southeast swell still wrapping in and the water on that side stuck in the upper 50s, it is a sand-eel-and-current-seam game, not a blitz game.

Inside the bay, the bite has clearly tipped from the early-spring chunking pattern into a more active presentation window. Bunker and river herring are thick in the bay and the warm afternoon flood is pulling bait up onto the flats off Canarsie Pier and the marsh edges behind Broad Channel. The plug and soft-plastic crowd is doing as well or better than the bait crowd now that water temps in the back are pushing into the low 60s during sunny afternoons — a bone-colored slim minnow or a 9-inch paddletail worked along the channel edges on the last two hours of the drop is the highest-percentage cast. Fluke have shown up on the shallowest, darkest-bottom flats inside the bay, and the keeper ratio is poor but improving — bucktail-and-teaser drifts in 8 to 15 feet over the mud are producing fish, with the occasional weakfish mixed in as a bonus that tells you the water has warmed enough to matter.

The Cross Bay Bridge area is fishing on a different clock than the Marine Parkway. Cross Bay sees its best window on the top of the incoming into the first of the ebb, when warm flat-water is being pushed back against the pilings; Marine Parkway is an outgoing bridge, full stop, and the last two hours before dead low into the first of the flood is when the better class of fish eats. From shore, the rocks on the Brooklyn side of Marine Parkway and the pocket west of the bridge are the access points worth walking. Breezy Point tip is fishable but the southeast swell is making the wash ugly — I would give it another two days.

Looking ahead three to five days, the northwest wind on the back side of this pressure system should knock down the ocean swell by the weekend and let the Rockaway beachfront clean up. If the bay holds at or above 62°F through the next warm afternoon cycle, expect the fluke bite to expand from the inside flats out toward the inlet proper, and watch for the first real weakfish push to set up around the channel edges behind Ruffle Bar. The June new moon is still a week and change out, but tides are already building, which favors the bridge bite on the back end of every ebb between now and then.

The pattern is simple and it is going to hold: fish the warm water, fish the moving water, and fish the structure where those two things intersect. The bay is doing the work right now. The ocean side will catch up when the swell lays down and the inshore SST climbs another three or four degrees.

reports.headline: Thermal break at Jones Inlet stacks bait inside while ocean stays raw
reports.subhead: NY Bight buoy 44025 holding 57°F with a 9-second southeast swell keeps the bite pinned to back-bay channels and the inlet throat.
reports.body_markdown:
The water is talking, and right now it's saying stay inside. NDBC 44025 in the NY Bight is reading 57.0°F with a 2.3-foot sea on a 9-second dominant period out of 122 degrees — that long-period southeast swell is the residual of the unsettled coastal regime that has been hammering the open beach for the better part of a week. NY Harbor Entrance buoy 44065 is sitting at 57.4°F with a northwest wind at 11.7 knots gusting to 15.6, pressure 1016 hPa, so the atmosphere is finally cleaning up even as the ocean stays lumpy. Sandy Hook tide-gauge water is already at 63.1°F and Kings Point at 58.6°F, which frames the controlling story: the back is four to six degrees warmer than the front. Hempstead Bay falls right inside that warm envelope. The offshore SST package is two days stale and 44039/44040 are offline, so we are reasoning off buoys and tide-station thermistors, but the gradient is unambiguous.

What that means for Jones Inlet is simple. The thermal break is doing the work of concentrating bait, and the bait is concentrating fish at the choke points. The inlet throat itself, the rip off the west jetty, and the deep slot just inside the green can on the east side are the prime real estate on the back half of the outgoing, when warm bay water dumps over that 18-to-24-foot trough and meets the colder ocean push. Bass are sitting on the seam. The Sloop Channel edges and the deeper holes behind Short Beach hold fluke on the incoming as that warm sheet floods back over the flats — but the ocean fluke drift out front of Jones Beach is still a week or two away from being worth the fuel, because nothing outside the bar has cracked 58°F yet.

The Wantagh corridor — the second and third Wantagh bridges down through Meadowbrook — is fishing the way it should fish at the end of May. Fluke are stacked but the size class is mostly shorts and an occasional 17- to 19-inch keeper, with the better fish coming on bigger profile baits: a white bucktail with a 4- to 5-inch Gulp or a smelt-tipped teaser, worked slow on the south side of the bridge abutments where the current scours out the deeper trough. Squid alone is feeding too many shorts. The bass picture is the louder one. With western Sound and East End surf both producing overslot and trophy-class fish on bunker and mackerel through the back half of May, the Jones corridor is squarely in the migration lane and the bunker schools have been holding inside the inlet on the morning slack. Live-lining a bunker on a 7/0 circle in the inlet bowl at first light, or pitching a wide-body soft plastic — a 9-inch white or bone Slug-Go on a 3/4-ounce head — along the jetty rocks on the dropping tide, is the high-percentage play for a slot or better.

The surf side is still compromised. That 9-second southeast period means the wash at Jones Beach proper is dirty and the bar is rolling, so the open-sand bite is restricted to the pocket water — the bowl just west of the inlet jetty, the cuts at Field 6, and any spot where you can find a defined current break. Weakfish are showing inside the bay, which tracks with the thermal story; the shallow mud east of the Meadowbrook on a warm afternoon ebb is the spot to throw a small pink or chartreuse paddletail on a quarter-ounce head and find out. Blackfish season is closed and porgies are still building inshore, so those are background notes, not headline acts.

Looking out three to five days, the northwest flow behind this system should knock the swell down by midweek and the ocean side will start to clean up. More importantly, with daytime highs forecast to push back into the 70s and light winds, the inside water will climb another degree or two and Democrat Point and the inlet flats will likely break 62°F by the weekend. That is the threshold where the ocean fluke drift south of the inlet starts to come alive and where weakfish activity in the bay shifts from sporadic to reliable. The new moon on June 6 brings stronger tides, which will rip the inlet harder on the outgoing and tighten the bass bite to the slack edges.

Fish the inside, fish the seams, and respect the swell. The inlet is where the engine is running right now, and it will keep running until the ocean catches up.

reports.headline: Estuary thermal engine fires Great South Bay as ocean stays cold and sloppy
reports.subhead: A 5- to 6-degree delta between back-bay flats and the NY Bight is stacking bass and bait inside the inlet while the open beach stays restricted.
reports.body_markdown:
The controlling number this week is the gap between inside and outside. Buoy 44025 in the NY Bight is sitting at 57.0°F with a 2.3-foot sea on a 9-second period out of the southeast, and 44065 at the Harbor Entrance is reading 57.4°F under a 12-knot northwest breeze gusting 16. Block Island's 44097 is colder still at 56.1°F. Meanwhile the inside stations tell a different story — Kings Point is already at 58.6°F and Montauk's tide gauge is at 59.4°F, and on a sun-soaked afternoon the back-bay flats from Babylon east to Patchogue are running warmer than either. Sandy Hook, our nearest analog to a fully estuarine bay station, has climbed to 63.1°F. That's a five- to six-degree thermal engine separating the bay from the open Atlantic, and it is doing all the work right now.

What that means on this beat is simple: the fish are inside, not outside. The ocean is cold, energetic, and the sea state from a residual southeast swell makes Democrat Point and the open Fire Island surf an uncomfortable, unproductive proposition for most boats and a tough wade for surfcasters. The bait — river herring still trickling out of the creeks, bunker schools that have pushed into the bay, and the resident spearing — is locked into the warm water, and the bass are locked onto the bait. Expect the cleanest bite on the outgoing, when that warm bay water funnels out through Fire Island Inlet and stacks against the cold ocean push, building a hard temperature seam right at the mouth. The Robert Moses bridges, the Sore Thumb rip, and the channel edges between Captree and the inlet are the structure to work, and the size class moving through is heavily weighted toward slot and overslot fish — the spring run is right on top of us.

The Captree night bite has shifted away from straight clam soaking toward soft plastics in the last couple of weeks, and that tracks with the water. As the bay climbs past 60, bass get more aggressive and more willing to chase, and a bucktail-and-Bass Assassin combo or a six-inch paddle tail on a half-ounce jighead is going to outproduce a clam belly on most tides. Clams are still earning their keep on the dead-low slack and the first push of the incoming for fish that want to feed lazy, but once that current loads up, switch to plastics and work the deeper edges of the channel — fifteen to twenty-two feet — where bass are staging on the seam.

Fluke are in the picture but the class is mixed and the keepers are still inside. The bay flats from Great Cove down to the Robert Moses flats are warming fastest, and that's where the legal fish are sitting. The deeper ocean fluke bite at the inlet mouth and the near-shore lumps needs another three to five degrees before it truly turns on. Weakfish are a real possibility on the warm-mud flats off Sayville and Patchogue on a slow-drifted pink Fin-S or a small bucktail tipped with squid — the inside water temperature is right in their wheelhouse. Bluefish chatter from the East End is loud enough that the first jumbo blues should be showing at the inlet inside a week if the bunker stay put.

The look-ahead hinges on wind. The current northwest flow is cold-air-over-warm-water, which actually helps the back bay by pushing surface water out and pulling deeper warm water up on the flats during the afternoon heating cycle. If we hold northwest to southwest through the weekend and into midweek, the bay temperature will climb another two to three degrees and that ocean-bay delta will only sharpen, intensifying the inlet seam bite. The risk is an east or southeast wind reloading the swell on 44025 — that shuts down the inlet mouth for small boats and pushes the bite deeper inside toward Captree and the bridges. Watch the NY Bight buoy water temperature; once it cracks 60, the ocean fluke and the beach bass open up, and the whole pattern slides outside.

For now, the play is the warm water. Fish the bay, work the seam on the dropping tide, throw plastics after dark, and let the ocean keep sorting itself out. The fish that matter are already where you can reach them.

reports.headline: Moriches thermal engine fires on the ebb as the ocean stays cold and lumpy
reports.subhead: NY Bight buoy 44025 holds 57°F with a 9-second swell, pushing the bite inside the inlet where back-bay water is climbing into the low 60s.
reports.body_markdown:
The ocean off Moriches is still wearing its winter coat. Buoy 44025 at the NY Bight is reading 57.0°F with a 2.3-foot sea on a 9.0-second dominant period — a long, lazy southeast groundswell that is breaking heavy on the outer bar and keeping the wash dirty from Cupsogue east through Westhampton. Block Island buoy 44097 is colder still at 56.1°F. Inshore, the picture flips: Montauk's tide station is at 59.4°F, Sandy Hook is at 63.1°F, and while NOAA does not publish a same-day reading at Moriches Inlet itself, the back-bay shallows from Tuthill Point west to the Mastic flats are unquestionably tracking with the warmer inside numbers — solar gain on three feet of water over dark bottom does that in late May. The result is a 4- to 6-degree thermal delta across the inlet throat on every ebb. 44017 at Montauk is offline, so the offshore swell picture east of us is partially blind, but 44025's period tells the story.

That delta is the whole game right now. Warm bay water dumping through Moriches Inlet on the outgoing creates a visible thermal plume that fans out across the ocean side bar, and bait — spearing, juvenile bunker, and the tail end of the river herring push out of Seatuck and Forge River — rides that plume out. Bass stack on the ocean-side edge of the east jetty and along the sand lobe that built west of the inlet after the winter's nor'easters reworked the cut. The fish are running heavily slot and overslot, consistent with the broader migratory wave moving the South Shore this week. Short fish are scarce; the class of fish in the inlet right now is the class that came north on mackerel and bunker, not resident schoolies.

The productive window has been the last two hours of the ebb into the first of the flood, worked from either the Cupsogue side or from a boat holding on the eastern edge of the channel in 14 to 22 feet. Bucktails in the 1.5- to 2-ounce range, white or chartreuse with a red Gulp grub, dragged across the sand-to-mud transition on the channel shoulder, have been the most consistent presentation — the same slow, rhythmic bottom retrieve that has been producing on the East End surf. From the beach at Cupsogue, the cleanest water has been on the inside of the rip line where the plume sets up; long bombs into the open ocean wash are wasted casts in this swell.

Fluke are a separate, parallel story and one entirely controlled by temperature. The ocean is too cold — 57°F will not turn on a sustained ocean fluke bite. Inside the bay, however, the skinny water from the east-west channel down through the slip gut and along the south-side flats off Pattersquash has warmed enough to hold fish on sunny afternoons. Drift the 4- to 8-foot edges with light jigs, and expect a heavy ratio of shorts to keepers until the bay pushes past 62°F bay-wide. Weakfish are showing in the same warm corners, particularly the deeper holes inside Tuthill on a late incoming when the warm flat empties into the channel. No meaningful blackfish or porgy intel from the inlet rocks yet — that's a June 5–10 story most years and there is no reason to think this one is different.

Look ahead to the next five days: surface pressure at 1016 hPa and a northwest breeze at 44065 suggest the sea state lays down by the back end of the week, which would clean up the Cupsogue wash and give the surf its first honest shot at the migratory bass moving through. The moon is building toward full, which means stronger ebbs and a more aggressive thermal flush through the inlet — the single best mechanism we have right now for concentrating fish. If the bay picks up another two degrees on the south-facing flats, the fluke pick inside the slip gut becomes a legitimate keeper-ratio bite rather than a numbers grind.

For the next week I would not waste a tide anywhere but within a half-mile of the inlet on the ebb. The ocean is too cold and too lumpy to reward range; the bay is warm enough to manufacture its own bait and its own bite, and the throat of Moriches Inlet is where those two truths meet.

reports.headline: Estuary thermal engine lights up Shinnecock as ocean stays cold and lumpy
reports.subhead: A four-degree delta between mid-50s ocean water and warming bay flats is concentrating bait and bass inside the inlet on the outgoing.
reports.body_markdown:
The ocean side of Shinnecock is still wearing its early-spring coat. Buoy 44025 in the NY Bight is reading 57.0°F with a 2.3-foot sea on a 9-second dominant period, and Block Island's 44097 is sitting at 56.1°F with a shorter, sharper 3-second wind chop out of 304°. Montauk's tide-station thermistor at 8510560 is the warmest open-water number on the East End at 59.4°F. The Shinnecock Inlet station itself is not reporting a usable water temp today, and the latest SST composite in the pipeline is three days stale (May 27), so the precise inside-versus-outside delta has to be inferred — but with Kings Point already at 58.6°F in the western Sound and the back bays here sitting in full sun on a light northwest breeze, the inside of the inlet is almost certainly running three to four degrees above the open beach. Pressure at the harbor entrance buoy is a flat 1016 hPa. Nothing about the synoptic picture is dramatic; the story is the thermal boundary, not the weather.

That boundary is the whole game for this beat right now. When the ocean is locked in the mid-50s and the bay is pushing 60, every ebb tide flushes a warm, bait-rich plume out through the inlet throat and stacks it against the colder ocean water on the seaward side of the jetties. Striped bass — and we are squarely in the slot-and-overslot window of the spring run, not the schoolie phase — will hold on the thermal seam and feed into the current. Fluke remain a back-bay story for at least another week; the ocean simply has not warmed enough to pull the better fish out to the 40-foot ridges off the beach. Weakfish are in the mix wherever there is a mud-bottom edge holding heat into the evening.

The inlet itself is fishing best on the back half of the outgoing, roughly the last three hours into slack, and the bite is firmly a night and low-light operation with surface water still this cool. The west jetty rip and the rockpile inside the east jetty are both holding fish; a 1.5-ounce bucktail with a red Gulp trailer worked across the channel and crawled back down the far edge is doing more than swimming plugs right now, because the bait is herring-class and the fish want something below the rip line, not skating on top. Larger bass — the 30- to 40-inch class showing up consistently in the eastern Long Island surf this past week — are taking bigger soft plastics and live eels on the deeper side of the outgoing seam in 18 to 24 feet of water just inside the throat.

Ponquogue Bridge is starting to wake up on the weakfish front, and that is a temperature story too. The pilings on the north side of the bridge sit over softer bottom that warms first, and the first real weakfish window of the year typically opens when bay water settles into the 60–62°F band — we are knocking on that door. Small pink and white plastics on a quarter-ounce head, drifted through the shadow line on the outgoing after dark, is the play. Fluke drifts in the bay are best on the channel edges off Tiana and the deeper cuts north of the inlet, with the warmest, sunniest afternoon ebbs producing the better keepers. The Shinnecock Canal remains the connector to the Peconic and the way fish are moving in and out of the system; bass are using it both directions this time of year.

Looking out three to five days, the variables to watch are wind and bay temperature. A sustained southwest, which the pattern wants to deliver later in the week, will pile warm surface water against the south shore and accelerate the bay's climb toward that 62°F weakfish threshold. If 44025 ticks past 60°F at the same time, the first real ocean-side fluke drifts off the beach become viable. A hard east wind — and the analyst's pattern flag on east-wind penalty is worth respecting — would shut down the outside and concentrate everything inside the inlet again. The new moon falls into the forecast window, which means stronger tides and a sharper rip at the inlet mouth on the overnight ebbs.

I would be on the inlet two hours before dead low this week, on the outgoing, bucktail in hand, working the seam where the warm bay water meets the cold ocean. That is where the fish are, that is where the bait is, and that is where the physics says they will stay until the ocean catches up.

reports.headline: Block Island holds at 56°F as thermal wall offshore concentrates bass on the Ledge edges
reports.subhead: Buoy 44097 reading 56.1°F keeps the open-ocean migration pinched against structure while Newport-side estuaries pull into the upper 50s.
reports.body_markdown:
Buoy 44097 off the southwest corner of the island is sitting at 56.1°F this morning with a 2.6-foot sea running on a short three-second period out of 304 degrees — a sloppy, wind-chopped northwest surface that flattens as you tuck under the lee of the island. Montauk's tide gauge across the way reads 59.4°F, the NY Bight buoy 44025 is 57.0°F with a cleaner nine-second swell, and New London at the mouth of the Race is still cold at 51.8°F. That spread tells the whole story: the open ocean south and east of the Ledge is locked in the mid-50s, the Rhode Island estuaries and Narragansett Bay shallows are warming into the high 50s on sun, and the deep cold water pouring out of Block Island Sound on the ebb is acting like a refrigerator door against the warmer Atlantic shelf water. The thermal wall is set up exactly where it should be for Memorial Day week.

For this zone, that means the migration is pinned. Bass coming up the shelf from the south are hitting that 56-degree line and tracking it east, and the Southwest Ledge is the single biggest piece of structure intercepting that flow. The fish are not yet spread thin across the rips — they are stacked on the western edge of the Ledge in 60 to 90 feet, working the temperature break on the dropping tide. Newport's Brenton Reef and the rocks off Castle Hill are firing on the same mechanism, with warmer Narragansett Bay outflow meeting cold ocean water on the ebb. Slot and overslot class is the dominant size right now; the dink schoolies that fill in midsummer are still two to three weeks behind this push.

The Ledge bite has been a live-eel and big-soft-plastic show on the last two hours of the dropping tide and the first hour of the flood. Wire-line trollers pulling tubes and sandworms along the 70-foot contour on the west side have been moving fish in the 20- to 30-pound class, with occasional 40s mixed in. Bigger fish — the 40-plus class that defines why this rock matters — are coming on live scup drifted on three-way rigs once the current really starts to rip. The North Rip is showing fish on the early flood but the bait sign is thinner there than it will be by mid-June; the squid push that supercharges the rips is still building east out of Nantucket Sound and has not fully arrived on the north side of the island.

Newport-side, the bass bite inside the bay mouth is running on the estuary thermal advantage. Bunker schools are thick from the Newport Bridge south to Beavertail, and the bass working them are eating big on the outgoing when the warmer bay water dumps past the points. Tog season is winding down for keepers but the structure off Brenton and around the Dumplings is loaded with shorts and the occasional resident keeper for anyone working green crabs on slack water. Fluke reports from the south side of the island remain soft — bottom temps on the 60-foot contour are still under 55°F by my read of the buoy data, and the doormat drift on the southwest grounds typically does not turn on until that number crosses 58.

Look ahead: the wind clocks south by Sunday afternoon and that is the switch I am watching. A two-day south breeze will push warmer shelf water up against the south side of the island, lift 44097 by two or three degrees, and start dragging the squid concentrations that are already staging east of Point Judith onto the Ledge proper. Once that happens — and I expect it inside five days — the rip bite at Southwest and at the North Rip on the night flood goes from good to the kind of fishing that puts this island on the map. The new moon on June 15 will stack a big tide on top of warming water and that is the window to circle. Until then, the southwest corner on the drop is the highest-percentage move on the island.

Fish the temperature break, not the chart. The bass are telling you exactly where the 56-degree line is, and on this island that line moves a quarter mile a day this time of year. Stay on it and the size class out here right now will reward the effort.

reports.headline: Montauk water at 59.4°F as spring trophy class stacks the rips
reports.subhead: A 3°F inside-to-outside thermal break is concentrating bait and overslot bass on the Point's current edges while Block Island Sound stays sloppy.
reports.body_markdown:
The Point is sitting on the leading edge of the spring transition this morning. NOAA's Montauk tide station (8510560) read 59.4°F at the 08:54 check, while just to the north the Block Island buoy (44097) was holding at 56.1°F with a 2.6-foot wind sea on a short 3-second period out of 304°. The NY Bight buoy (44025) was at 57.0°F with 2.3-foot seas on a longer 9-second swell. New London (8461490) is still dragging at 51.8°F, which tells you the cold reservoir to the north hasn't yet flushed into the Sound side. The takeaway: there is a real 3-degree thermal step from the inside of the Point out to the open Atlantic, and a sharper step from Montauk water into the western Block Island Sound. Offshore SST imagery hasn't refreshed since the 27th, but the buoy network is consistent enough to read the structure without it.

That thermal geometry is exactly what stacks fish on the Point in late May. The warmer water riding the south side and wrapping around the Lighthouse is pulling squid and the front edge of the bunker push into the rips, while the colder Sound water on the north side acts as a wall the bait won't cross until it warms another few degrees. That sets up the classic early-season pattern: the south side from Turtle Cove east to the Lighthouse is the high-percentage zone on the dropping tide, North Bar comes alive on the last of the flood as that warmer south-side water sweeps around the corner, and Shagwong is a tide-and-bait play rather than a sure thing because the water out there is still on the cool side of the break. Sea state at 44097 is the limiter — a 3-second period out of the northwest means the north side and the eastern rip lines will be confused and short, ugly water for a small boat but actually useful for the surf crowd working the bowls.

The size class showing up right now is the headline. This is migratory trophy water — slot fish to legitimate fifty-pounders are inside the rips, with very few shorts mixed in. That matches what's coming out of the western Sound and tracks with the squid expansion working west from Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound. When squid get into the rips at the Lighthouse in any volume, the bigger fish key on them hard, and the productive presentation collapses down to two things: a bucktail in the 1.5 to 3 ounce range worked slow on the down-current side of the rip, and a soft plastic or eel skin on a leadhead fished the same way. Live eels after dark, drifted on the south side off the Lighthouse boulder field on the first of the dropping tide, is the highest-percentage shot at a fish over forty. Bluefish in the jumbo class are running with these bass and will shred soft baits, so a wire leader is back in the program for anyone who cares about tackle.

Fluke is still a back-bay and shallow-water game. The 59.4°F reading at the Montauk station is right at the threshold where the south side ocean drifts start producing, but the deeper water hasn't caught up yet. Fort Pond Bay and the inside of the harbor are the better play for a keeper flattie until the open ocean climbs another three to five degrees. Porgies are setting up on the rockpiles inside the harbor and along the Sound shoreline. Blackfish season is winding down on the spring side but the bigger boulder fields off the Lighthouse will still give up a slob on green crabs if the swell lays down.

The next three to five days hinge on whether the northwest flow at 44097 backs off and the short-period sea in the Sound flattens. If it does, the eastern rip lines and Shagwong come into play as the warmer south-side water wraps further north.
